translation_en:
Book of Changes

“The king attains a household: they love one another.”

Wu Han

Associate Examiner Yang, Instructor, comments: “The topic is not inherently difficult to write on, yet the candidates in the examination hall proved unable, when discussing ‘attaining a household,’ to recast even a single phrase from the Original Meaning commentary. Some even brought ‘Do not worry; auspicious’ into their exposition. When they reached ‘loving one another,’ their language and meaning inevitably became labored and repetitive, wearying readers today [?]. This essay is otherwise and deserves inclusion.”
Associate Examiner Deng, School Instructor, comments: “The language is orderly and polished—a pleasure to read.”
Examiner Wang, School Instructor, comments: “The conclusion has force; this is no careless composition.”
Examiner Lu, Professor, comments: “A well-executed essay on the meaning of the Changes.”

The Commentary on the Images cites the words concerning a king’s taking a queen and makes manifest the feelings that unite the two. In the relationships among members of a household, what matters is that those within and those without share the same virtue. The nine in the fifth place establishes a household and obtains the right person; their feelings of mutual love can thus be understood.

Formerly, the Master, in the Lesser Images, explained the meaning of the nine in the fifth place of the Family hexagram. This nine is firm and vigorous, central and correct: it represents the man occupying his proper place outside. Below, it corresponds to the six in the second place, yielding and compliant, central and correct: it represents the woman occupying her proper place within. When they seek one another on this basis, this upright man reaches the time for wedding a gentle bride [?], and theirs is a match made by Heaven: the provision of food within the household finds its rightful mistress. The queen possesses the goodness of a modest and graceful woman; the betrothal rites establish the auspicious union, and the gentleman finds harmony with his mate.

The rites governing women are duly observed; there is neither wrongdoing nor misconduct, and the inner chambers thereby become solemn and dignified. The mother’s instructions [?] are not forgotten: ‘Be reverent; be cautious.’ The state …

title: 正德八年河南鄉試錄
text:
家可期於順成矣周公之意如此蓋以夫能正
室由內之和婦克宜家乃德之化今九五之家
內外皆得其人吾知一剛一柔以德合德心孚
意契而險詖私謁之不形一健一順以賢配賢
氣同情協而儆戒相成之有道內助之懿夫實
愛之固非昵於慾也此唱彼隨琴瑟鍾鼓曾是
以爲樂乎刑家之化婦寔變焉亦不失其正也
彼感此應觿燧箴管其足以爲好乎於乎五之
於二相求之理既正而相與之情自篤占者有
===
其德則勿用憂恤而吉也信可必矣抑聞之傳
曰夫婦人倫之始上以事宗廟下以繼後世也
匹夫疇人必懷有家一或不能以德相愛鮮不
顛殞厥類而况於有國與天下者乎王者之道
始於家而閨門之化達之天下天下治忽於此
乎繫聖人序易配咸恒於乾坤而家人之卦又
拳拳焉姬氏八百年之長曆文王太姒關雎之
德實啓之所謂正始之道王化之基有天下者
施于家之首政信矣
punctuated:
家可期於順成矣。周公之意如此。蓋以夫能正室，由內之和；婦克宜家，乃德之化。今九五之家，內外皆得其人。吾知一剛一柔，以德合德，心孚意契，而險詖私謁之不形；一健一順，以賢配賢，氣同情協，而儆戒相成之有道。內助之懿，夫實愛之，固非昵於慾也。此唱彼隨，琴瑟鍾鼓，曾是以爲樂乎？刑家之化，婦寔變焉，亦不失其正也。彼感此應，觿燧箴管，其足以爲好乎？於乎！五之於二，相求之理既正，而相與之情自篤。占者有其德，則勿用憂恤而吉也，信可必矣。

抑聞之，傳曰：「夫婦，人倫之始，上以事宗廟，下以繼後世也。」匹夫疇人，必懷有家，一或不能以德相愛，鮮不顛殞厥類，而况於有國與天下者乎？王者之道始於家，而閨門之化達之天下，天下治忽於此乎繫。聖人序易，配咸恒於乾坤，而家人之卦又拳拳焉。姬氏八百年之長曆，文王太姒關雎之德實啓之。所謂正始之道，王化之基，有天下者施于家之首政，信矣。
translation_en:
…may be expected to attain harmonious order. Such was the Duke of Zhou’s meaning. A husband’s ability to set his household right proceeds from harmony within; a wife’s ability to bring well-being to her family results from the transforming influence of virtue. Now, in the household represented by the nine in the fifth place, both the inner and outer spheres have the right person. I know that the firm and the yielding unite virtue with virtue: their hearts trust one another and their intentions accord, leaving no occasion for malicious or biased words or private solicitations. The strong and the compliant match worthiness with worthiness: their dispositions agree and their feelings harmonize, providing a way for them to perfect one another through admonition and warning. The husband truly loves the excellence of her assistance within the household; this assuredly is no indulgence in desire. He leads and she follows—but could their joy consist merely in zithers, bells, and drums? Through his transforming influence as an example to the family, the wife is indeed changed, likewise without departing from what is right. He moves her and she responds—but could the cord-loosening awl, fire-kindling implements, needles, and cases suffice to constitute their affection? Ah! As regards the fifth line’s relationship with the second, since the principle by which they seek one another is correct, the affection with which they associate is naturally deep. If the person consulting the oracle possesses this virtue, then there is no need for anxiety, and the outcome will be auspicious. This can indeed be counted upon.

Furthermore, I have heard it said in the commentary: “Husband and wife constitute the beginning of human relationships: above, they serve the ancestral temple; below, they continue the generations to come.” Even ordinary men and common people necessarily cherish the wish to have a family. If they should fail to love one another through virtue, few avoid bringing ruin upon their kin. How much more does this apply to those who possess a state or all under Heaven! The way of the true king begins in the family, and the transforming influence of the inner household extends throughout the realm. Whether all under Heaven is well governed or neglected depends upon this. When the sage arranged the Changes, he paired Influence and Constancy with The Creative and The Receptive, and in the hexagram The Family he again showed the deepest concern for this matter. The eight-hundred-year span of the Ji ruling house was truly inaugurated by the virtue of King Wen and Tai Si celebrated in “The Ospreys’ Cry.” What is called the way of rectifying the beginning, the foundation of kingly transformation, is indeed the foremost act of government that the possessor of all under Heaven must carry out in his own family.

title: 正德八年河南鄉試錄
text:
謙也者致恭以存其位者也
車寵
同考試官教諭楊 批〔塲中作者於謙與致恭處類無異詞其異之者又遠于章旨獨此篇體貼得出說存位危分曉故錄之〕
同考試官學正鄧 批〔氣充詞贍而不失簡淨精微之旨作手作手〕
考試官學正王 批〔謙之爲德發揮盡矣〕
考試官教授陸 批〔明暢可錄〕
===
大傳論君子能不居其有乃所以保其有也盖
有而不居人之所難能也君子之行如是其得
有終而吉也固宜昔大傳聖人釋謙九三爻義
至此謂夫儆凶德也而人不可有謙美行也而
人不可無彼九三君子有勞不伐而有功不德
處心於厚而以功下人內之所積德則欲其盛
而充實之如山外之所施禮則欲其恭而卑下
之如地是謙也者非致恭以存其位之道邪何
則九三君子上下所歸使有功勞而自伐門德
punctuated:
謙也者，致恭以存其位者也。
車寵
同考試官教諭楊批〔塲中作者於謙與致恭處類無異詞，其異之者又遠于章旨。獨此篇體貼得出，說存位危分曉，故錄之。〕
同考試官學正鄧批〔氣充詞贍，而不失簡淨精微之旨。作手！作手！〕
考試官學正王批〔謙之爲德，發揮盡矣。〕
考試官教授陸批〔明暢可錄。〕
大傳論君子能不居其有，乃所以保其有也。盖有而不居，人之所難能也。君子之行如是，其得有終而吉也固宜。昔大傳聖人釋謙九三爻義，至此謂夫儆，凶德也，而人不可有；謙，美行也，而人不可無。彼九三君子，有勞不伐，而有功不德，處心於厚，而以功下人。內之所積德，則欲其盛而充實之如山；外之所施禮，則欲其恭而卑下之如地。是謙也者，非致恭以存其位之道邪？何則？九三君子，上下所歸，使有功勞而自伐門德，
translation_en:
“Modesty means exercising reverence to preserve one’s position.”
Che Chong
Associate Examiner Yang, Instructor, comments: “Candidates in the examination generally say much the same thing about ‘modesty’ and ‘exercising reverence’; those who differ stray far from the passage’s meaning. This essay alone grasps it closely and brings it out, clearly explaining the preservation and endangerment of one’s position [?]. Hence its inclusion.”
Associate Examiner Deng, School Instructor, comments: “Its energy is full and its language rich, yet it retains the purport’s concision, clarity, subtlety, and precision. A master writer! A master writer!”
Examiner Wang, School Instructor, comments: “The virtue of modesty has been expounded to the fullest.”
Examiner Lu, Professor, comments: “Clear and fluent; worthy of inclusion.”
The Great Commentary explains that a gentleman’s ability to refrain from claiming what he possesses as his own achievement is precisely how he preserves it. For possessing something without claiming credit for it is difficult for people to accomplish. When a gentleman acts in this way, it is surely fitting that he should bring matters to completion and enjoy good fortune. In the Great Commentary, when the sage explained the meaning of the third, yang line of the Modesty hexagram, he reached this point and said that vigilance [?] is a baleful quality that people must not possess, whereas modesty is an admirable practice that people must not lack. The gentleman represented by this line performs services without boasting and achieves merit without claiming credit. His intentions are grounded in generosity, and despite his achievements he places himself below others. As for the virtue he accumulates within, he wishes it to flourish and makes it as substantial as a mountain; as for the ritual propriety he displays outwardly, he wishes it to be reverent and makes it as lowly as the earth. Is not such modesty the way of exercising reverence to preserve one’s position? Why is this so? The gentleman represented by the third, yang line is the one to whom those above and below turn. If, having accomplishments and services to his credit, he were to boast of himself and vaunt his virtue [?] …

title: 正德八年河南鄉試錄
text:
必不可以持滿故謙而致恭不忘乎下人之心
焉於德禮而不盛不恭必將至於招損故致恭
于謙常謹乎甲牧之志焉其事上也坎之自牖
睽之于巷事不敢以直遂上其不信任之乎其
臨下也之下賤大有之尚賢行不敢以驕傲
下豈不悅服之乎吾知其位雖極於富也滿而
不溢可以常守其富有朋龜之益而無鼫鼠之
厲矣吾見其位雖處於貴也高而不危可以常
保其貴有朱紱之慶而無鞶帶之褫矣噫此君
===
子之謙而位之所以存也有終而吉之道爲何
如哉雖然謙者君子之常行豈爲欲存其位而
爲之而言存其位者程子謂能致恭所以能存
其位謙之道其效固如是耳學非爲祿也而祿
在其中善非爲名也而名由此立脩天爵而人
爵至矣君子何心焉而或者乃欲持祿養資柔
筋曲體甘骸骸以求容悅託名於謙以爲固位
之術非九三之罪人歟
書
punctuated:
必不可以持滿，故謙而致恭，不忘乎下人之心焉。於德禮而不盛不恭，必將至於招損，故致恭于謙，常謹乎甲牧之志焉。其事上也，坎之自牖，睽之于巷，事不敢以直遂，上其不信任之乎？其臨下也，之下賤，大有之尚賢，行不敢以驕傲，下豈不悅服之乎？吾知其位雖極於富也，滿而不溢，可以常守其富，有朋龜之益而無鼫鼠之厲矣。吾見其位雖處於貴也，高而不危，可以常保其貴，有朱紱之慶而無鞶帶之褫矣。噫！此君子之謙而位之所以存也。有終而吉之道爲何如哉？雖然，謙者君子之常行，豈爲欲存其位而爲之？而言存其位者，程子謂能致恭，所以能存其位，謙之道，其效固如是耳。學非爲祿也，而祿在其中；善非爲名也，而名由此立。脩天爵而人爵至矣，君子何心焉？而或者乃欲持祿養資，柔筋曲體，甘骸骸以求容悅，託名於謙，以爲固位之術，非九三之罪人歟？

書
translation_en:
…he certainly could not preserve his fullness. Thus he remains humble and exercises reverence, never forgetting the resolve to place himself below others. If his virtue were not abundant and his ritual conduct not reverent, he would inevitably invite loss. Thus he exercises reverence through humility, always attending carefully to his resolve to govern himself [?]. In serving his superiors, he follows the example of approaching through the window in the hexagram Kan (The Abysmal), and of meeting in the lane in Kui (Opposition): he dares not press directly ahead in conducting affairs. Would his superiors not trust him? In overseeing his subordinates, he follows the example of placing himself below the lowly [?], and of honoring the worthy in Dayou (Great Possession): he dares not act arrogantly. Would his subordinates not gladly submit to him? I know that, even if his position brings him the utmost wealth, he can remain full without overflowing and always preserve that wealth, enjoying the gain of precious tortoise shells without the peril of the great rat. I see that, even if his position places him among the eminent, he can stand high without danger and always preserve his eminence, enjoying the blessing of the vermilion knee covering without having his ceremonial belt stripped away. Ah! Such is the gentleman’s humility, and this is how his position is preserved. What, then, is the way to reach a good end with auspicious results?

Nevertheless, humility is the gentleman’s constant practice. How could he practice it merely from a desire to preserve his position? As for speaking of preserving one’s position, Master Cheng says that the ability to exercise reverence is what enables one to preserve one’s position. Such is simply the natural effect of the way of humility. Learning is not undertaken for an official stipend, yet a stipend lies within it; goodness is not practiced for reputation, yet reputation is thereby established. Cultivate the nobility bestowed by Heaven, and human rank will follow. What ulterior intention does the gentleman have? Yet some wish to retain their stipends and nurture their standing, relaxing their sinews and bending their bodies, willingly abasing themselves [?] to win acceptance and favor. They invoke the name of humility as a technique for securing their positions. Are they not offenders against the teaching of the Nine in the Third Place?

Book of Documents

title: 正德八年河南鄉試錄
text:
欽厥止率乃祖攸行
李濂
同考試官訓導秦　批〔題本平易作者多牽致于儉〕
〔德從事之說殊失本旨此作一本傳註且能體貼伊尹告君之意是用〕
〔錄之〕
同考試官教諭桑　批〔詞約理明不事雕琢如此篇〕
〔者亦少矣〕
考試官學正王　批〔發揮敬止法祖處甚明白佳作也〕
考試官教授陸　批〔伊尹告君之意合是如此〕
===
大臣告君以處事惟欲敬其度之本然遵其度
之已然也甚矣事必有度也人君處事可不于
吾心之本然與前人之已然者交致其力耶昔
伊尹作書以訓太甲至此意謂虞人之射且省
括于度矣人君處事豈無度可省乎是故吾心
所止足以綱維乎事物者即本然之度也不知
所以敬之則本不立矣要必方寸之中有嚴有
翼一肅恭而無縱弛虛靈之境亦臨亦保常收
斂而無放肆勿貳以二勿參以三使天理昭融
punctuated:
欽厥止，率乃祖攸行。
李濂
同考試官訓導秦批〔題本平易，作者多牽致于儉〕〔德從事之說，殊失本旨。此作一本傳註，且能體貼伊尹告君之意，是用〕〔錄之。〕
同考試官教諭桑批〔詞約理明，不事雕琢，如此篇〕〔者亦少矣。〕
考試官學正王批〔發揮敬止法祖處甚明白，佳作也。〕
考試官教授陸批〔伊尹告君之意，合是如此。〕
大臣告君以處事，惟欲敬其度之本然，遵其度之已然也。甚矣，事必有度也！人君處事，可不于吾心之本然與前人之已然者交致其力耶？昔伊尹作書以訓太甲，至此意謂：虞人之射，且省括于度矣；人君處事，豈無度可省乎？是故吾心所止，足以綱維乎事物者，即本然之度也。不知所以敬之，則本不立矣。要必方寸之中，有嚴有翼，一肅恭而無縱弛；虛靈之境，亦臨亦保，常收斂而無放肆。勿貳以二，勿參以三，使天理昭融
translation_en:
“Reverently attend to where you should rest, and follow what your ancestor practiced.”
Li Lian

Associate Examiner Qin, Assistant Instructor, comments: “The topic is straightforward, yet many writers strain to connect it with the teaching about undertaking affairs with frugal virtue, thereby seriously missing its original purport. This composition follows the commentaries throughout and also aptly conveys Yi Yin’s intention in admonishing his ruler. For this reason it has been selected.”

Associate Examiner Sang, Instructor, comments: “Its language is concise and its reasoning clear, without elaborate embellishment. Compositions like this are rare.”

Examiner Wang, School Instructor, comments: “It very clearly expounds reverently attending to where one should rest and taking one’s ancestor as a model. An excellent composition.”

Examiner Lu, Professor, comments: “This is precisely what Yi Yin must have intended in admonishing his ruler.”

When a great minister instructs his ruler in handling affairs, he wishes only that the ruler should revere the standard as it inherently is and follow that standard as it has already been put into practice. How essential it is that affairs must have a standard! In handling affairs, can a ruler fail to exert himself both toward what is inherent in his own mind and toward what his predecessors have already practiced? Long ago, Yi Yin composed a document to instruct Tai Jia. At this point, his meaning was this: even a forester shooting an arrow checks its nock against a standard; when a ruler handles affairs, can there be no standard against which to check his conduct?

Thus, that in which my mind rests, which suffices to govern and order things and affairs, is the inherent standard. If I do not know how to revere it, the foundation will not be established. Within the mind there must be gravity and vigilance, unfailing solemnity and respect, without laxity or slackness. Over its empty and numinous realm one must both keep watch and maintain guardianship, constantly gathering oneself inward without license or abandon. Do not divide it by introducing a second object; do not fragment it by introducing a third. Let Heaven’s principle shine forth clearly and pervasively …

title: 正德八年河南鄉試錄
text:
而不爲外誘之移無有作好無有作惡俾至善
渾全而不爲人欲之累所謂敬吾心之本然者
如此先王所行足以啓佑予後人者乃已然之
度也不知所以循之則吾不行矣又必仰惟時
若不愆不忘而舊章之率由篤于前烈是矜是
式而成憲之必監以義制事以禮制心乃祖之
家法具在勿作聰明以亂之懋敬厥德克配上
帝乃祖之令緒可嗣罔以側言而改之所謂遵
先王之已然者如此吁敬止以立本法祖以致
用處事之度不外是矣吾王能于是兩盡焉尚
何過舉之有哉抑考太甲自厎不類欲敗度縱
敗禮其於所謂本然之度與夫已然之度蓋胥
失之矣伊尹有見于此故已投以受病之藥而
又喻以處事之要忠愛之言不一而足老成之
告君類如此卒之克終允德而配天之澤上與
湯並謂非阿衡啓迪之力哉
是訓是行以近天子之光
田滋
punctuated:
而不爲外誘之移，無有作好，無有作惡，俾至善渾全而不爲人欲之累。所謂敬吾心之本然者如此。先王所行，足以啓佑予後人者，乃已然之度也。不知所以循之，則吾不行矣。又必仰惟時若，不愆不忘，而舊章之率由；篤于前烈，是矜是式，而成憲之必監。以義制事，以禮制心，乃祖之家法具在，勿作聰明以亂之；懋敬厥德，克配上帝，乃祖之令緒可嗣，罔以側言而改之。所謂遵先王之已然者如此。吁！敬止以立本，法祖以致用，處事之度不外是矣。吾王能于是兩盡焉，尚何過舉之有哉？抑考太甲自厎不類，欲敗度，縱敗禮，其於所謂本然之度與夫已然之度，蓋胥失之矣。伊尹有見于此，故已投以受病之藥，而又喻以處事之要。忠愛之言，不一而足，老成之告君類如此。卒之克終允德，而配天之澤上與湯並，謂非阿衡啓迪之力哉？

是訓是行，以近天子之光。
田滋
translation_en:
…and remain unmoved by external temptations. Let there be no willful likes or dislikes, so that the highest good remains whole and unencumbered by human desires. Such is what is meant by reverently preserving the original condition of one’s own heart. What the former kings practiced, sufficient to enlighten and aid us who come after them, constitutes the established standard. Unless I know how to follow it, I cannot act accordingly. One must therefore look reverently upward and follow their example, neither transgressing nor forgetting, adhering to the old statutes; one must remain devoted to their former achievements, honoring and emulating them, and invariably taking their established regulations as a guide. Regulate affairs through righteousness and regulate the heart through ritual propriety: your forefather’s dynastic rules are all there; do not disrupt them by devising clever innovations. Strive reverently to cultivate virtue and become worthy of the Lord on High: your forefather’s splendid legacy can be continued; do not alter it because of misleading words. Such is what is meant by following the established practices of the former kings.

Ah! Reverently abiding in the proper resting place establishes the foundation; modeling oneself on one’s ancestors brings it into practice. The standards for handling affairs extend no further than these. If our king can fulfill both completely, what mistaken action could there still be? Yet consider how Tai Jia brought himself to act unworthily: desire undermined the standards, and self-indulgence undermined ritual propriety. He had thus lost both the standard inherent in the heart and the standard established by precedent. Yi Yin perceived this; hence, having already administered medicine for the affliction, he further instructed him in the essentials of handling affairs. His words of loyalty and love were too numerous for a single instance to suffice. Such is the way seasoned elders counsel their rulers. In the end, Tai Jia was able to remain truly virtuous to the last, and his beneficence, worthy of Heaven, equaled that of Tang before him. Could one say that this was not due to the enlightening guidance of the A-heng, Yi Yin?

“Follow this instruction and put it into practice, thereby drawing near to the radiance of the Son of Heaven.”
By Tian Zi.

title: 正德八年河南鄉試錄
text:
同考試官訓導秦　批〔恭傳言是訓是行可以近天子道德之光華此作形容覩切〕
同考試官教諭桑　批〔布置齊整而不腐不晦自是作家手段〕
考試官學正王　批〔文有典則氣甚渾雄科場中佳士也〕
考試官教授陸　批〔爾雅沉着無踰此篇〕
民不違乎君之教斯不遠乎君之德蓋敷言之
教所以納民於極也民既由之而不違則於君
德其庶幾乎昔箕子衍皇極之疇以告武王至
此若謂君以建極爲教民以好德爲心是以民
===
於極之敷言以諷以誦而佩服之不違宛然耳
提面命也以歌以詠而思念之不忘恍然口傳
心授也不徒知之必躬行之而俛焉以盡其力
既允蹈之必心得之而執焉以復其性遵義遵
道遵路會其有極者異其人而同心蕩蕩平平
正直歸其有極者殊其途而一致然民之性皆
復于善如此則可以近天子道德之光矣吾知
人慾消而天理明道德同而風俗一日月照臨
之地孰不依餘光以自新雲漢昭回之天孰不
punctuated:
同考試官訓導秦，批〔恭傳言「是訓是行，可以近天子道德之光華」，此作形容覩切。〕
同考試官教諭桑，批〔布置齊整，而不腐不晦，自是作家手段。〕
考試官學正王，批〔文有典則，氣甚渾雄，科場中佳士也。〕
考試官教授陸，批〔爾雅沉着，無踰此篇。〕
民不違乎君之教，斯不遠乎君之德。蓋敷言之教，所以納民於極也。民既由之而不違，則於君德，其庶幾乎！昔箕子衍皇極之疇以告武王，至此若謂：君以建極爲教，民以好德爲心。是以民於極之敷言，以諷以誦，而佩服之不違，宛然耳提面命也；以歌以詠，而思念之不忘，恍然口傳心授也。不徒知之，必躬行之，而俛焉以盡其力；既允蹈之，必心得之，而執焉以復其性。遵義遵道遵路，會其有極者，異其人而同心；蕩蕩平平正直，歸其有極者，殊其途而一致。然民之性皆復于善如此，則可以近天子道德之光矣。吾知人慾消而天理明，道德同而風俗一。日月照臨之地，孰不依餘光以自新？雲漢昭回之天，孰不
translation_en:
Associate Examiner Qin, Assistant Instructor, comments: 〔The commentary [?] says, “Follow this instruction and put it into practice, and you may approach the radiance of the Son of Heaven’s moral virtue.” This composition portrays this vividly and aptly [?].〕
Associate Examiner Sang, Instructor, comments: 〔The arrangement is orderly, yet neither stale nor obscure: unmistakably the work of an accomplished writer.〕
Examiner Wang, School Instructor, comments: 〔His writing has classical standards, and its force is remarkably full and vigorous. He is an outstanding scholar among the examination candidates.〕
Examiner Lu, Prefectural School Professor, comments: 〔For refinement and composure, nothing surpasses this piece.〕
When the people do not depart from their ruler’s teaching, they are not far from their ruler’s virtue. For teaching through promulgated pronouncements serves to bring the people to the supreme standard. Once the people follow it without departing from it, surely they come close to their ruler’s virtue! Formerly, when Jizi elaborated the section on the August Standard to instruct King Wu, at this point he seemed to be saying: the ruler teaches by establishing the standard, and the people set their hearts on loving virtue.
Thus, regarding the pronouncements that expound the standard, the people recite and rehearse them, cherishing and observing them without deviation, as though the ruler were drawing them close by the ear and instructing them face to face. They sing and chant them, keeping them in mind without forgetting, as though receiving them from his lips directly into their hearts. They do not merely understand them: they must put them personally into practice, diligently exerting their full strength. Having truly acted upon them, they must grasp them in their hearts and hold fast to them, thereby recovering their original nature. Following righteousness, following the Way, and following the road, those who converge upon the established standard are different people of one mind. Moving broadly, evenly, uprightly, and directly, those who return to the established standard travel different paths toward one end. When the people’s natures have all thus returned to goodness, they may approach the radiance of the Son of Heaven’s moral virtue.
I know that human desires will diminish and Heaven’s principle become clear; the Way and virtue will be shared, and customs unified. Throughout the lands illuminated by the sun and moon, who would not draw upon that radiance to renew themselves? Beneath the sky where the River of Stars shines and turns, who would not…

title: 正德八年河南鄉試錄
text:
覽德輝以自耀秉彝之心人所同得君有之而
民化之位雖異而性則同矣天子道德之光華
不旣相近矣乎降衷之理人所均稟上行之而
下效之分雖殊而理則一矣惟皇道德之光輝
夫豈相遠矣乎吁在上者脩道以立教在下者
率性以爲道此成周之民所以爲皇極之民也
歟抑考傳曰堯舜帥天下以仁而民從之桀紂
帥天下以暴而民從之其所令反其所好而民
不從是則民之從化于其所行而不于其所言
===
也敷言之感豈特言語之所致哉蓋皇極之君
躬行心得有以爲之地耳後世詔令蓋紛紛矣
詞非不美法非不密而民終不能感化者何益
於治故爲政不在多言
詩
衆維魚矣實維豐年旐維旟矣室家溱溱
李茂元
同考試官教諭黃　批〔宣王承饑饉流離之後所顧者歲熟民滋耳此篇摸寫詩人語意如身親見者然可謂善言詩矣〕
punctuated:
覽德輝以自耀？秉彝之心，人所同得；君有之而民化之，位雖異而性則同矣。天子道德之光華，不旣相近矣乎？降衷之理，人所均稟；上行之而下效之，分雖殊而理則一矣。惟皇道德之光輝，夫豈相遠矣乎？吁！在上者脩道以立教，在下者率性以爲道，此成周之民所以爲皇極之民也歟！抑考傳曰：「堯舜帥天下以仁，而民從之；桀紂帥天下以暴，而民從之。其所令反其所好，而民不從。」是則民之從化，于其所行而不于其所言也。敷言之感，豈特言語之所致哉？蓋皇極之君，躬行心得，有以爲之地耳。後世詔令蓋紛紛矣，詞非不美，法非不密，而民終不能感化者，何益於治？故爲政不在多言。

《詩》
衆維魚矣，實維豐年；旐維旟矣，室家溱溱。
李茂元

同考試官教諭黃　批〔宣王承饑饉流離之後，所顧者歲熟民滋耳。此篇摸寫詩人語意，如身親見者然，可謂善言詩矣。〕
translation_en:
… behold the radiance of virtue and thereby shine themselves? The heart that holds fast to constant moral principles is something all people alike possess. The ruler possesses it, and the people are transformed by him: although their positions differ, their nature is the same. Have they not already drawn near to the brilliance of the Son of Heaven’s moral virtue? The principles of the moral nature bestowed by Heaven are equally endowed in everyone. Those above put them into practice, and those below emulate them: although their stations differ, these principles are one. How, then, could they be far from the radiance of the sovereign’s moral virtue? Ah! Those above cultivate the Way to establish instruction; those below follow their nature to practice the Way. Is this not why the people of Chengzhou became people who conformed to the Sovereign’s Ultimate Standard?

Furthermore, consider what the Commentary says: “Yao and Shun led the realm through benevolence, and the people followed them. Jie and Zhou led the realm through violence, and the people followed them. When their commands contradicted what they themselves favored, the people did not follow.” Thus, the people follow and are transformed by what their rulers do, rather than by what they say. Can the moving influence of proclaimed words arise solely from speech? Surely it is the ruler who embodies the Sovereign’s Ultimate Standard, through personal practice and inward understanding, who provides their foundation. In later ages, edicts and commands have proliferated. Their wording has certainly been fine, and their regulations meticulous; yet if the people ultimately remain unmoved and untransformed, what benefit do these bring to government? Thus, governing does not depend on many words.

Book of Odes
“The multitudes become fish: truly, this foretells an abundant year. The tortoise-and-snake banners become falcon banners: households will be thronged with people.”
Li Maoyuan

Comment by Associate Examiner Huang, Instructor: “King Xuan succeeded to rule after famine and displacement. His concern was simply that the harvests should ripen and the people increase. This essay renders the poet’s words and meaning as though its author had witnessed these things in person. He may indeed be said to interpret the Odes well.”

title: 正德八年河南鄉試錄
text:
同考試官教諭鄒　批〔周人獻吉夢于王正如此或謂考牧之詩設夢爲之頌禱非也録此以祛羣疑〕
考試官學正王　批〔意思悠遠而語致從容視他作特異〕
考試官教授陸　批〔文從理順讀之令人灑然〕
即牧人夢兆之異占國家富庶之祥蓋既富且
庶有國家者所深願也牧人夢兆有祥而所占
乃爾詩人得不備述以獻于上哉是詩言牧事
有成而牛羊衆多至此意曰國家之興必有禎
===
祥吉夢之占必有徵應蓋人惟萬物之靈魚特
鱗介之類則夫人所生固不如魚所生之多也
牧人夢人爲魚是維以少變多之象其占也不
將爲豐年之穰穰乎殆見饑饉之餘豐稔疊至
陰陽以和風雨以時自天降康雲漢無旱魃之
災也五穀以熟百物以充迄用康年桑柔無捋
采之憂也然夢兆之祥不特此耳在郊野則載
旐在州里則建旟則夫旐所統固不如旟所統
之衆也牧人夢旐爲旟是又以寡得衆之象其
punctuated:
同考試官教諭鄒，批〔周人獻吉夢于王，正如此。或謂考牧之詩，設夢爲之頌禱，非也。録此以祛羣疑。〕
考試官學正王，批〔意思悠遠，而語致從容，視他作特異。〕
考試官教授陸，批〔文從理順，讀之令人灑然。〕
即牧人夢兆之異，占國家富庶之祥。蓋既富且庶，有國家者所深願也。牧人夢兆有祥，而所占乃爾，詩人得不備述以獻于上哉？是詩言牧事有成，而牛羊衆多。至此，意曰：國家之興，必有禎祥；吉夢之占，必有徵應。蓋人惟萬物之靈，魚特鱗介之類，則夫人所生，固不如魚所生之多也。牧人夢人爲魚，是維以少變多之象，其占也，不將爲豐年之穰穰乎？殆見饑饉之餘，豐稔疊至，陰陽以和，風雨以時，自天降康，《雲漢》無旱魃之災也；五穀以熟，百物以充，迄用康年，《桑柔》無捋采之憂也。然夢兆之祥，不特此耳。在郊野則載旐，在州里則建旟，則夫旐所統，固不如旟所統之衆也。牧人夢旐爲旟，是又以寡得衆之象，其
translation_en:
Associate Examiner Zou, Instructor, comments: 〔This is precisely how the people of Zhou presented an auspicious dream to their king. Some say that this poem on inspecting the herds invents a dream as a means of offering praise and prayers. That is incorrect. I have recorded this to dispel such doubts.〕
Examiner Wang, School Instructor, comments: 〔Its ideas have far-reaching resonance, while its expression is unhurried. Compared with other compositions, it is outstanding.〕
Examiner Lu, Professor, comments: 〔The writing flows smoothly and the reasoning proceeds coherently; reading it leaves one refreshed.〕
From the extraordinary omens in the herdsmen’s dreams, one divines auspicious signs of the state’s wealth and populousness. For wealth and a numerous population are what the ruler of a state deeply desires. The herdsmen’s dreams contained auspicious omens, and their interpretation was such as this: how could the poet fail to recount them fully and present them to his sovereign? This poem speaks of success in tending the herds, with cattle and sheep becoming numerous. At this point its meaning is: when a state rises to prosperity, there must be auspicious signs; the interpretation of a fortunate dream must find confirming fulfillment. Now humans are the most spiritually endowed of all creatures, while fish are merely creatures of the scaled and shelled kinds; yet the number of offspring humans produce is certainly smaller than that produced by fish. The herdsmen dream that people become fish: this is an image of the few becoming many. Would its interpretation not foretell the abundance of a plentiful year? We may expect that, after famine, plentiful harvests will come in succession. Yin and yang will be harmonious, wind and rain timely, and well-being will descend from Heaven: there will be none of the calamity wrought by the drought demon in “The Milky Way” (Yunhan). The five grains will ripen, all produce will abound, and a year of plenty will at last arrive: there will be none of the distress over stripped foliage in “The Luxuriant Mulberry” (Sangrou). Yet the auspicious omens in the dreams are not confined to this. In the outlying countryside the tortoise-and-serpent banner is raised; in the districts and villages the falcon banner is erected. Those marshaled under the former are certainly fewer than those marshaled under the latter. The herdsmen dream that tortoise-and-serpent banners become falcon banners: this too is an image of gaining many from few. Its…

title: 正德八年河南鄉試錄
text:
占也不將爲室家之溱溱𠎝殆見流離之後生
聚日繁往者還之擾者定之究安宅而閭閻相
望鴻鴈無中澤之勞也危者安之散者復之達
四境而鷄犬相聞黃鳥無此邦之嘆也是知年
豐則國用以足民衆則國本以固宣王牧事有
成而獻吉夢者如是中興氣象亦可以想見也
夫抑考厲王之時百姓背叛四夷交侵宗周之
業已板蕩矣宣王即位遇災而懼撥亂反正內
脩外攘天下喜於王化復行而頌禱之詩洋洋
===
盈耳矣何末年失政僨千畝之師料太原之民
拒樊穆仲之諫而令終不保此牂羊之歌作而
無羊之迹熄矣可不畏哉
休矣皇考以保明其身
杜桐
同考試官教諭貫 批〔成王始即政深懲管蔡之事恒〕
〔以不能保明其身是懼故惓惓以是延訪羣臣學詩者多不能體認卒〕
〔洋詞長語敷衍其義殊較可厭及得是卷爲之喜見顏色〕
同考試官教諭鄒 批〔詩人思慕意氣發揮親切然〕
punctuated:
占也，不將爲室家之溱溱𠎝？殆見流離之後，生聚日繁，往者還之，擾者定之，究安宅而閭閻相望，《鴻鴈》無中澤之勞也；危者安之，散者復之，達四境而鷄犬相聞，《黃鳥》無此邦之嘆也。是知年豐則國用以足，民衆則國本以固。宣王牧事有成，而獻吉夢者如是，中興氣象亦可以想見也夫！抑考厲王之時，百姓背叛，四夷交侵，宗周之業已板蕩矣。宣王即位，遇災而懼，撥亂反正，內脩外攘，天下喜於王化復行，而頌禱之詩洋洋盈耳矣。何末年失政，僨千畝之師，料太原之民，拒樊穆仲之諫，而令終不保？此《牂羊》之歌作，而《無羊》之迹熄矣。可不畏哉！
休矣皇考，以保明其身。
杜桐
同考試官教諭貫，批〔成王始即政，深懲管蔡之事，恒〕〔以不能保明其身是懼，故惓惓以是延訪羣臣。學詩者多不能體認，卒〕〔洋詞長語，敷衍其義，殊較可厭。及得是卷，爲之喜見顏色。〕
同考試官教諭鄒，批〔詩人思慕意氣，發揮親切，然〕
translation_en:
…would not its prognostication be that households would multiply abundantly [?]? One might indeed see, after displacement and wandering, a population growing daily: those who had departed brought back, those in turmoil settled, all finding secure dwellings, with village homes in sight of one another. There would be none of the hardship in the marshes described in “Wild Geese” (Hongyan). Those in danger would be made secure, and those scattered restored; throughout the realm, chickens and dogs could be heard from one settlement to the next. There would be none of the lament over “this country” found in “Yellow Birds” (Huangniao). Thus we know that abundant harvests provide sufficient resources for the state, while a numerous population secures its foundations. King Xuan achieved success in animal husbandry, and such were the auspicious dreams presented to him. From these one can also imagine the atmosphere of his restoration!
Yet consider the time of King Li: the people rebelled, the surrounding foreign peoples invaded from every direction, and the royal Zhou enterprise had already fallen into disorder. When King Xuan ascended the throne, he responded to calamities with fear, quelled disorder and restored proper government, cultivated affairs within and repelled enemies without. All under Heaven rejoiced that the king’s transforming influence prevailed once more, and poems of praise and prayer filled the ears in profusion. Why, then, did he govern badly in his final years, suffer the defeat of his army at Qianmu, take a census of the people of Taiyuan, and reject Fan Muzhong’s remonstrance, failing to preserve a good end to his reign? Thus the song “The Ewe” (Zangyang) arose, and the achievements celebrated in “No Sheep” (Wuyang) vanished. Is this not cause for fear?
“Glorious was my august deceased father; thereby may I preserve and enlighten my person.”
Du Tong
Associate Examiner Guan, Instructor, comments: 〔When King Cheng first assumed government, he took profound warning from the affair of Guan and Cai, constantly〕〔fearing that he would be unable to preserve and enlighten his person. He therefore earnestly summoned his ministers to consult them on this matter. Students of the Book of Odes often fail to grasp this, and end up〕〔expounding its meaning in verbose phrases and lengthy speeches, which are particularly tiresome [?]. On obtaining this script, however, my delight showed in my face.〕
Associate Examiner Zou, Instructor, comments: 〔The poet’s feelings of longing and remembrance are expressed with intimacy and aptness. Yet…〕

title: 正德八年河南鄉試錄
text:
幾可與說詩者
考試官學正王　批〔冊本色語組織成章舉子中之熟於經學者〕
考試官教授陸　批〔寫出訪落之意〕
嗣王之延訪羣臣惟欲賴先王之休以自善而
已夫保明其身則嗣王之所以爲善者有其道
矣然非仰賴先王之遺休抑亦何由而致此乎
昔成王既朝武王之廟因作詩以道延訪羣臣
之意至此意謂我昭考武王之道仰之而不可
===
及就之而未能合然豈無以恤我乎哉蓋上下
於庭乃昭考燕翼之迹于此而思所以紹之庶
幾賴其休於上下之時臨之如在前也質之如
在旁也陟降於家乃昭考貽謀之地于此而思
所以嗣之庶幾籍其休於陟降之餘坐則見於
墻也食則見於羮也夫我以家之多難國方罹
危殆之憂質之不聰又未免昏塞之患幸而昭
考遺休足爲顧籍是引是翼有以保吾身於不
危患生而能備害至而能防九重之尊即吾優
punctuated:
幾可與說詩者。
考試官學正王，批〔冊本色語組織成章，舉子中之熟於經學者。〕
考試官教授陸，批〔寫出訪落之意。〕
嗣王之延訪羣臣，惟欲賴先王之休以自善而已。夫保明其身，則嗣王之所以爲善者有其道矣。然非仰賴先王之遺休，抑亦何由而致此乎？昔成王既朝武王之廟，因作詩以道延訪羣臣之意。至此，意謂我昭考武王之道，仰之而不可及，就之而未能合，然豈無以恤我乎哉？蓋上下於庭，乃昭考燕翼之迹，于此而思所以紹之，庶幾賴其休。於上下之時，臨之如在前也，質之如在旁也。陟降於家，乃昭考貽謀之地，于此而思所以嗣之，庶幾籍其休。於陟降之餘，坐則見於墻也，食則見於羮也。夫我以家之多難，國方罹危殆之憂；質之不聰，又未免昏塞之患。幸而昭考遺休，足爲顧籍，是引是翼，有以保吾身於不危。患生而能備，害至而能防，九重之尊，即吾優
translation_en:
…one with whom it is almost possible to discuss the Odes.
Examiner Wang, Instructor, comments: 〔The wording of the text [?], in its native idiom, is woven into a coherent composition. This is a candidate well versed in classical learning.〕
Examiner Lu, Professor, comments: 〔It brings out the meaning of “Seeking Counsel at the Beginning” (Fang luo).〕
The succeeding king’s purpose in inviting and consulting his ministers was simply to rely on the former king’s beneficence to perfect himself. To preserve his person and make it enlightened: herein lay the way by which the succeeding king could achieve goodness. Yet without looking up to and relying upon the beneficence bequeathed by the former king, how could he accomplish this? After King Cheng had paid homage at King Wu’s ancestral temple, he composed a poem to express his intention of inviting and consulting his ministers. At this point, his meaning was: “The Way of my illustrious deceased father, King Wu—I look up to it but cannot reach it; I approach it but cannot yet accord with it. Yet can it have no means of caring for me?
“As I move up and down through the court, here are the traces of my illustrious father’s provision for the peace and protection of his descendants. Here I consider how to carry on his work, hoping thereby to rely on his beneficence. As I move about, I stand before him as though he were in front of me, and submit my conduct to his judgment as though he were beside me. As I ascend and descend within the house, this is the place where my illustrious father left plans for his descendants. Here I consider how to succeed him, hoping thereby to draw upon his beneficence. In the intervals of my movements, when I sit, I see him upon the wall; when I eat, I see him in my broth.
“Because of the many troubles of my royal house, my state is now beset by the anxiety of peril. Being by nature wanting in understanding, I am also not free from the affliction of mental darkness and obstruction. Fortunately, the beneficence left by my illustrious father is sufficient to sustain my reliance upon him. Guiding and assisting me, it enables me to preserve my person from danger. When trouble arises, I can prepare for it; when harm arrives, I can guard against it. The exalted station within the ninefold palace becomes a place where I may be at ease…”

title: 正德八年河南鄉試錄
text:
游之境矣莽蜂辛螫寧復自求矣乎是將是迪
有以明吾身於不昧物來而先知事至而先覺
萬幾之務在吾洞察之中矣桃蟲拚飛寧不自
戢矣乎噫先王之道遠矣即其事而求之則道
之在先王者在吾身也爾羣臣尚堪爲我一助
焉大抵成王以幼冲踐祚乃能延訪羣臣如此
此其所以緝熈有容而能安靖天下他日訓迪
百官既曰制治未亂保邦未危又曰亂爾有政
以佑乃辟亦知慎終如始而永保大命也已持
===
盈守成者當以成王爲法
春秋
諸侯遂救許〔僖公六年〕諸侯遂圍許〔僖公〕
二十有八年
張景
考試官學正王 批〔聖筆褒貶於一字之間此作闡揚微　意既明且盡而下筆不迂不追整之文體甚爲雅重是可以式矣〕
考試官教授陸 批〔春秋經世大旨重在夷夏君臣之間此　但文救許圍許之事所以可著是篇筆力簡健而經旨甚明必深有得於春秋者〕
punctuated:
游之境矣，莽蜂辛螫，寧復自求矣乎？是將是迪，有以明吾身於不昧，物來而先知，事至而先覺，萬幾之務在吾洞察之中矣。桃蟲拚飛，寧不自戢矣乎？噫！先王之道遠矣，即其事而求之，則道之在先王者在吾身也。爾羣臣尚堪爲我一助焉。大抵成王以幼冲踐祚，乃能延訪羣臣如此，此其所以緝熈有容而能安靖天下。他日訓迪百官，既曰「制治未亂，保邦未危」，又曰「亂爾有政，以佑乃辟」，亦知慎終如始而永保大命也已。持盈守成者，當以成王爲法。

春秋

諸侯遂救許〔僖公六年〕。諸侯遂圍許〔僖公〕二十有八年。

張景

考試官學正王批〔聖筆褒貶於一字之間，此作闡揚微意，既明且盡，而下筆不迂不追，整之文體甚爲雅重，是可以式矣〕。

考試官教授陸批〔春秋經世大旨，重在夷夏君臣之間，此但文救許圍許之事，所以可著。是篇筆力簡健，而經旨甚明，必深有得於春秋者〕。
translation_en:
…a realm in which I may dwell at ease. Would I again bring upon myself the painful sting of the bee [?]? With this support and guidance, I can keep myself enlightened and free from obscurity: I shall understand things before they arrive and discern affairs before they arise. The myriad affairs of government will all lie within my penetrating understanding. Should I not restrain myself, mindful of the small bird that takes wing and grows great? Ah! The Way of the former kings is distant indeed. Yet if I seek it through their deeds, the Way that resided in them will reside in me. You, my assembled ministers, may yet give me your assistance.

King Cheng ascended the throne while still a young child, yet he was able to summon and consult his ministers in this manner. This was how he continued to cultivate enlightened virtue and magnanimity and brought peace and stability to the realm. Later, in instructing the officials, he said, “Establish order before disorder arises; safeguard the state before danger appears.” He also said, “Set your administration in order, thereby assisting your sovereign.” He thus understood how to be as cautious at the end as at the beginning and preserve the great Mandate forever. Those who would maintain prosperity and preserve what has been achieved should take King Cheng as their model.

Spring and Autumn Annals

“The feudal lords thereupon went to the rescue of Xu.” 〔Sixth year of Duke Xi.〕 “The feudal lords thereupon besieged Xu.” 〔Duke Xi.〕 Twenty-eighth year.

Zhang Jing

Examiner Wang, School Instructor, comments: 〔The sage’s brush conveys praise and blame within a single word. This composition elucidates that subtle meaning both clearly and fully. Its writing is neither circuitous nor forced [?], and its orderly literary form is most refined and dignified. It may serve as a model.〕

Examiner Lu, Prefectural School Professor, comments: 〔The great purpose of the Spring and Autumn Annals in ordering the world lies chiefly in the distinctions between the non-Chinese and the Chinese, and between ruler and minister. Here, merely recording the rescue and siege of Xu makes this apparent [?]. This essay’s writing is concise and vigorous, and the meaning of the Classic is very clear. Its author must have attained a profound understanding of the Spring and Autumn Annals.〕

title: 正德八年河南鄉試錄
text:
霸主急於恤患春秋深善之霸主明於討罪春
秋亦善之此齊桓之遂救許晉文之遂圍許皆
有得於大義之所當為者何莫而非春秋之所
善也哉且伐鄭新城之役非許所專楚人欲救
而圍乃及許固將以撓我師也然當是時鄭尚
未服雖緩恤之也何嫌桓以為救分之禮在所
當急夷得猾夏伊誰之咎況致圍者以吾收貳
之故乎吾寧舍鄭不可以負吾許于是遂解新
城之圍徃為許人之救水火之害惟恐其拯之
===
不早簡書之畏惟恐其為之不力雖墮楚之詭
計不恤也是非勇於義者其能急人之急如此
桓之此舉安攘之功於是為大春秋書曰遂救
許救固為善其曰遂救者善之尤者也非深善
之而何若踐土河陽之地於許為近天子再至
而朝獨無許固可謂慢其職也然當是時蹕巳
反旋雖姑置之也何傷文則以征討之決在所
當明豈敢慢君人得而討況出覲者又吾舉廢
之志乎吾欲尊周不可以追此許于是遂率于
punctuated:
霸主急於恤患，春秋深善之；霸主明於討罪，春秋亦善之。此齊桓之遂救許、晉文之遂圍許，皆有得於大義之所當為者，何莫而非春秋之所善也哉？且伐鄭新城之役，非許所專，楚人欲救，而圍乃及許，固將以撓我師也。然當是時，鄭尚未服，雖緩恤之也何嫌？桓以為救分之禮，在所當急；夷得猾夏，伊誰之咎？況致圍者，以吾收貳之故乎？吾寧舍鄭，不可以負吾許。于是遂解新城之圍，徃為許人之救。水火之害，惟恐其拯之不早；簡書之畏，惟恐其為之不力。雖墮楚之詭計，不恤也。是非勇於義者，其能急人之急如此？桓之此舉，安攘之功於是為大。春秋書曰：「遂救許。」救固為善，其曰「遂救」者，善之尤者也。非深善之而何？

若踐土、河陽之地，於許為近，天子再至，而朝獨無許，固可謂慢其職也。然當是時，蹕巳反旋，雖姑置之也何傷？文則以征討之決，在所當明。豈敢慢君？人得而討。況出覲者，又吾舉廢之志乎？吾欲尊周，不可以追此許。于是遂率于
translation_en:
When a hegemon hastens to relieve distress, the Spring and Autumn Annals deeply approves; when a hegemon clearly discerns whom to punish for wrongdoing, the Annals likewise approves. Thus Duke Huan of Qi’s proceeding to rescue Xu and Duke Wen of Jin’s proceeding to besiege Xu both accorded with what great righteousness required. How could either fail to receive the Annals’ approval?

Now, the campaign against Zheng at Xincheng was not Xu’s undertaking alone. The men of Chu wished to rescue Zheng, but their siege instead fell upon Xu: their intention was certainly to disrupt our army. At that time, however, Zheng had not yet submitted. What objection could there have been to delaying relief for Xu? Duke Huan considered the ritual obligation to give assistance [?] a matter of urgency: “If the barbarians are allowed to disturb the Chinese states, whose fault is that? Moreover, has Xu not been besieged because I sought to bring a wavering state back into allegiance? I would rather leave Zheng alone than fail our ally Xu.” Accordingly, he lifted the siege of Xincheng and went to rescue the people of Xu. Faced with their peril, like that of fire and flood, he feared only that rescue would come too late; mindful of the obligations conveyed in written commands, he feared only that his efforts would be insufficient. Even falling into Chu’s cunning trap was no concern to him. Could anyone lacking courage in righteousness have treated another’s emergency with such urgency? Through this action, Duke Huan’s achievement in securing the Chinese states and repelling the barbarians became great. The Annals records: “They thereupon rescued Xu.” Rescue was certainly commendable; its wording “thereupon rescued” expresses particular approval. What could this be but deep approval?

As for Jiantu and Heyang, these places were near Xu. The Son of Heaven came twice, yet Xu alone was absent from the audience: this could certainly be called neglect of its duty. At that time, however, the royal carriage had already returned. What harm would there have been in setting the matter aside for the moment? Duke Wen, however, considered that the resolve to undertake punitive action must be made clear: “How dare anyone slight his ruler? Others are entitled to punish him. Moreover, was bringing the Son of Heaven out to receive homage not also an expression of my intention to revive neglected institutions? I wish to honor Zhou; I cannot pursue this Xu [?].” Accordingly, he proceeded to lead those at…

title: 正德八年河南鄉試錄
text:
溫之衆徃爲許人之圍數其一不朝也而不臣
之罪以聲數其再不朝也而無君之惡以懲雖
非周之發禁不討也是非明於義者其能不後
其君如此文之此舉尊奬之名於是爲正春秋
書曰遂圍許圍不爲甚其曰遂者繼事之詞也
又非善之而何是則許之遂救也而夷夏之大
防以立其遂圍也而君臣之大分以明桓文之
霸此其所以爲可稱與雖然救許善矣臧黃敗
徐之坐視何不克終圍許可矣翟泉子虎之上
===
盟何不自考要之均未聞王者之道而不免假
之者也君子於二公取人之恕衛道之嚴又可
兩備也哉
公二年
齊侯使國佐如師　及國佐盟于袁婁〔成〕
考試官學正王　批
鄭重
〔是作依經據傳筆下操縱老徤說出晉人服敵待敵之失詳盡無遺非得春秋心法者不能薦之必有用〕
之學
punctuated:
溫之衆，徃爲許人之圍，數其一不朝也，而不臣之罪以聲；數其再不朝也，而無君之惡以懲。雖非周之發禁，不討也？是非明於義者，其能不後其君如此？文之此舉，尊奬之名於是爲正。《春秋》書曰：「遂圍許。」圍不爲甚，其曰「遂」者，繼事之詞也，又非善之而何？是則許之遂救也，而夷夏之大防以立；其遂圍也，而君臣之大分以明。桓文之霸，此其所以爲可稱與！雖然，救許善矣，臧黃敗徐之坐視，何不克終？圍許可矣，翟泉子虎之上盟，何不自考？要之，均未聞王者之道，而不免假之者也。君子於二公，取人之恕、衛道之嚴，又可兩備也哉！
公二年。
齊侯使國佐如師，及國佐盟于袁婁。〔成〕
考試官學正王，批：
鄭重〔是作依經據傳，筆下操縱老徤，說出晉人服敵待敵之失，詳盡無遺。非得春秋心法者不能。薦之，必有用〕之學。
translation_en:
…the forces at Wen and went to besiege Xu. He enumerated its first failure to attend court, thereby proclaiming its offense of refusing a subject’s allegiance; he enumerated its second failure to attend court, thereby punishing its wicked disregard for its sovereign. Even though Zhou had not issued the prohibition, could he leave it unpunished [?]? Could anyone who did not clearly understand righteousness have been so unwilling to put his sovereign second? Through this action, Duke Wen rightly earned a reputation for honoring and supporting the sovereign. The Spring and Autumn Annals records: “He then besieged Xu.” The siege was not excessive; “then” is a word linking successive undertakings. How could this, too, signify anything other than approval? Thus, by proceeding to rescue Xu, the great boundary between the Yi peoples and the Xia was established; by proceeding to besiege Xu, the fundamental distinction between ruler and subject was clarified. Is this not what makes the hegemony of Dukes Huan and Wen worthy of praise?
Nevertheless, rescuing Xu was good, but why did Huan fail to carry this goodness through to the end, standing idly by over Zang and Huang [?] and the defeat of Xu? Besieging Xu was acceptable, but why did Wen fail to examine his own conduct when, at the covenant at Diquan, he took precedence over Zihu? Ultimately, neither had heard the Way of true kingship, and neither escaped merely borrowing its appearance. In judging these two dukes, can the gentleman not fully combine generosity in recognizing others’ merits with strictness in defending the Way?
Second year of Duke … [The duke’s name, Cheng, appears below in an annotation.]
“The Marquis of Qi sent Guo Zuo to the army. A covenant was concluded with Guo Zuo at Yuanlou.”〔Cheng〕
Comment by Examiner Wang, School Instructor:
Earnest and serious learning.〔This composition rests upon the Classic and draws its evidence from the commentaries. Its handling of the argument is mature and vigorous. It explains fully, leaving nothing out, the errors of the men of Jin in subduing and dealing with their enemy. Only someone who has grasped the essential principles of the Spring and Autumn Annals could accomplish this. Recommend him: he will certainly prove useful.〕

title: 正德八年河南鄉試錄
text:
考試官教授陸　批〔不熟讀三傳恐不能作此〕
春秋紀霸臣於敵至而要信也原其無服人之
義責其無待人之禮此國佐之如師晉但能使
之求免而衰婁之及盟晉不能制之甘心此春
秋致意於是良有以哉嘅昔于鞌有戰齊師敗
北侵車東巡晉忿未息於是齊有國佐之遣而
晉因為衰婁之盟焉夫以齊之強而晉能致之
人固謂其與齊桓之致屈完者等爾不知服人
有義以力屈者非所謂服也齊之暴不如楚而
===
憤不可遏晉苟負擊強扶弱之心數其罪而不
加兵焉則所伐者正而齊固自服矣今者得國
佐之如師是畢義以服人乎雪一笑之恥至於
殘民毒衆之慘不道之加為暴已甚亦何以厭
其心哉但見賂持甗磬惟知求免雖曰如我師
也彼特懼吾之迫而勉強於一時焉耳在晉也
者豈知所以服齊若屈完之欵者哉夫國佐既
返而晉乃盟之人亦謂其與齊桓之盟召陵者
等爾不知待人有禮以盟要者非所謂待也國
punctuated:
考試官教授陸批〔不熟讀三傳，恐不能作此。〕

春秋紀霸臣於敵至而要信也，原其無服人之義，責其無待人之禮。此國佐之如師，晉但能使之求免，而衰婁之及盟，晉不能制之甘心。此春秋致意於是，良有以哉！嘅昔于鞌有戰，齊師敗北，侵車東巡，晉忿未息。於是齊有國佐之遣，而晉因為衰婁之盟焉。夫以齊之強，而晉能致之，人固謂其與齊桓之致屈完者等爾。不知服人有義，以力屈者非所謂服也。齊之暴不如楚，而憤不可遏。晉苟負擊強扶弱之心，數其罪而不加兵焉，則所伐者正，而齊固自服矣。今者得國佐之如師，是畢義以服人乎？雪一笑之恥，至於殘民毒衆之慘，不道之加，為暴已甚，亦何以厭其心哉？但見賂持甗磬，惟知求免。雖曰如我師也，彼特懼吾之迫，而勉強於一時焉耳。在晉也者，豈知所以服齊若屈完之欵者哉？夫國佐既返，而晉乃盟之，人亦謂其與齊桓之盟召陵者等爾。不知待人有禮，以盟要者非所謂待也。國
translation_en:
Comment by Examiner Lu, Professor: 〔Without a thorough reading of the Three Commentaries, one could scarcely compose this.〕

The Spring and Autumn Annals records how a minister of a hegemonic state exacted a pledge when an enemy’s envoy arrived: it examines his lack of righteousness in securing submission and censures his lack of ritual propriety in treating others. When Guo Zuo came to the army, Jin could only make him seek deliverance; when they concluded the covenant at Shuailou [袁婁, Yuanlou, apparently intended], Jin could not make him assent willingly. The attention the Spring and Autumn Annals gives this matter surely has good reason! Alas, in the battle at An, the army of Qi was defeated and fled. The invading chariots advanced eastward, and Jin’s anger remained unappeased. Qi therefore dispatched Guo Zuo, and Jin consequently concluded the covenant at Shuailou.

Given Qi’s strength, people naturally considered Jin’s ability to bring its envoy to appear equivalent to Duke Huan of Qi’s bringing Qu Wan to appear. They did not understand that securing submission requires righteousness: subjugation by force is not what is meant by submission. Qi’s violence did not equal Chu’s, yet Jin’s fury could not be restrained. Had Jin harbored the intention of striking the strong and supporting the weak, enumerating Qi’s offenses without further attacking it, its punitive action would have been just, and Qi would naturally have submitted. Now that Jin had obtained Guo Zuo’s visit to its army, had it thereby fully discharged the demands of righteousness in securing submission [?]? To avenge the humiliation of a single laugh, it went so far as cruelly to ravage the people and afflict the multitude. Such unrighteous treatment was already excessively violent; how could it satisfy Qi’s heart? We see only an envoy bearing a yan cooking vessel and a musical stone as gifts, intent solely on obtaining deliverance. Although he is said to have ‘come to our army,’ he merely feared our coercion and reluctantly complied for the moment. How could those on Jin’s side understand how to secure Qi’s submission with sincerity like Qu Wan’s?

After Guo Zuo had returned, Jin made a covenant with him. People likewise considered this equivalent to Duke Huan of Qi’s covenant at Shaoling. They did not understand that treating others requires ritual propriety: coercing them through a covenant is not what is meant by proper treatment. Guo…

title: 正德八年河南鄉試錄
text:
佐之服不如完而勢不可挾晉苟知招携懷貳
之德綏以誠而不敢遂焉則所示者大而齊固
自幸矣今者逮袁婁以與盟是果禮以下敵乎
特一戰之捷至有質母東畝之命不衷之發爲
悖已甚亦何以免其倨哉卒之假使魯衛去而
復要雖曰聽于盟也彼蓋陋吾之識而勉强於
盟者哉聖人以爲制敵莫如仗義天下莫大於
一與焉爾在晉也者豈知所以待齊若召陵之
理而强有力不與焉故於國佐如師之下而反
===
以及盟在晉若曰晉之不義不能致其服而其
悖理徒以强其盟也一變文間而晉之曲於此
焉見春秋曲直之繩墨有如是夫雖然齊果無
罪乎房帷不謹而至於喪師失地幾見執獲固
先有以自取矣特郤克挾主盟之勢行其私憤
是以反爲國佐所折非齊之本直也噫晉有郤
克雖嘗敗齊也而已大至於損威齊有國佐雖
嘗見敗也而亦差能以伸氣此于蒲之盟晉不
免於收拾而雞澤以後齊率至於抗衡矣國
punctuated: 佐之服不如完，而勢不可挾。晉苟知招携懷貳之德，綏以誠而不敢遂焉，則所示者大，而齊固自幸矣。今者逮袁婁以與盟，是果禮以下敵乎？特一戰之捷，至有質母東畝之命，不衷之發爲悖已甚，亦何以免其倨哉？卒之假使魯衛去而復要，雖曰聽于盟也，彼蓋陋吾之識而勉强於盟者哉？聖人以爲制敵莫如仗義，天下莫大於一，與焉爾。在晉也者，豈知所以待齊若召陵之理，而强有力不與焉？故於國佐如師之下，而反以及盟在晉，若曰晉之不義不能致其服，而其悖理徒以强其盟也。一變文間，而晉之曲於此焉見。《春秋》曲直之繩墨有如是夫！雖然，齊果無罪乎？房帷不謹，而至於喪師失地，幾見執獲，固先有以自取矣。特郤克挾主盟之勢，行其私憤，是以反爲國佐所折，非齊之本直也。噫！晉有郤克，雖嘗敗齊也，而已大至於損威；齊有國佐，雖嘗見敗也，而亦差能以伸氣。此于蒲之盟，晉不免於收拾，而雞澤以後，齊率至於抗衡矣。國
translation_en:
…Zuo’s submission was not like that of Qu Wan, and superior power must not be used to coerce others. Had Jin understood the virtue of drawing in the estranged and winning over the wavering, reassuring them with sincerity and not daring to press its advantage, it would have demonstrated magnanimity, and Qi would certainly have considered itself fortunate. Yet now it went as far as Yuanlou to conclude a covenant. Was this truly treating an enemy with ritual courtesy and humility? On the strength of a single victory, it went so far as to demand a mother as hostage and the reorientation of field boundaries eastward. Such unreasonable demands were flagrantly perverse; how could Jin escape the charge of arrogance? In the end, it employed Lu and Wei as intermediaries, withdrew, and again pressed for an agreement [?]. Although Qi was said to have accepted the covenant, surely it merely despised Jin’s judgment and entered the covenant unwillingly?

The Sage held that nothing surpassed reliance on righteousness in bringing an enemy under control, and that nothing under Heaven was greater than unity: this alone he approved [?]. How could those in Jin have understood how to treat Qi according to the principles exemplified at Shaoling? Yet brute strength receives no approval [?]. Thus, after recording that Guo Zuo went to the army, the text reverses the phrasing and assigns the initiative in concluding the covenant to Jin. It is as though it says that Jin’s unrighteousness could not secure Qi’s submission, and that its violation of principle served only to force Qi into a covenant. Through a single change in wording, Jin’s being in the wrong becomes apparent. Such is the standard by which the Spring and Autumn Annals distinguishes wrong from right!

Even so, was Qi truly without fault? A failure to maintain propriety within the women’s quarters led to the loss of its army and territory, and nearly to its ruler’s capture. Certainly, it had first brought these things upon itself. It was only because Xi Ke exploited his position as leader of the covenant to vent his private resentment that Guo Zuo was able to rebuff him; it was not that Qi had been in the right from the outset. Alas! With Xi Ke, Jin defeated Qi, yet went so far as gravely to diminish its own prestige. With Guo Zuo, Qi suffered defeat, yet was still somewhat able to recover its spirit. Thus, at the covenant of Pu, Jin could not avoid having to put matters back in order; after Jize, Qi generally came to contend with it on equal terms. A state…

title: 正德八年河南鄉試錄
text:
之於人所繫亦匪輕哉
禮記
故曰生民之道樂爲大焉
同考試官教諭林　批〔樂記一書多論樂道化人之義然未有如此章直指君子小人同歸道化之妙者此作備見聖樂之化存於〕
〔聲容之意宛然在目回視直述上文牽合他章經語成文而了無歸宿者大〕
〔不侔矣是宜錄出〕
考試官學正王　批〔樂記義類此作者絕少〕
===
考試官教授陸　批〔講既明悉結亦有見〕
記者引言人道莫大於樂以其爲化民之本也
夫樂之於人其感化也至矣昔謂生民之道而
不以是爲大乎樂記君子固論樂舞寓化民之
理而引古語以結之意謂樂之爲道發於聖人
而感於天下至大而無尚也何以見之是故民
之有生心未必皆一也非有以一之則民風不
能移情未必皆同也非有以同之則民俗不能
易然欲一民心而同民情其惟樂之爲道乎樂
punctuated:
之於人，所繫亦匪輕哉！

禮記

故曰：「生民之道，樂爲大焉。」

同考試官教諭林批〔樂記一書，多論樂道化人之義，然未有如此章直指君子小人同歸道化之妙者。此作備見聖樂之化存於〕〔聲容之意，宛然在目。回視直述上文、牽合他章經語成文而了無歸宿者，大〕〔不侔矣。是宜錄出。〕

考試官學正王批〔樂記義類此作者絕少。〕

考試官教授陸批〔講既明悉，結亦有見。〕

記者引言，人道莫大於樂，以其爲化民之本也。夫樂之於人，其感化也至矣。昔謂生民之道，而不以是爲大乎？樂記君子固論樂舞寓化民之理，而引古語以結之。意謂樂之爲道，發於聖人，而感於天下，至大而無尚也。何以見之？是故民之有生，心未必皆一也，非有以一之，則民風不能移；情未必皆同也，非有以同之，則民俗不能易。然欲一民心而同民情，其惟樂之爲道乎？樂
translation_en:
…what a state depends upon in its people is indeed no small matter!

Book of Rites

“Thus it is said: ‘Among the ways of nurturing the people, music is paramount.’”

Comment by Associate Examiner Lin, Instructor: 〔The Record of Music frequently discusses how the Way of music transforms people. Yet no passage so directly reveals as this chapter the subtle workings by which gentlemen and common people alike come under the transforming influence of the Way. This essay fully displays how the transforming power of the sages’ music resides in〕〔the meaning conveyed by sounds and movements, bringing it vividly before our eyes. Compared with essays that merely restate the preceding text and forcibly stitch together canonical phrases from other chapters without arriving at any conclusion, it is greatly〕〔superior. It therefore deserves to be selected for inclusion.〕

Comment by Examiner Wang, Instructor: 〔Expositions of the meaning of the Record of Music comparable to this essay are exceedingly rare.〕

Comment by Examiner Lu, Professor: 〔The exposition is clear and thorough, and the conclusion also shows insight.〕

The recorder quotes a saying that, among the ways governing human life, nothing is greater than music, because it is the foundation for transforming the people. Music’s power to move and transform human beings is indeed consummate. When people of old spoke of the way of nurturing the people, did they not regard music as paramount? The gentleman who composed the Record of Music discussed how music and dance embody the principles for transforming the people, and quoted an ancient saying to conclude his account. His meaning was that the Way of music originates with the sages and moves all under Heaven: it is supremely great, with nothing above it. How can this be seen?

People are born with hearts that are not necessarily united. Unless there is something to unite them, their prevailing ways cannot be changed. Their feelings are not necessarily alike. Unless there is something to bring them into accord, their customs cannot be altered. Yet if one wishes to unite the people’s hearts and harmonize their feelings, must this not be accomplished through the Way of music? Music…

title: 正德八年河南鄉試錄
text:
也者本諸復情和志之功而有窮本知變之妙
其作也極聲音之和而鐘鼓管磬之相宣凡心
之所動莫不形見而無遺所謂天地之命者在
是極動靜之變而羽籥干戚之迭舞凡情之所
蘊莫不表暴而無餘所謂中和之紀者在是人
惟無閒於樂也一有聞焉則慾心自釋躁心自
平君子以之而好善非特使學之者不厭其道
而已矣人惟無聽於樂也一有聽焉則佚能思
初安能惟始小人以之而知過非特使救之者
===
不私其欲而已矣夫化於此或遺於彼非大也
君子化之而小人亦化之則心一情同有舉世
甄陶之氣象小補不足以並稱也感於彼或遺
於此非大也小人感之而君子亦感之則風移
俗易有同歸道化之規模小康不足以儷美也
謂之曰樂爲大大焉不亦信哉抑又論之人道以
樂爲大固也然自節事天地之神辨君臣上下
長幼之位別男女父子兄弟之親昏姻疏數之
交而言則有禮以爲大自夫婦別父子親君臣
punctuated:
也者，本諸復情和志之功，而有窮本知變之妙。其作也，極聲音之和，而鐘鼓管磬之相宣，凡心之所動，莫不形見而無遺，所謂天地之命者在是。極動靜之變，而羽籥干戚之迭舞，凡情之所蘊，莫不表暴而無餘，所謂中和之紀者在是。人惟無閒於樂也，一有聞焉，則慾心自釋，躁心自平。君子以之而好善，非特使學之者不厭其道而已矣。人惟無聽於樂也，一有聽焉，則佚能思初，安能惟始。小人以之而知過，非特使救之者不私其欲而已矣。
夫化於此，或遺於彼，非大也。君子化之，而小人亦化之，則心一情同，有舉世甄陶之氣象，小補不足以並稱也。感於彼，或遺於此，非大也。小人感之，而君子亦感之，則風移俗易，有同歸道化之規模，小康不足以儷美也。謂之曰樂爲大大焉，不亦信哉？抑又論之，人道以樂爲大，固也。然自節事天地之神，辨君臣上下長幼之位，別男女父子兄弟之親、昏姻疏數之交而言，則有禮以爲大。自夫婦別、父子親、君臣
translation_en:
…is rooted in the work of restoring the emotions and harmonizing the will, and possesses the subtle efficacy of fathoming origins and understanding change. When music is performed, it brings the harmony of sounds to its utmost, with bells, drums, pipes, and chime stones giving expression to one another. Whatever stirs within the heart is thus made manifest, with nothing omitted: herein lies what is called “the mandate of Heaven and Earth.” It exhausts the variations of movement and stillness through alternating dances with feathers and flutes, shields and axes. Everything harbored in the emotions is thus brought forth, with nothing remaining concealed: herein lies what is called “the ordering principle of equilibrium and harmony.” People need only have occasion to hear music [?]; once they hear it, their desires naturally dissolve and their agitation naturally subsides. Through it, the gentleman comes to love goodness: its effect is not merely to keep those who study it from tiring of its Way. People may simply have failed to listen to music; once they listen, in ease they can reflect upon their beginnings, and in security they can recall their origins. Through it, the petty person comes to recognize his faults: its effect is not merely to keep those who seek to remedy them from indulging their private desires.
If it transforms those here but perhaps leaves out those there, it is not great. When gentlemen are transformed by it and petty people are likewise transformed, hearts become united and feelings become shared. There is then the prospect of molding the whole world; a minor improvement cannot be spoken of in the same terms. If it moves those there but perhaps leaves out those here, it is not great. When petty people are moved by it and gentlemen are likewise moved, prevailing practices change and customs are transformed. There is then a pattern of all returning together to the transforming influence of the Way; modest well-being cannot rival its excellence. Is it not indeed true, then, to call music the greatest [?]? Yet let us consider this further. It is certainly true that music is greatest among the ways of human life. But if we speak of regulating service to the spirits of Heaven and Earth, distinguishing the positions of ruler and minister, superior and subordinate, elder and younger, and differentiating the familial relationships of men and women, fathers and sons, and elder and younger brothers, as well as marital connections and the frequency of social intercourse, then ritual is what is greatest. If we speak of distinction between husband and wife, affection between father and son, and ruler and minister…

Comment by Associate Examiner Lin, Instructor: 〔The topic is fundamentally straightforward. Writers fail to understand the meaning of the word “sincerity” in the commentary and consequently base their arguments on the claim that words and deeds must be rooted in sincerity. This seriously contravenes the original meaning. This essay simply follows the literal wording of the topic.〕

Wang Qian

[Continuation of Lin’s comment:] It proceeds with a plain exposition that is perfectly coherent; therefore it is printed here as a model.

Comment by Examiner Wang, Instructor: 〔The meaning of the topic forms an integral whole, making it especially difficult to formulate an argument. This essay comes close to preserving its comprehensive treatment of words and deeds, and therefore deserves inclusion.〕

Where words and deeds actually manifest themselves, there must be evidence of those words and deeds. For wherever such a thing exists, its corresponding effects must exist. Can what makes people hear its sound and see its accomplishment lie anywhere other than in words and deeds? Long ago, those who recorded the rites recounted our Master’s words on this point. Their meaning was that the gentleman takes words and deeds as his pivot and trigger, while the ears and eyes take keen hearing and clear sight as their constant rule. Thus, just as the pivot and trigger are set in motion within me, others have already perceived them through their hearing and sight. There is naturally something here that cannot be checked…

title: 正德八年河南鄉試錄
text:
者矣彼人於日用常行之間莫不有言焉言也
者物感於外情動於中本之氣以宣其藴者也
使言藏於心則無迹之可求固有傾耳而聽之
不可得而聞者矣惟宣之言也則因文以達其
志而清濁高下之有倫由辭以發其情而喜怒
哀樂之殊應故善言出則仁義之聲入於人不
善之言出則非僻之聲入於人未有言而無
聲有聲而無聞者也言之有徵也蓋如此人於
應事接物之際亦莫不有行焉行也者有踐履
===
之方施爲之序本諸身以體夫事者也使言而
不行則無形之可驗固有正明目而視之不可
得而見者矣惟涉於行也則發乎邇而見乎遠
有卓然不易之規加於身而措於前有嶷然不
動之象故行之而善則人莫不見其德之成行
之而弗善則人莫不見其過之成未有有行而
無成有成而無見者也行之有徵也又如此吁
言必有聲行必有成然則君子於言行可不謹
哉抑考此章上文有曰苟有車必見其軾苟有
punctuated: 者矣。彼人於日用常行之間，莫不有言焉。言也者，物感於外，情動於中，本之氣以宣其藴者也。使言藏於心，則無迹之可求，固有傾耳而聽之不可得而聞者矣。惟宣之言也，則因文以達其志，而清濁高下之有倫；由辭以發其情，而喜怒哀樂之殊應。故善言出，則仁義之聲入於人；不善之言出，則非僻之聲入於人。未有言而無聲、有聲而無聞者也。言之有徵也，蓋如此。人於應事接物之際，亦莫不有行焉。行也者，有踐履之方、施爲之序，本諸身以體夫事者也。使言而不行，則無形之可驗，固有正明目而視之不可得而見者矣。惟涉於行也，則發乎邇而見乎遠，有卓然不易之規；加於身而措於前，有嶷然不動之象。故行之而善，則人莫不見其德之成；行之而弗善，則人莫不見其過之成。未有有行而無成、有成而無見者也。行之有徵也，又如此。吁！言必有聲，行必有成，然則君子於言行可不謹哉？抑考此章上文有曰：「苟有車，必見其軾；苟有
translation_en:
…cannot be checked. In the ordinary course of daily life, everyone speaks. Speech arises when external things affect us and feelings stir within; drawing upon vital energy, it gives expression to what lies within. If words remain hidden in the heart, there is no trace to seek: even someone who inclines an ear to listen cannot hear them. Once they are expressed in speech, however, patterned expression conveys one's intentions, with clear and turbid, high and low tones duly ordered; words give vent to one's feelings, with distinct responses corresponding to joy, anger, sorrow, and pleasure. Thus, when good words issue forth, the sounds of benevolence and righteousness enter others' ears; when bad words issue forth, the sounds of wrongdoing and perversity enter others' ears. There has never been speech without sound, or sound without its being heard. Such is the evidence that speech produces.

In responding to affairs and dealing with things, everyone also acts. Action has methods of practice and an order of execution; it takes the person as its basis and gives concrete embodiment to affairs. If one speaks but does not act, there is no visible form to examine: even someone who looks directly with clear eyes [?] cannot see it. Once something enters the realm of action, however, it begins nearby and becomes apparent far away, displaying a conspicuous and unchanging pattern; it is enacted in one's person and set forth before others, presenting a lofty and unwavering appearance. Thus, if one's actions are good, everyone sees one's virtue brought to fruition; if one's actions are not good, everyone sees one's faults brought to fruition. There has never been action without an outcome, or an outcome without its being seen. Such, too, is the evidence that action produces.

title: 正德八年河南鄉試錄
text:
衣必見其敝皆言有是物必有是事也車誠設
不可欺人以無軾衣誠服不可欺人以無敝況
言行乎君子知其不可欺也故言擇其可而非
法不道行擇其可而非道弗行焉夫子於此引
其端不竟其說蓋欲學者體會於心而自得之
耳不然言非其法行非其道平旦之思獨無自
作於心乎
第貳場
論
===
聖人能使天下順治
同考試官訓導秦　批　論場正要於議論中看人
見識論理要得理趣論事要得事情又覆委曲含蓄痛快乃
見胸次乃見筆力而近時士子科舉之作承習學究一種活套文
字遇題不問出處但字面有近似者輒移其意以入其說陳俗
腐爛有所不計主司以其說偶合而備選者多矣古人以言觀人之法
將何所施此弊何時而改邪檢閱數日食次忽得此論為之三歎其
人胸次筆力俱不凡必是學有根據且能為古文者錄之可以祛場中
punctuated:
衣必見其敝，皆言有是物必有是事也。車誠設，不可欺人以無軾；衣誠服，不可欺人以無敝。況言行乎？君子知其不可欺也，故言擇其可而非法不道，行擇其可而非道弗行焉。夫子於此引其端，不竟其說，蓋欲學者體會於心而自得之耳。不然，言非其法，行非其道，平旦之思獨無自作於心乎？

第貳場
論

聖人能使天下順治

同考試官訓導秦批：論場正要於議論中看人見識。論理要得理趣，論事要得事情，又覆委曲含蓄痛快，乃見胸次，乃見筆力。而近時士子科舉之作，承習學究一種活套文字，遇題不問出處，但字面有近似者，輒移其意以入其說，陳俗腐爛有所不計。主司以其說偶合而備選者多矣。古人以言觀人之法，將何所施？此弊何時而改邪？檢閱數日，食次忽得此論，為之三歎。其人胸次筆力俱不凡，必是學有根據且能為古文者。錄之可以祛場中
translation_en:
…clothing, its wear must become visible.” Both statements mean that where a thing exists, its consequences must follow. Once a carriage is set out, one cannot deceive others by claiming it has no crossbar; once clothing is worn, one cannot deceive others by claiming it has no wear. How much more is this true of speech and conduct! Knowing that these cannot be concealed, the gentleman chooses what is appropriate to say and says nothing contrary to proper standards; he chooses what is appropriate to do and does nothing contrary to the Way. Here the Master introduces the point without exhausting its explanation, presumably wishing learners to apprehend it in their hearts and attain understanding for themselves. Otherwise, if their speech violates proper standards and their conduct violates the Way, could reflection in the early morning fail to arise spontaneously in their hearts?

Second Session
Discourse

“The Sage Can Bring All Under Heaven into Harmonious Order”

Comment by Associate Examiner Qin, Assistant Instructor: In the discourse session, the essential task is to discern a candidate’s insight through his argument. Discussion of principles must capture their underlying meaning; discussion of affairs must grasp their actual circumstances. Furthermore, it should be nuanced, restrained, and forceful [?]: only then does the writer’s intellectual breadth become apparent, and only then does his command of writing emerge. Yet examination compositions by candidates in recent times perpetuate a kind of stock formula used by pedantic scholars. On encountering a topic, they do not inquire into its source. Whenever its wording bears some resemblance to something familiar, they simply transfer that meaning into their argument, heedless of its being stale, vulgar, and thoroughly hackneyed. Many have been selected by the examiners because their arguments happened to fit. Where, then, can the ancients’ method of judging people by their words be applied? When will this abuse be corrected? After several days of reviewing scripts, I unexpectedly came upon this discourse at mealtime and sighed three times in admiration. Its author’s intellectual breadth and command of writing are both exceptional. He must be someone whose learning has firm foundations and who can also write ancient-style prose. Including it in the record can dispel from the examination hall…

text:

===

有所止無所止則不得其所歸止必有所
據無所據則不得其所止聖人天下之所
歸也聖人之止將以歸天下者也天下於

所矣爲我止矣而不爲之據其能爲我安
乎我之止有未得其所我之止之所有未

That all under Heaven find repose where the sage comes to rest is simply because principle provides its foundation. Under Heaven there are no things outside principle, and no principle outside affairs. The myriad things and the multitude of affairs must have a place at which to rest; without such a place, they cannot find where they belong. title: 正德八年河南鄉試錄
text:
止之所聖人之所據而與天下共之者也
天下事物莫不有理莫不各有其所理之
所在事物所當止之所也聖人於此以爲
天下所與共之者也是故其所止也不敢
以私于其身而止之也亦非有强於人是
故聖人之止天下之止也聖人止之天下
無不安之程子曰聖人能使天下順治其
理如此甚矣天下之生也物有萬焉事有
萬焉有萬其情喜怒哀樂發焉有萬其變
===
吉凶悔吝出焉尊卑異臨大小異行親疎
異分内外異制遠近異視衆獨異處重輕
異置今故異襲久暫異習同異異識孰者
爲得孰者爲失孰者爲過孰爲不及孰是
孰非孰美孰惡孰公孰私孰順孰逆紛紜
膠轕將迎滿目舉天下何等非物物接乎
我何等非事擾擾貿貿於何所歸聖人者
出若之何而歸之歸之未易若之何而止
之止之未易又若之何安之噫是亦有理
punctuated: 止之所，聖人之所據而與天下共之者也。天下事物莫不有理，莫不各有其所。理之所在，事物所當止之所也。聖人於此，以爲天下所與共之者也。是故其所止也，不敢以私于其身；而止之也，亦非有强於人。是故聖人之止，天下之止也。聖人止之，天下無不安之。程子曰：「聖人能使天下順治，其理如此。」甚矣，天下之生也！物有萬焉，事有萬焉，有萬其情，喜怒哀樂發焉；有萬其變，吉凶悔吝出焉。尊卑異臨，大小異行，親疎異分，内外異制，遠近異視，衆獨異處，重輕異置，今故異襲，久暫異習，同異異識。孰者爲得？孰者爲失？孰者爲過？孰爲不及？孰是孰非？孰美孰惡？孰公孰私？孰順孰逆？紛紜膠轕，將迎滿目。舉天下，何等非物？物接乎我，何等非事？擾擾貿貿，於何所歸？聖人者出，若之何而歸之？歸之未易，若之何而止之？止之未易，又若之何安之？噫！是亦有理
translation_en: …the place in which to rest is what the sage relies upon and shares with all under Heaven. Among the affairs and things of the world, none lacks principle, and each has its proper place. Where principle resides is the place in which affairs and things ought to rest. The sage regards this as something to be shared with all under Heaven. Thus, in finding his resting place, he dares not reserve it for himself alone; and in bringing others to rest there, he does not impose anything upon them. Hence the sage’s resting place is the resting place of all under Heaven. When the sage rests there, none under Heaven fails to find peace there. Master Cheng said: “The sage can bring all under Heaven into harmonious order; the principle is like this.” How vast is the unfolding of life under Heaven! Things are myriad, affairs are myriad, and their feelings are myriad: joy, anger, sorrow, and pleasure arise from them. Their changes are myriad: good fortune, misfortune, regret, and humiliation emerge from them. The honored and the lowly are approached differently; the great and the small are dealt with differently; the close and the distant have different allotted relationships; those within and those without are governed by different rules; the far and the near are viewed differently; the multitude and the solitary are treated differently; the weighty and the slight are assigned different places; the new and the old are taken up differently; the enduring and the temporary are practiced differently; the like and the unlike are distinguished differently. Which constitutes attainment? Which constitutes failure? Which goes too far? Which falls short? Which is right and which wrong? Which is good and which bad? Which serves the common good and which private interests? Which accords with the proper order and which opposes it? Tangled and intertwined, things to be sent off and welcomed fill the eyes. Throughout the world, what is not a thing? When things come into contact with me, what is not an affair? Amid this bustle and confusion, where can one turn? When a sage emerges, how can he bring them to their proper destination? Since bringing them there is not easy, how can he bring them to rest? Since bringing them to rest is not easy, how, moreover, can he bring them peace? Ah! Here too there is principle…

title: 正德八年河南鄉試錄
text:
焉爾矣理在天下在萬物在萬事理在聖
人在其身心天下事物有一物即有一物
理有一理即有一理事事物有萬理亦有
萬萬物備於聖人而聖人之心具乎萬理
聖人所治舉天下萬物庶事又何莘而非
理之所在耶嗚呼此聖人所以爲天下歸
聖人之止之所之所據所以共乎天下天
下事物所以各有當止之所而聖人止之
所以安其所而止也無尊卑無大小無親
===
踈無内外無遠近無衆獨無重輕無今故
無久暫無同異而能得之是審之是察
謹抑其過勉其不及去非即是棄惡成美
革私從公遠逆依順隨所居之位而不違
乎當然之則嗚呼此固聖人所以公天下
之人而爲止之之理也止之而止止之得
其所也止得其所得其理也其理則其所
據之具也物得當然之則以爲之據金之
於範泥之於鈞奔者之於机休者之於喬
punctuated: 焉爾矣。理在天下，在萬物，在萬事；理在聖人，在其身心。天下事物，有一物即有一物理，有一理即有一理事；事物有萬，理亦有萬。萬物備於聖人，而聖人之心具乎萬理。聖人所治，舉天下萬物庶事，又何莘而非理之所在耶？嗚呼！此聖人所以爲天下歸，聖人之止之所之所據，所以共乎天下，天下事物所以各有當止之所，而聖人止之，所以安其所而止也。無尊卑，無大小，無親踈，無内外，無遠近，無衆獨，無重輕，無今故，無久暫，無同異，而能得之，是審之，是察，謹抑其過，勉其不及，去非即是，棄惡成美，革私從公，遠逆依順，隨所居之位而不違乎當然之則。嗚呼！此固聖人所以公天下之人而爲止之之理也。止之而止，止之得其所也；止得其所，得其理也。其理則其所據之具也。物得當然之則以爲之據，金之於範，泥之於鈞，奔者之於机，休者之於喬
translation_en:
…there is simply principle within them. Principle resides in all under Heaven, in the myriad things, and in every affair; principle resides in the sage, in his person and mind. Among the affairs and things of the world, wherever there is a thing, there is that thing’s principle; wherever there is a principle, there is an affair corresponding to it. Affairs and things number in the myriad, and so do principles. The myriad things are complete within the sage, and the sage’s mind possesses the myriad principles. Of all the myriad things and manifold affairs under Heaven that the sage governs, which could fail to be a locus of principle [?]? Ah! This is why all under Heaven turn to the sage. The basis of the place in which the sage brings things to rest [?] is shared throughout the world. Thus the affairs and things of the world each have a place where they ought to rest; the sage brings them to rest so that they settle securely in their places.

Without distinction between noble and lowly, great and small, close and distant kin, inner and outer, near and far, the multitude and the solitary, weighty and light, present and past, lasting and temporary, or same and different, he can apprehend this principle. He examines and scrutinizes it, carefully restraining excess and encouraging what falls short, removing wrong and adopting right, discarding evil and bringing goodness to fruition, reforming selfishness and following impartiality, shunning contrariness and adhering to what accords with principle. Whatever position he occupies, he does not depart from the rule of what ought to be. Ah! This indeed is the principle by which the sage treats the people of the world impartially and brings them to rest. When he brings them to rest and they rest, he has brought them to rest in their proper places. To rest in the proper place is to attain its principle. That principle supplies the basis on which they rely. Things obtain the rule of what ought to be as their support: metal in relation to its mold, clay to the potter’s wheel, one who runs to a supporting stand [?], and one who rests to a lofty…

title: 正德八年河南鄉試錄
text:
木而有不止不安者乎是理也在書曰皇
極在詩曰物則在周易之艮則所謂背而
孔氏於大學直指為至善者也昔者聖人
作易次艮於震而吾夫子傳之於止之而
止之理言之悉矣猶懼學者或有所未達
也於是授門人以大學之道其綱領三其
條目八二百五字之間泄露無餘其示虞
人之的而授匠氏之規矩乎聖人至善之
止不獨止乎其德之明將民之新也物格
===
知至意誠心正而身之脩固將家之齊國
之治而天下之平也易有之曰艮其背矣
曰艮其身矣艮其背其止以天下天下之
止聖人之止也艮其身其止一身而已聖
人弗取也聖人之止公乎天下如是理
固聖人所與天下共之非可得私而所謂
明德者聖人與人同得於天不此有彼無
不彼豐此嗇者也特人不能無氣質物欲
之累而無以充其全體故天下之明德不
punctuated:
木，而有不止不安者乎？是理也，在《書》曰皇極，在《詩》曰物則，在《周易》之《艮》則所謂背，而孔氏於《大學》直指為至善者也。昔者聖人作《易》，次《艮》於《震》，而吾夫子傳之，於止之而止之理言之悉矣。猶懼學者或有所未達也，於是授門人以《大學》之道，其綱領三，其條目八，二百五字之間，泄露無餘。其示虞人之的而授匠氏之規矩乎？聖人至善之止，不獨止乎其德之明，將民之新也。物格、知至、意誠、心正，而身之脩，固將家之齊、國之治，而天下之平也。《易》有之，曰「艮其背」矣，曰「艮其身」矣。艮其背，其止以天下，天下之止，聖人之止也；艮其身，其止一身而已，聖人弗取也。

聖人之止，公乎天下如是。理固聖人所與天下共之，非可得私，而所謂明德者，聖人與人同得於天，不此有彼無，不彼豐此嗇者也。特人不能無氣質物欲之累，而無以充其全體，故天下之明德不
translation_en:
…trees: could any fail to come to rest and find repose? This principle is called the Supreme Standard in the Book of Documents and the norm of things in the Book of Odes. In Keeping Still (Gen) in the Book of Changes, it is what is meant by the back; in the Great Learning, Confucius points directly to it as the highest good. Formerly, when the sage composed the Changes, he placed Keeping Still after The Arousing (Zhen). Our Master then wrote a commentary on it, fully explaining the principle by which one is brought to rest and rests. Still fearing that learners might not fully understand, he taught his disciples the Way of the Great Learning. Its three guiding principles and eight steps are fully disclosed within its 205 characters, with nothing left unrevealed. Was this not like showing a forester his target [?] and giving a craftsman his compass and square? The sage’s resting in the highest good does not end merely with making his own virtue bright; it extends to renewing the people. Investigating things, extending knowledge, making intentions sincere, rectifying the mind, and cultivating oneself are indeed directed toward regulating the family, governing the state, and bringing peace to all under Heaven. The Changes says both “Keeping his back still” and “Keeping his person still.” Keeping his back still means taking all under Heaven as the scope of his repose: the repose of all under Heaven is the sage’s repose. Keeping his person still means resting only in one’s own person; the sage does not adopt this.

Such is the impartiality with which the sage extends his repose to all under Heaven. Principle is inherently shared by the sage with all under Heaven and cannot be privately appropriated. As for what is called bright virtue, the sage and other people alike receive it from Heaven. It is not present in one and absent in another, nor abundant in one and scant in another. It is simply that people cannot avoid the encumbrances of their physical endowment and material desires, and so cannot fully realize it in its entirety. Thus the bright virtue of all under Heaven cannot…

title: 正德八年河南鄉試錄
text:
能不賴于聖人以明而新民之責聖人不
得不以之自任雖然非人力私意有所付
畀增益之也人有之不及知知之不及行
而行之者不及至也聖人於是歸之于當
止之所而止之以當然之則立必俱立成
不獨成亦何事於強哉至善之止聖人無
分己所有於人之惠而人亦無受其所有
於聖人之謝止之各於其所而已矣止之
不於其所則無可止之理天下事物得其
===
所則安失其所則悖其安其悖一視乎理
而已矣愚故曰天下安聖人之所止者有
理爲之據耳止則治安則順矣此程子順
治之說所以爲易艮止而發而有及乎孔
氏門人傳釋大學所引之言朱子深有契
焉二書之註交明互舉曲暢旁通伊川示
我無欲無思之境紫陽勉我必至不遷之
地當止之所於是爲極學者於是地而求
之可以立仁宅可以闢義路可以設禮門
punctuated: 能不賴于聖人以明，而新民之責，聖人不得不以之自任。雖然，非人力私意有所付畀增益之也。人有之，不及知；知之，不及行；而行之者，不及至也。聖人於是歸之于當止之所，而止之以當然之則。立必俱立，成不獨成，亦何事於強哉？至善之止，聖人無分己所有於人之惠，而人亦無受其所有於聖人之謝，止之各於其所而已矣。止之不於其所，則無可止之理。天下事物得其所則安，失其所則悖。其安其悖，一視乎理而已矣。愚故曰：「天下安聖人之所止者，有理爲之據耳。」止則治，安則順矣。此程子順治之說，所以爲《易》艮止而發，而有及乎孔氏門人傳釋《大學》所引之言，朱子深有契焉。二書之註，交明互舉，曲暢旁通。伊川示我無欲無思之境，紫陽勉我必至不遷之地，當止之所於是爲極。學者於是地而求之，可以立仁宅，可以闢義路，可以設禮門。
translation_en:
…cannot but depend on the sage to illuminate it, and the sage cannot but take upon himself the responsibility of renewing the people. Yet this does not mean that human effort or private intention can bestow something upon them or add to what they possess. People possess it but fail to know it; they know it but fail to put it into practice; and those who practice it fail to reach its fullest realization. The sage therefore brings them back to where they ought to rest and settles them there according to the standards of what is right. In establishing himself, he must establish others too; in attaining fulfillment, he does not attain it alone. What need, then, is there for coercion? In resting in the highest good, the sage confers no favor by sharing with others something belonging to himself, nor do people owe him thanks for receiving from him what they themselves already possess. Each simply rests in the proper place. If one rests somewhere other than the proper place, there is no principle warranting that resting. All affairs and things under Heaven are at peace when they find their proper place, and fall into disorder when they lose it. Whether they are at peace or in disorder depends entirely upon principle.

Thus I humbly say: “That all under Heaven find peace where the sage rests is simply because principle provides the foundation.” Resting brings order; being at peace brings accord. This is why Master Cheng’s explanation of accord and order, developed to elucidate the meaning of Gen—resting—in the Book of Changes, also bears upon the words quoted in the commentary explaining the Great Learning by the disciples of Confucius. Master Zhu profoundly grasped this connection. The annotations to the two books illuminate and invoke one another, fully unfolding their subtleties and revealing connections throughout. Yichuan [Cheng Yi] shows us the realm free of desire and deliberation; Ziyang [Zhu Xi] urges us toward the ground we must reach and never leave. The place where one ought to rest thus becomes the ultimate standard. By seeking it on this ground, students can establish the dwelling of benevolence, open the road of righteousness, and erect the gate of ritual propriety…

text:
可□間智牖可以升孔子之堂而入其室

光稽首頓首上言伏惟堯舜之事載于典
謨循之可以致治文武之政布在方策舉
之存乎得人歷觀既往之盛衰足為將來

脩而卷帙猶多叙述詳而檢閱難徧乃自
punctuated:

translation_en:
…one may [open?] the window of wisdom [?], ascend into Confucius’s hall, and enter his inner chamber. Respectfully submitted as a discourse.

Memorial

A memorial in the voice of Sima Guang of the Song dynasty, presenting the Record of Investigations into Antiquity (Jigu lu) [First year of Yuanyou, 1086].
By Che Fu.

Comment by Associate Examiner Yang, Instructor: [Lord Sima’s own memorial presenting the Record of Investigations into Antiquity survives in his writing.] This piece imitates it and bears a considerable resemblance.

Comment by Associate Examiner Deng, Instructor: [The parallel phrasing follows proper rules; the author is certainly capable of writing four-and-six prose.]

Comment by Examiner Wang, Instructor: [Every word and sentence is grounded in substance, vividly capturing the Duke of Wen, Sima Guang.]

Comment by Examiner Lu, Professor: [In composing a memorial, avoid forced arrangement, empty language, abject accommodation [?], and violations of the patterns of level and oblique tones.] It conveys considerable devotion to the sovereign as father. This composition is most appropriate in form and manner.

Your servant Guang, Grand Master for Proper Deliberation, Acting Left Vice Director of the Department of State Affairs and concurrently Vice Director of the Chancellery, bows his head to the ground and repeatedly prostrates himself, submitting these words:

title: 正德八年河南鄉試錄
text:
羲農以入戰國由秦漢以至
本朝上下幾四千年記纂纔二十卷微春秋
之筆削愧乏三長竭旦暮之劬勞較有一
得恭遇
○○○○
繼離出震
旋乾轉坤纘
太祖太宗之基圖而負荷不墜承
太皇太后之佑啓而孝養不違
===
式尚典刑
延登耆舊臣已廢復起既老且衰扶病趨
班豈堪重任捐軀報
國用畢愚誠凡今日所當盡之心皆平生可
對人之語冒陳鄙拙仰荅
恩私伏願
明目達聰改新法而竟除四害隱惡揚善察
邇言而試用五規力回慶曆之徽風無蹈
熙豐之覆轍臣無任懇切願望戰汗屏營
punctuated: 羲農以入戰國，由秦漢以至本朝，上下幾四千年，記纂纔二十卷。微春秋之筆削，愧乏三長；竭旦暮之劬勞，較有一得。恭遇○○○○，繼離出震，旋乾轉坤，纘太祖太宗之基圖而負荷不墜，承太皇太后之佑啓而孝養不違，式尚典刑，延登耆舊。臣已廢復起，既老且衰，扶病趨班，豈堪重任？捐軀報國，用畢愚誠。凡今日所當盡之心，皆平生可對人之語。冒陳鄙拙，仰荅恩私。伏願明目達聰，改新法而竟除四害；隱惡揚善，察邇言而試用五規。力回慶曆之徽風，無蹈熙豐之覆轍。臣無任懇切願望、戰汗屏營
translation_en: …from Fuxi and Shennong into the Warring States period, and from the Qin and Han down to our present dynasty—a span of nearly four thousand years—the record I have compiled amounts to only twenty juan. Lacking the editorial discernment of the Spring and Autumn Annals, I am ashamed to fall short in the three strengths of a historian. Yet, exhausting myself in labor from morning to night, I have perhaps achieved something of value. I have reverently had the good fortune to encounter ○○○○ [?], who continues the imperial radiance and emerges as sovereign, turns Heaven and Earth about, and carries forward the foundations and grand design of Taizu and Taizong, bearing that charge without letting it fall. Receiving the protection and guidance of the Grand Empress Dowager, you have never failed in filial care; you honor established precedents and bring venerable former servants back into office. Your servant, once dismissed, has been recalled, but is now old and frail. Supporting my sick body as I hasten to take my place at court, how could I bear a weighty responsibility? I would give my life to repay the state, thereby offering all my humble sincerity. Everything that I should now express from my heart consists of words that, throughout my life, I could openly speak before others. I venture to present this crude and clumsy work in gratitude for your personal favor. I humbly pray that you will open your eyes and ears to all, revise the New Policies and completely eliminate the four harms; conceal others’ faults and proclaim their virtues, examine even ordinary people’s words, and try putting the five admonitions into practice. Strive to restore the admirable spirit of the Qingli reign, and do not repeat the disastrous course of the Xining and Yuanfeng reigns. Your servant cannot contain his earnest hopes and longing, trembling, sweating, and deeply apprehensive…

Third Session
Policy Essay
First Question

Comment by Associate Examiner Huang, Instructor
Essay by Li Maoyuan

〔The words of Yao have been proclaimed throughout the realm; everyone ought to be able to recite them. Yet few examination candidates know the book Method of the Mind (Xinfa). This policy essay alone expounds it fully, leaving nothing out.
