title: 正德八年河南鄉試錄
text:
第壹塲
四書
富與貴是人之所欲也不以其道得之不
處也貧與賤是人之所惡也不以其道
得之不去也
李濂
同考試官訓導秦　批〔他作多形容富貴貧賤而於不以其道處却無一言發揮此作知輕重有斟酌筆力且老健宜取以置高等〕
同考試官教諭桑　批〔典雅溫厚詞不費而理自足佳〕
===
作也
考試官學正王　批〔體貼審富貴而安貧賤處甚有分曉〕
考試官教授陸　批〔講爲仁親切非獨優於經學者〕
聖人論君子之爲仁在審富貴而安貧賤也蓋
富貴貧賤取舍之間實用力於仁之所也君子
能審之以義而安之於命則取舍之分明矣爲
仁固如是夫昔聖人之意若曰仁體物而不遺
人無往而可忽彼富與貴皆順境雖有志者不
能無覬覦之私人孰不欲之然有義存焉在審
punctuated:
第壹塲
四書
「富與貴，是人之所欲也；不以其道得之，不處也。貧與賤，是人之所惡也；不以其道得之，不去也。」
李濂
同考試官訓導秦，批〔他作多形容富貴貧賤，而於不以其道處却無一言發揮。此作知輕重，有斟酌，筆力且老健，宜取以置高等。〕
同考試官教諭桑，批〔典雅溫厚，詞不費而理自足，佳〕作也。
考試官學正王，批〔體貼審富貴而安貧賤處，甚有分曉。〕
考試官教授陸，批〔講爲仁親切，非獨優於經學者。〕
聖人論君子之爲仁，在審富貴而安貧賤也。蓋富貴貧賤取舍之間，實用力於仁之所也。君子能審之以義，而安之於命，則取舍之分明矣。爲仁固如是夫！昔聖人之意若曰：仁體物而不遺，人無往而可忽。彼富與貴，皆順境，雖有志者不能無覬覦之私，人孰不欲之？然有義存焉，在審
translation_en:
First Session
Four Books

“Wealth and high station are what people desire. If they are obtained otherwise than by the proper Way, one does not remain in them. Poverty and low station are what people dislike. If they are obtained otherwise than by the proper Way, one does not leave them.”

Li Lian

Associate Examiner Qin, Assistant Instructor, comments: “Other compositions mostly describe wealth and high station, poverty and low station, but offer not a word of elaboration on ‘otherwise than by the proper Way.’ This composition understands the relative importance of the issues and weighs them carefully. Its writing is also mature and vigorous. It should be selected and placed in a high grade.”

Associate Examiner Sang, Instructor, comments: “Classically elegant, gentle, and generous in tone; without wasting words, it fully conveys the principle. A fine composition.”

Examiner Wang, Instructor, comments: “Its close treatment of scrutinizing wealth and high station and resting content in poverty and low station makes the distinctions very clear.”

Examiner Lu, Professor, comments: “Its discussion of practicing benevolence is closely pertinent; the author excels in more than classical scholarship alone.”

The Sage explains that the gentleman’s practice of benevolence lies in scrutinizing wealth and high station and resting content in poverty and low station. For it is precisely in choosing what to accept and reject amid wealth, high station, poverty, and low station that one applies effort to benevolence. If the gentleman can scrutinize these in accordance with righteousness and rest content in what is allotted by Heaven, the distinction between what to accept and what to reject becomes clear. Surely this is how benevolence is practiced!

The Sage’s meaning was as though he had said: “Benevolence embodies all things, leaving none out; wherever people find themselves, they must never neglect it. Wealth and high station are both favorable circumstances. Even those with firm aspirations cannot be entirely free of private desires to obtain them. Who does not desire them? Yet righteousness bears upon this, and what matters is scrutinizing …”

title: 正德八年河南鄉試錄
text:
之而已苟或授受不合於禮進退不由其道是
富貴所不當得而得之君子則曰富
貴可欲而吾心之仁尤可欲於此而處之寧不
害吾仁乎于是繫馬千駟視之如浮雲也祿以
萬鍾棄之如敝蹝也其審富貴而不處也如此
若貧與賤皆逆境雖有守者不能無憂戚之態
人孰不惡之然有命存焉在安之而已苟或事
勢出於不虞變故起於無妄是貧賤所不當得
矣不當得而得之君子則曰貧賤可惡而吾之
===
不仁尤可惡於此而去之寧不違吾仁乎于是
飯糗茹草若將終身也困窮拂鬱若固有之也
其安貧賤而不去也如此夫審於所欲則非決
性命之情以饕富貴安於所惡則非徇人欲之
私以厭貧賤取舍之分明而本心之仁全矣此
其所以能成君子之名而獨有以異於衆人也
歟大抵富貴貧賤好惡異情取舍異向自非樂
天知命君子孰肯舍其所好而取其所惡哉求
之於古吾於孔孟見之矣觀其不主彌子與不
punctuated:
之而已。苟或授受不合於禮，進退不由其道，是富貴所不當得而得之。君子則曰：「富貴可欲，而吾心之仁尤可欲，於此而處之，寧不害吾仁乎？」于是繫馬千駟，視之如浮雲也；祿以萬鍾，棄之如敝蹝也。其審富貴而不處也如此。
若貧與賤，皆逆境，雖有守者不能無憂戚之態，人孰不惡之？然有命存焉，在安之而已。苟或事勢出於不虞，變故起於無妄，是貧賤所不當得矣。不當得而得之，君子則曰：「貧賤可惡，而吾之不仁尤可惡，於此而去之，寧不違吾仁乎？」于是飯糗茹草，若將終身也；困窮拂鬱，若固有之也。其安貧賤而不去也如此。
夫審於所欲，則非決性命之情以饕富貴；安於所惡，則非徇人欲之私以厭貧賤。取舍之分明，而本心之仁全矣。此其所以能成君子之名，而獨有以異於衆人也歟！大抵富貴貧賤，好惡異情，取舍異向。自非樂天知命君子，孰肯舍其所好而取其所惡哉？求之於古，吾於孔孟見之矣。觀其不主彌子與不
translation_en:
…one need only examine them carefully. If giving and receiving do not accord with ritual propriety, or advancement and withdrawal do not follow the proper Way, then these are riches and honors acquired when they ought not to be acquired. The gentleman says: “Riches and honors are desirable, but the benevolence of my own heart is still more desirable. Were I to remain in such a position, would I not impair my benevolence?” Thus he regards a thousand teams of tethered horses as floating clouds; he casts aside a stipend of ten thousand measures of grain as worn-out sandals. Such is his careful scrutiny of riches and honors and his refusal to remain in them.
Poverty and low station are both adverse circumstances. Even those who hold firmly to their principles cannot entirely avoid showing distress: who does not dislike them? Yet there is a destined allotment to acknowledge; one need only rest content in it. If circumstances arise unexpectedly and misfortune comes without fault on one’s part, this is poverty and low station that one ought not to incur. When he incurs them nonetheless, the gentleman says: “Poverty and low station are hateful, but my own lack of benevolence would be still more hateful. Were I to escape them under these circumstances, would I not depart from my benevolence?” Thus he eats parched grain and wild greens as though he would do so all his life; he endures hardship and frustration as though they were his natural lot. Such is his acceptance of poverty and low station and his refusal to escape them.
By carefully scrutinizing what he desires, he does not injure the true dispositions of his nature and allotted life to glut himself on riches and honors. By resting content in what he dislikes, he does not indulge selfish human desires in his aversion to poverty and low station. The distinction between what to accept and what to reject is clear, and the benevolence of his original heart remains whole. Is this not how he earns the name of gentleman and distinguishes himself from ordinary people? In general, riches and honors, poverty and low station elicit different feelings of liking and dislike, and different inclinations to accept or reject. Unless one is a gentleman who delights in Heaven and understands his destined allotment, who would willingly relinquish what he likes and accept what he dislikes? Seeking examples among the ancients, I find them in Kongzi and Mengzi. Consider the refusal to take Mizi as host and the refusal to…

title: 正德八年河南鄉試錄
text:
受齊卿之祿君子固窮與不遇曾侯之說同一
審富貴而安貧賤耳他如子貢猶不免於貨殖
而冉求亦為之聚斂其餘可知也已噫仁與不
仁之分公私義利之間而已矣學者不可不辨
苟不固聰明聖知達天德者其孰能知之
吳瀚
同考試官教諭楊　批〔場中作者破多不斷正意而講多不順本文俱失經義之體故錄此作以為之式〕
同考試官學正鄧　批〔中庸文字亙須句句理會過〕
===
考試官學正王　批〔合全篇之旨講本題之義而詞不繁此亦潛心於性理之學者〕
考試官教授陸　批〔理勝於文複非初學之士所能到〕
實有至聖之德能契至誠之道甚矣唯聖人能
知聖人也然則至誠之道非至聖其孰能與於
斯乎中庸三十二章承上章大德敦化而言天
道至此意謂至誠之道妙知化於窮神至聖之
德充踐形之惟肖苟非有聖人者與具聰明聖
punctuated:
受齊卿之祿，君子固窮與不遇曾侯之說，同一審富貴而安貧賤耳。他如子貢猶不免於貨殖，而冉求亦為之聚斂，其餘可知也已。噫！仁與不仁之分，公私義利之間而已矣，學者不可不辨。

「苟不固聰明聖知達天德者，其孰能知之？」
吳瀚
同考試官教諭楊　批〔場中作者破多不斷正意，而講多不順本文，俱失經義之體，故錄此作以為之式。〕
同考試官學正鄧　批〔中庸文字亙須句句理會過。〕
考試官學正王　批〔合全篇之旨，講本題之義，而詞不繁，此亦潛心於性理之學者。〕
考試官教授陸　批〔理勝於文，複非初學之士所能到。〕

實有至聖之德，能契至誠之道。甚矣，唯聖人能知聖人也！然則至誠之道，非至聖，其孰能與於斯乎？《中庸》三十二章承上章大德敦化而言天道。至此，意謂至誠之道，妙知化於窮神；至聖之德，充踐形之惟肖。苟非有聖人者與，具聰明聖
translation_en:
…accepting the stipend of a minister of Qi, and the sayings that “the gentleman remains steadfast in poverty” and that he “did not encounter the Marquis of Zeng” [?], all alike concern weighing wealth and rank carefully and remaining content in poverty and low station. Others, such as Zigong, could not escape involvement in commerce, while Ran Qiu even amassed wealth for his patron; the rest may readily be imagined. Alas! The distinction between benevolence and its absence lies simply between public-mindedness and selfishness, righteousness and profit. Students must distinguish these.

“Unless one is truly [?] perceptive, sagacious, and possessed of an understanding of Heaven’s virtue, who can know it?”
Wu Han
Associate Examiner Yang, Instructor, comments: 〔Among the candidates in the examination, most fail in their opening statements to identify the precise central meaning, and their expositions mostly fail to follow the original text. Both faults violate the proper form of an essay on the Classics. This composition has therefore been selected as a model.〕
Associate Examiner Deng, School Assistant, comments: 〔The wording of the Doctrine of the Mean must [?] be understood sentence by sentence.〕
Examiner Wang, School Assistant, comments: 〔He brings together the purport of the entire work to explain the meaning of this topic, without excessive wording. This too is someone who has devoted himself to the study of human nature and principle.〕
Examiner Lu, Professor, comments: 〔Principle outweighs literary ornament; this, again [?], is beyond the attainment of a beginner.〕

One who truly possesses the virtue of utmost sagehood can accord with the Way of utmost sincerity. How profound it is that only a sage can know a sage! Thus, as for the Way of utmost sincerity, who but the utmost sage could participate in it? Chapter thirty-two of the Doctrine of the Mean continues the preceding chapter’s statement that “great virtue brings abundant transformation,” and speaks of the Way of Heaven. Here its meaning is that the Way of utmost sincerity wondrously knows transformation by plumbing the spiritual, while the virtue of utmost sagehood fully realizes the bodily form in perfect correspondence [with Heaven]. Unless there is a sage endowed with perceptiveness and sagely…

title: 正德八年河南鄉試錄
text:
知之資而天之所賦於已者備其全而不偏達
仁義禮智之德而性之所出於天者究其極而
不昧吾見質非生知則無以為凝聚培植之基
德非至聖則無以為融會貫通之地體之未至
見之未真歧性命於兩途而天之與人判然其
間隔矣行矣不著習矣不察視道器為二物而
人之於天邈然其懸絶矣想像於形迹之粗所
謂經綸大經而與仁無二之妙探之而愈遠也
測之而愈深也孰能超詣頓悟而真知其藴奥
===
邪議擬於口耳之間所謂立本知化而天淵合
一之妙仰之而彌高也鑽之而彌堅也孰能神
會默契而洞見其精微邪夫至誠之道非至聖
不能知至聖之德非至誠不能為則亦非二物
矣子思子發明聖人天道之極致尚何以加于
此哉抑又論之天下之言二有有德之言有造
道之言中庸所謂大德敦化小德川流發明聖
人天道至此而無以加矣求其可以當之者惟
吾夫子焉耳故非夫子之聖不足以知之亦不
punctuated:
知之資，而天之所賦於已者備其全而不偏，達仁義禮智之德，而性之所出於天者究其極而不昧。吾見質非生知，則無以為凝聚培植之基；德非至聖，則無以為融會貫通之地。體之未至，見之未真，歧性命於兩途，而天之與人判然其間隔矣。行矣不著，習矣不察，視道器為二物，而人之於天邈然其懸絶矣。想像於形迹之粗，所謂經綸大經而與仁無二之妙，探之而愈遠也，測之而愈深也，孰能超詣頓悟而真知其藴奥邪？議擬於口耳之間，所謂立本知化而天淵合一之妙，仰之而彌高也，鑽之而彌堅也，孰能神會默契而洞見其精微邪？夫至誠之道，非至聖不能知；至聖之德，非至誠不能為，則亦非二物矣。子思子發明聖人天道之極致，尚何以加于此哉？

抑又論之，天下之言二：有有德之言，有造道之言。《中庸》所謂大德敦化，小德川流，發明聖人天道至此而無以加矣。求其可以當之者，惟吾夫子焉耳。故非夫子之聖，不足以知之，亦不
translation_en:
…the endowment of wisdom, possessing fully and without partiality all that Heaven has bestowed upon oneself; comprehending the virtues of benevolence, righteousness, ritual propriety, and wisdom, and fathoming to its utmost, without obscurity, the nature that comes from Heaven. I see that unless one’s native endowment includes knowledge possessed from birth, there is no foundation for consolidation and cultivation; unless one’s virtue is that of the utmost sage, there is no basis for comprehensive understanding. If one has not fully embodied it or truly perceived it, one separates human nature and Heaven’s mandate into two paths, leaving Heaven and humanity distinctly divided. Acting without understanding, practicing without discernment, one regards the Way and concrete things as two separate entities, leaving humanity and Heaven remote from one another, with an immense gulf between them. If one merely imagines it through the coarse outward traces, then the subtlety of what is called ordering the great guiding relationships, while being one with benevolence, grows more distant the further one probes, and deeper the further one sounds it. Who could attain a transcendent insight and sudden awakening, and truly understand its hidden profundities? If one deliberates and conjectures merely through what is spoken and heard, then the subtlety of what is called establishing the foundation and knowing transformation, in which Heaven and the depths unite as one, becomes higher the more one looks up to it and firmer the more one bores into it. Who could apprehend it spiritually, accord with it silently, and see deeply into its finest subtleties? The Way of utmost sincerity can be known only by the utmost sage; the virtue of the utmost sage can be achieved only through utmost sincerity. Thus these, too, are not two separate things. Master Zisi has elucidated the ultimate attainment of the sage and the Way of Heaven: what more could be added to this?

Yet let us discuss this further. There are two kinds of utterances in the world: those of people possessing virtue, and those of people who have attained the Way. What the Doctrine of the Mean calls “great virtue bringing about abundant transformation” and “lesser virtues flowing like rivers” elucidates the sage and the Way of Heaven to a point beyond which nothing can be added. If we seek someone who could measure up to this, there is only our Master, Confucius. Thus, without the sageliness of our Master, one could not adequately understand it, nor could one…

title: 正德八年河南鄉試錄
text:
能以體之而子思子又𢿘如此之悉邪夫中庸
之知乃至聖之知非聞見之知也子思之言其
亦造道之言也歟
聖人治天下使有菽粟如水火菽粟如水
火而民焉有不仁者乎
李茂元
同考試官教諭黃　批〔說使字上說治天下之意最是且不眩於挫吝不仁之說此直有學識者〕
同考試官教諭鄭　批〔場中作此題者多以教養立說〕
===
考試官學正王　批〔脫去浮華而歸於雅淡若此篇者殊不多見蓋有意於不求而出之〕
考試官教授陸　批〔文字着實見識超邁非苟作者亦鮮矣〕
聖人之治世惟有以裕乎民因有以化乎民蓋
民富則善心生善心生則於治亦易矣君天下
者曷亦自其先者而圖之乎昔孟子述意蓋謂
民可使之富也亦可使之仁也聖人有見於此
故其治天下也必使易田疇薄稅斂庶可以厚
punctuated:
能以體之，而子思子又𢿘如此之悉邪？夫中庸之知，乃至聖之知，非聞見之知也。子思之言，其亦造道之言也歟？
聖人治天下，使有菽粟如水火。菽粟如水火，而民焉有不仁者乎？
李茂元
同考試官教諭黃，批〔說使字上說治天下之意最是，且不眩於挫吝不仁之說，此直有學識者。〕
同考試官教諭鄭，批〔場中作此題者，多以教養立說。〕
考試官學正王，批〔脫去浮華而歸於雅淡，若此篇者殊不多見，蓋有意於不求而出之。〕
考試官教授陸，批〔文字着實，見識超邁，非苟作者，亦鮮矣。〕
聖人之治世，惟有以裕乎民，因有以化乎民。蓋民富則善心生，善心生則於治亦易矣。君天下者，曷亦自其先者而圖之乎？昔孟子述意，蓋謂民可使之富也，亦可使之仁也。聖人有見於此，故其治天下也，必使易田疇，薄稅斂，庶可以厚
translation_en:
…nor could one embody it. And did Master Zisi also expound this [?] in such exhaustive detail? The understanding spoken of in the Doctrine of the Mean is the understanding of the utmost sage, not knowledge acquired through hearing and seeing. Might Zisi’s words also be the words of one who has attained the Way?
“When a sage governs All-under-Heaven, he ensures that beans and grain are as plentiful as water and fire. When beans and grain are as plentiful as water and fire, how could any of the people fail to be benevolent?”
Li Maoyuan
Associate Examiner Huang, Instructor, comments: 〔The explanation of the meaning of governing All-under-Heaven through the word ‘ensures’ is particularly sound. Moreover, the writer is not misled by the interpretation concerning ‘挫吝’ [?] and lack of benevolence. This is plainly someone with learning and discernment.〕
Associate Examiner Zheng, Instructor, comments: 〔Most candidates in the examination hall who wrote on this topic based their arguments on education and material provision.〕
Examiner Wang, School Director, comments: 〔Essays like this, which cast off florid embellishment and return to elegant simplicity, are decidedly uncommon. The writer evidently intends to achieve this effect without seeming to strive for it.〕
Examiner Lu, Professor, comments: 〔The writing is substantial, and the insight surpasses the ordinary. Writers who do not compose carelessly are indeed rare.〕
In governing the world, a sage first finds the means to bring prosperity to the people and thereby finds the means to transform them. For when the people are prosperous, good dispositions arise; when good dispositions arise, governing becomes easy. Why should those who rule All-under-Heaven not make their plans by beginning with what must come first? When Mengzi formerly expressed this idea, his meaning was that the people can be made prosperous and can also be made benevolent. The sage perceives this. Thus, in governing All-under-Heaven, he invariably ensures that the fields are well cultivated and taxes and levies are light, employing whatever means may enrich…

title: 正德八年河南鄉試錄
text:
民生者無不用也食以時用以禮凡可以教民
儉者無不至也藏富于民而菽粟之入隨用隨
有譬諸水火至足求者無弗與矣散財于下而
菽粟之積隨取隨足譬諸水火之多與者無或
惜矣夫如是吾知財用饒洽之餘既有以遂其
俯仰之願飽煖安逸之後又得以存其固有之
天禮義之心生而淳龐之風著會極歸極沛然
德化之大同也焉有偷薄而為不仁者乎廉耻
之俗振而雍熙之化成遵道遵路藹然德教之
===
洋溢也曾有放僻而為不仁者乎吁不患民心
之未仁而患民用之不足民用既足則民心自
仁而治道畢矣聖人之治天下孰有急於此者
邪雖然禮義生於富足固也後世乃有頭會箕
歛而為富國之計者殆亦弗思之甚歟夫君民
一體君苟富矣而民貧焉則刦奪之禍起而所
謂仁心者喪矣雖有粟吾得而食諸此孟子所
以拳拳欲人君先足乎民也有若告哀公亦曰
百姓足君孰與不足合而觀之益信
punctuated: 民生者，無不用也。食以時，用以禮，凡可以教民儉者，無不至也。藏富于民，而菽粟之入隨用隨有，譬諸水火至足，求者無弗與矣。散財于下，而菽粟之積隨取隨足，譬諸水火之多，與者無或惜矣。夫如是，吾知財用饒洽之餘，既有以遂其俯仰之願；飽煖安逸之後，又得以存其固有之天。禮義之心生，而淳龐之風著，會極歸極，沛然德化之大同也，焉有偷薄而為不仁者乎？廉耻之俗振，而雍熙之化成，遵道遵路，藹然德教之洋溢也，曾有放僻而為不仁者乎？吁！不患民心之未仁，而患民用之不足。民用既足，則民心自仁，而治道畢矣。聖人之治天下，孰有急於此者邪？雖然，禮義生於富足，固也。後世乃有頭會箕歛而為富國之計者，殆亦弗思之甚歟！夫君民一體，君苟富矣，而民貧焉，則刦奪之禍起，而所謂仁心者喪矣。雖有粟，吾得而食諸？此孟子所以拳拳欲人君先足乎民也。有若告哀公亦曰：「百姓足，君孰與不足？」合而觀之，益信。
translation_en:
…there is no means of enriching the people's livelihood that he does not employ. Eating at the proper times and using resources in accordance with ritual propriety, he leaves nothing undone that might teach the people frugality. He lodges wealth among the people, so that supplies of beans and grain are available whenever needed, as plentiful as water and fire: none who asks is refused. He distributes wealth among those below, so that stores of beans and grain remain sufficient however much is taken, as abundant as water and fire: those who give have no cause to begrudge it. When things are thus, I know that abundant resources enable the people to fulfill their wish to support their parents above and their dependants below; once well fed, warmly clothed, secure, and at ease, they can also preserve their inherent Heaven-endowed nature. Minds attentive to ritual propriety and righteousness arise, and a sincere and generous spirit becomes manifest. All converge upon and return to the supreme standard, achieving a great concord through the full flow of moral transformation. How could anyone become mean and shallow and act without benevolence? The practice of integrity and a sense of shame flourish, and harmonious, prosperous government is achieved. All follow the Way and its paths, while moral instruction spreads everywhere in abundance. Could anyone indulge in perversity and act without benevolence?

Ah! The concern is not that the people's hearts are not yet benevolent, but that their means of subsistence are insufficient. Once their means are sufficient, their hearts will naturally become benevolent, and the way of government will be fully realized. In the sage's government of the world, what could be more urgent than this? Nevertheless, although ritual propriety and righteousness indeed arise from material sufficiency, in later ages there have been those who devised plans to enrich the state by levying taxes by the head and gathering wealth by the basketful. Surely this shows an extreme failure to reflect! Ruler and people form one body. If the ruler is rich while the people are poor, the calamity of plunder and robbery will arise, and what we call the benevolent heart will be lost. Though I have grain, will I be able to eat it? This is why Mengzi so earnestly wished rulers first to ensure that the people had enough. You Ruo likewise told Duke Ai: “If the common people have enough, how could their ruler alone lack enough?” Considered together, these statements inspire still greater conviction.

title: 正德八年河南鄉試錄
text:
易
王假有家交相愛也
吳瀚
同考試官教諭楊　批〔題本不難作而塲中士子於假家處竟不能化本義一語有併勿恤吉而入講者至交相愛處不免語意滯複今人厭觀此作不然是宜錄出〕
同考試官學正鄧　批〔文詞整潔可喜〕
考試官學正王　批〔結有力非苟作者〕
考試官教授陸　批〔易義合作〕
===
象傳舉王者納后之辭而著其兩相與之情也
夫家人相與貴乎內外有同德也九五有家而
得其人焉其情之相愛也可知昔夫子小象釋
家人九五爻義謂夫九五剛健中正男之正位
乎外者也下應六二之柔順中正女之正位乎
內者也以是相求則是王者及嬪婉之辰而天
作之合中饋獲歸於所主后妃有窈窕之淑而
文定厥祥君子獲諧其所配陰禮聿脩無非無
儀閨壼于焉而肅穆矣毋訓不忘必敬必戒邦
punctuated:
易

王假有家，交相愛也。

吳瀚

同考試官教諭楊　批〔題本不難作，而塲中士子於假家處竟不能化本義一語，有併勿恤吉而入講者。至交相愛處，不免語意滯複，今人厭觀。此作不然，是宜錄出。〕
同考試官學正鄧　批〔文詞整潔可喜。〕
考試官學正王　批〔結有力，非苟作者。〕
考試官教授陸　批〔易義合作。〕

象傳舉王者納后之辭，而著其兩相與之情也。夫家人相與，貴乎內外有同德也。九五有家，而得其人焉，其情之相愛也可知。昔夫子小象釋家人九五爻義，謂夫九五剛健中正，男之正位乎外者也；下應六二之柔順中正，女之正位乎內者也。以是相求，則是王者及嬪婉之辰，而天作之合，中饋獲歸於所主；后妃有窈窕之淑，而文定厥祥，君子獲諧其所配。陰禮聿脩，無非無儀，閨壼于焉而肅穆矣。毋訓不忘，必敬必戒，邦
translation_en:
Book of Changes

“The king attains a household: they love one another.”

Wu Han

Associate Examiner Yang, Instructor, comments: “The topic is not inherently difficult to write on. Yet candidates in the examination hall proved unable, in treating ‘attains a household,’ to recast even a phrase from the Original Meaning commentary. Some even brought ‘Do not worry; auspicious’ into their exposition. When they reached ‘love one another,’ their language and ideas inevitably became labored and repetitive, wearying readers [?]. This composition is different and deserves inclusion.”
Associate Examiner Deng, School Instructor, comments: “The diction is orderly and polished—a pleasure to read.”
Examiner Wang, School Instructor, comments: “The conclusion has force; this is no careless composition.”
Examiner Lu, Professor, comments: “A well-executed essay on the meaning of the Changes.”

The Commentary on the Images cites the words concerning a king’s taking a queen, making manifest the affection with which the two associate. In the relations between members of a household, what matters is that those within and those without possess the same virtue. The nine in the fifth place establishes a household and obtains the right person; their mutual affection can thus be understood. Formerly, the Master, in the Lesser Images, explained the meaning of the nine in the fifth place of the Family hexagram: the nine in the fifth place is firm and vigorous, central and correct—the man occupying his proper position outside. Below, it corresponds to the six in the second place, yielding and compliant, central and correct—the woman occupying her proper position inside. When they seek each other on this basis, the king reaches the time of taking a gracious bride [?], and theirs is a match made by Heaven: responsibility for the household’s food finds its proper mistress. The queen possesses the goodness of a modest, retiring woman; ceremonial gifts establish the auspicious marriage, and the gentleman finds harmony with his mate. The rites pertaining to women are duly observed; there is neither wrongdoing nor ostentatious conduct, and the inner chambers thereby become solemn and peaceful. Not forgetting her mother’s instruction [?], she must be reverent and must be watchful; the state…

title: 正德八年河南鄉試錄
text:
家可期於順成矣周公之意如此蓋以夫能正
室由內之和婦克宜家乃德之化令九五之家
內外皆得其人吾知一剛一柔以德合德心孚
意契而險詖私謁之不形一健一順以賢配賢
氣同情協而儆戒相成之有道內助之懿夫實
愛之固非昵於慾也此唱彼隨琴瑟鍾鼓曾是
以爲樂乎刑家之化婦寔愛焉亦不失其正也
彼感此應觿燧箴管其足以爲好乎於乎五之
於二相求之理既正而相與之情自篤占者有
===
其德則勿用憂恤而吉也信可必矣抑聞之傳
曰夫婦人倫之始上以事宗廟下以繼後世也
匹夫匹婦人必懷有家一或不能以德相愛鮮不
顛殞厥類而況於有國與天下者乎王者之道
始於家而閨門之化達之天下天下治忽於此
乎繫聖人序易配咸恒於乾坤而家人之卦又
拳拳焉姬氏八百年之長曆文王太姒關雎之
德實啓之所謂正始之道王化之基有天下者
施于家之首政信矣
punctuated:
家可期於順成矣。周公之意如此。蓋以夫能正室，由內之和；婦克宜家，乃德之化。令九五之家，內外皆得其人，吾知一剛一柔，以德合德，心孚意契，而險詖私謁之不形；一健一順，以賢配賢，氣同情協，而儆戒相成之有道。內助之懿，夫實愛之，固非昵於慾也。此唱彼隨，琴瑟鍾鼓，曾是以爲樂乎？刑家之化，婦寔愛焉，亦不失其正也。彼感此應，觿燧箴管，其足以爲好乎？於乎！五之於二，相求之理既正，而相與之情自篤。占者有其德，則勿用憂恤而吉也，信可必矣。

抑聞之，傳曰：「夫婦，人倫之始，上以事宗廟，下以繼後世也。」匹夫匹婦，人必懷有家，一或不能以德相愛，鮮不顛殞厥類，而況於有國與天下者乎？王者之道，始於家，而閨門之化達之天下，天下治忽於此乎繫。聖人序易，配咸恒於乾坤，而家人之卦又拳拳焉。姬氏八百年之長曆，文王、太姒《關雎》之德實啓之。所謂正始之道，王化之基，有天下者施于家之首政，信矣。
translation_en:
…the state and household may be expected to attain harmonious order. Such was the Duke of Zhou’s meaning. A husband’s ability to set his household right depends on harmony within; a wife’s ability to bring harmony to the family is the transforming effect of virtue. Now [?], in the household represented by the nine in the fifth place, the proper persons occupy both the inner and outer spheres. I know that the firm and the yielding unite virtue with virtue: their hearts trust one another and their intentions accord, leaving no room for devious partiality or private solicitations. The strong and the compliant match worthiness with worthiness: their spirits agree and their affections harmonize, providing a way for each to perfect the other through admonition and warning. The husband truly loves the excellence of his wife’s assistance within the household; this is certainly no indulgence in desire. When one leads and the other follows, can their joy really consist merely in zithers, bells, and drums? The wife truly loves the transforming influence of her husband’s example in the household, and her love likewise remains correct. When one moves the other and the other responds, can knot-looseners, fire-making implements, needles, and cases suffice to constitute their affection? Ah! In the relation between the fifth and second places, the principle governing their seeking one another is correct, and so their affection in their life together is naturally profound. If the person consulting the oracle possesses this virtue, then there is no need for worry, and there will be good fortune. This can indeed be counted upon.

Furthermore, I have heard it said in the Commentary: “Husband and wife constitute the beginning of human relationships: above, they serve the ancestral temple; below, they continue the line for later generations.” Every ordinary man and woman cherishes the wish to establish a family. If either fails to love the other through virtue, rarely do they avoid bringing their own kind to ruin. How much more is this true of those who possess a state or all under Heaven! The Way of the king begins in the family, and the transforming influence of the inner chambers extends throughout the realm. Whether all under Heaven is well governed or neglected depends upon this. In arranging the Changes, the sage paired Influence (Xian) and Constancy (Heng) with the Creative (Qian) and the Receptive (Kun), and in the hexagram the Family (Jiaren) he again dwelt earnestly on this matter. The long, eight-hundred-year rule of the Ji house was truly inaugurated by the virtue of King Wen and Tai Si celebrated in “The Ospreys” (Guanju). What is called the way of rectifying the beginning, the foundation of kingly transformation, is indeed the foremost measure that the possessor of all under Heaven must apply to his own household.

title: 正德八年河南鄉試錄
text:
謙也者致恭以存其位者也
卓寵
同考試官教諭楊　批〔塲中作者於謙與致恭處類無異詞其異之者又遠于章旨獨此篇體貼得出說存位尤分曉故　錄之〕
同考試官學正鄧　批〔氣充詞贍而不失潔凈精微之旨作手作手〕
考試官學正王　批〔謙之爲德發揮盡矣〕
考試官教授陸　批〔明暢可錄〕
===
大傳論君子能不居其有乃所以保其有也蓋
有而不居人之所難能也君子之行如是其得
有終而吉也固宜昔大傳聖人釋謙九三爻義
至此謂夫儆凶德也而人不可有謙美行也而
人不可無彼九三君子有勞不伐而有功不德
處心於厚而以功下人內之所積德則欲其盛
而充實之如山外之所施禮則欲其恭而卑下
之如地是謙也者非致恭以存其位之道邪何
則九三君子上下所歸使有功勞而自伐自德
punctuated:
謙也者，致恭以存其位者也。
卓寵
同考試官教諭楊批〔塲中作者於謙與致恭處類無異詞，其異之者又遠于章旨。獨此篇體貼得出，說存位尤分曉，故錄之。〕
同考試官學正鄧批〔氣充詞贍，而不失潔凈精微之旨。作手！作手！〕
考試官學正王批〔謙之爲德，發揮盡矣。〕
考試官教授陸批〔明暢可錄。〕

大傳論君子能不居其有，乃所以保其有也。蓋有而不居，人之所難能也。君子之行如是，其得有終而吉也，固宜。昔大傳聖人釋謙九三爻義，至此謂夫儆，凶德也，而人不可有；謙，美行也，而人不可無。彼九三君子，有勞不伐，而有功不德，處心於厚，而以功下人。內之所積，德則欲其盛，而充實之如山；外之所施，禮則欲其恭，而卑下之如地。是謙也者，非致恭以存其位之道邪？何則？九三君子，上下所歸，使有功勞而自伐自德，
translation_en:
“Humility is the means by which one carries reverence to the utmost and thereby preserves one’s position.”
Zhuo Chong
Associate Examiner Yang, Instructor, comments: 〔The candidates in this examination mostly say the same things about humility and carrying reverence to the utmost; those who differ stray far from the passage’s meaning. This essay alone grasps and brings out its meaning, and its explanation of preserving one’s position is particularly clear. I have therefore selected it for inclusion.〕
Associate Examiner Deng, Director of Studies, comments: 〔Its force is full and its language rich, yet it retains the import of purity and subtle precision. A master writer! A master writer!〕
Examiner Wang, Director of Studies, comments: 〔The virtue of humility is expounded to the full.〕
Examiner Lu, Professor, comments: 〔Clear and fluent; worthy of inclusion.〕

The Great Commentary explains that a gentleman’s ability not to claim credit for what he possesses is precisely how he preserves it. To possess something without claiming credit for it is difficult for people to accomplish. When a gentleman conducts himself in this way, it is surely fitting that he should bring matters to completion and attain good fortune. In the Great Commentary, when the sage explained the meaning of the third, yang line of the hexagram Humility, he came to this point: vigilance [?] is a pernicious quality that people must not possess; humility is an admirable practice that people must not lack. The gentleman represented by this third, yang line has labored but does not boast, and has achieved merit but does not take credit. He grounds his intentions in generosity and, despite his achievements, places himself below others. In what he accumulates within, he seeks abundance of virtue, making it full and substantial like a mountain. In the ritual propriety he practices outwardly, he seeks reverence, making himself lowly like the earth. Is not such humility the way to carry reverence to the utmost and thereby preserve one’s position? Why is this so? The gentleman of the third, yang line is the one to whom those above and below turn. If, having achieved merit through his labors, he were to boast and take credit for himself…

title: 正德八年河南鄉試錄
text:
必不可以持滿故謙而致恭不忘乎下人之心
焉於德禮而不盛不恭必將至於招損故致恭
乎謙常謹乎卑牧之志焉其事上也坎之自牖
睽之于巷事不敢以直遂上其不信任之乎其
臨下也屯之下賤大有之尚賢行不敢以驕傲
下豈不悅服之乎吾知其位雖極於富而
不溢可以常守其富有朋龜之益而無鼫鼠之
厲矣吾見其位雖處於貴也高而不危可以常
保其貴有朱紱之慶而無鞶帶之褫矣噫此君
===
子之謙而位之所以存也有終而吉之道爲何
如哉雖然謙者君子之常行豈爲欲存其位而
爲之而言存其位者程子謂能致恭所以能存
其位謙之道其效固如是耳學非爲祿也而祿
在其中善非爲名也而名由此立脩天爵而人
爵至矣君子何心焉而或者乃欲持祿養資柔
筋曲體甘骸骫以求容悅託名於謙以爲固位
之術非九三之罪人歟
書
punctuated:
必不可以持滿，故謙而致恭，不忘乎下人之心焉。於德禮而不盛不恭，必將至於招損，故致恭乎謙，常謹乎卑牧之志焉。其事上也，坎之自牖、睽之于巷，事不敢以直遂，上其不信任之乎？其臨下也，屯之下賤、大有之尚賢，行不敢以驕傲，下豈不悅服之乎？吾知其位雖極於富而不溢，可以常守其富，有朋龜之益而無鼫鼠之厲矣。吾見其位雖處於貴也，高而不危，可以常保其貴，有朱紱之慶而無鞶帶之褫矣。噫！此君子之謙而位之所以存也。有終而吉之道爲何如哉？雖然，謙者君子之常行，豈爲欲存其位而爲之？而言存其位者，程子謂能致恭，所以能存其位，謙之道其效固如是耳。學非爲祿也，而祿在其中；善非爲名也，而名由此立；脩天爵而人爵至矣。君子何心焉？而或者乃欲持祿養資，柔筋曲體，甘骸骫以求容悅，託名於謙以爲固位之術，非九三之罪人歟？

書
translation_en:
…he surely could not preserve his fullness. Thus he is humble and shows reverence, never forgetting his resolve to place himself below others. If his virtue were not abundant and his ritual conduct not reverent, he would inevitably invite loss. Thus he expresses reverence through humility, always carefully maintaining his resolve to nurture himself through lowliness. In serving those above him, he follows the examples of entering “through the window” in Kan and meeting “in the lane” in Kui: he does not dare press straight ahead in conducting affairs. Would those above him not trust him? In governing those below him, he follows the examples of placing oneself below the lowly in Zhun and honoring the worthy in Dayou: he does not dare behave arrogantly. How could those below him fail to submit gladly? I know that, though his position brings him the utmost wealth, he does not overflow and can always preserve his riches: he enjoys the gain of valuable tortoise shells without the peril of the great rat. I see that, though his position is exalted, he stands high without danger and can always preserve his distinction: he enjoys the felicity of the vermilion knee-cover without suffering the stripping away of the great belt.

Ah! Such is the gentleman’s humility, and this is how his position is preserved. What, then, is the way to reach a fortunate conclusion? Yet humility is the gentleman’s constant practice. How could he practice it merely from a desire to preserve his position? As for the statement that he preserves his position, Master Cheng explains that his ability to show reverence is what enables him to preserve it. Such, indeed, is simply the effect of the way of humility. Learning is not undertaken for an official stipend, yet a stipend is found within it; goodness is not practiced for reputation, yet reputation is thereby established. Cultivate Heaven’s nobility, and human nobility will follow. What ulterior intention does the gentleman have? Yet some seek to retain their stipends and nurture their standing, making their sinews pliant and bending their bodies, willingly twisting their very bones [?] to win acceptance and favor. They claim the name of humility and use it as a technique for securing their positions. Are they not offenders against the teaching of the Nine in the Third Place?

Book of Documents

title: 正德八年河南鄉試錄
text:
欽厥止率乃祖攸行
李濂
同考試官訓導秦　批〔題本平易作者多率致于俭〕
〔德從事之說殊於本旨此作一本傳註且能體貼伊尹告君之意是用〕
〔錄之〕
同考試官教諭桑　批〔詞約理明不事雕琢如此篇〕
〔者亦少矣〕
考試官學正王　批〔發揮敬止法祖處甚明白佳作也〕
考試官教授陸　批〔伊尹告君之意合是如此〕
===
大臣告君以處事惟欲敬其度之本然遵其度
之已然也甚矣事必有度也人君處事可不于
吾心之本然與前人之已然者交致其力邪昔
伊尹作書以訓太甲至此意謂虞人之射且省
括于度矣人君處事豈無度可省乎是故吾心
所止足以綱維乎事物者即本然之度也不知
所以敬之則本不立矣要必方寸之中有嚴有
翼一肅恭而無縱弛虛靈之境亦臨亦保常收
斂而無放肆勿貳以二勿參以三使天理昭融
punctuated:
「欽厥止，率乃祖攸行。」
李濂
同考試官訓導秦批〔題本平易，作者多率致于俭〕〔德從事之說，殊於本旨。此作一本傳註，且能體貼伊尹告君之意，是用〕〔錄之。〕
同考試官教諭桑批〔詞約理明，不事雕琢，如此篇〕〔者亦少矣。〕
考試官學正王批〔發揮敬止法祖處甚明白，佳作也。〕
考試官教授陸批〔伊尹告君之意，合是如此。〕
大臣告君以處事，惟欲敬其度之本然，遵其度之已然也。甚矣，事必有度也！人君處事，可不于吾心之本然與前人之已然者交致其力邪？昔伊尹作書以訓太甲，至此意謂：虞人之射，且省括于度矣；人君處事，豈無度可省乎？是故吾心所止，足以綱維乎事物者，即本然之度也。不知所以敬之，則本不立矣。要必方寸之中，有嚴有翼，一肅恭而無縱弛；虛靈之境，亦臨亦保，常收斂而無放肆。勿貳以二，勿參以三，使天理昭融
translation_en:
“Reverently abide in your proper resting place, and follow what your ancestor practised.”
Li Lian 李濂
Associate Examiner Qin, Assistant Instructor, comments: “The topic is straightforward, but writers mostly turn it toward an explanation of acting with frugal virtue [?], departing from its original purport. This composition rests entirely on the received commentaries and also captures Yi Yin’s intention in admonishing his ruler. For these reasons it has been selected.”
Associate Examiner Sang, Instructor, comments: “Its language is concise and its reasoning clear, without striving for ornate embellishment. Compositions like this are rare.”
Examiner Wang, School Instructor, comments: “Its exposition of reverently abiding in the proper resting place and taking one’s ancestor as a model is extremely clear. This is an excellent composition.”
Examiner Lu, Professor, comments: “This is precisely how Yi Yin’s intention in admonishing his ruler should be understood.”
When a great minister instructs his ruler in handling affairs, he wishes only that the ruler revere the standard as it inherently is and follow that standard as it has already been embodied in practice. How essential it is that affairs have a standard! In handling affairs, can a ruler fail to exert himself both toward what is inherent in his own mind and toward what his predecessors have already put into practice? Formerly, Yi Yin composed a written admonition to instruct Tai Jia. At this point, his meaning was this: even a forester shooting an arrow checks its nock against a standard; when a ruler handles affairs, can there be no standard against which to check them?
Thus, the resting place of my mind, which suffices to order and uphold affairs and things, is precisely the inherent standard. If I do not know how to revere it, the foundation will not be established. Within the heart there must therefore be solemnity and vigilance, consistent reverence without laxity. Over the mind’s empty and numinous realm one must both stand watch and keep guard, constantly gathering oneself inward without giving way to licence. Do not divide it into two by entertaining a second concern, nor into three by entertaining a third; let Heaven’s principle shine forth in harmonious clarity…

title: 正德八年河南鄉試錄
text:
而不爲外誘之移無有作好無有作惡俾至善
渾全而不爲人欲之累所謂敬吾心之本然者
如此先王所行足以啓佑于後人者乃已然之
度也不知所以循之則厎不行矣又必仰惟時
若不愆不忘而舊章之率由篤于前烈是矜是
式而成憲之必監以義制事以禮制心乃祖之
家法具在勿作聰明以亂之懋敬厥德克配上
帝乃祖之令緒可嗣罔以側言而改之所謂遵
先王之已然者如此吁敬止以立本法祖以致
===
用處事之度不外是矣吾王能于是兩盡焉尚
何過舉之有哉抑考太甲自厎不類欲敗度縱
敗禮其於所謂本然之度與夫已然之度蓋胥
失之矣伊尹有見于此故已投以受病之藥而
又喻以處事之要忠愛之言不一而足老成之
告君類如此卒之克終允德而配天之澤上與
湯並謂非阿衡啓迪之力哉
是訓是行以近天子之光
田滋
punctuated:
而不爲外誘之移，無有作好，無有作惡，俾至善渾全，而不爲人欲之累。所謂敬吾心之本然者如此。先王所行，足以啓佑于後人者，乃已然之度也。不知所以循之，則厎不行矣。又必仰惟時若，不愆不忘，而舊章之率由；篤于前烈，是矜是式，而成憲之必監。以義制事，以禮制心，乃祖之家法具在，勿作聰明以亂之；懋敬厥德，克配上帝，乃祖之令緒可嗣，罔以側言而改之。所謂遵先王之已然者如此。吁！敬止以立本，法祖以致用，處事之度不外是矣。吾王能于是兩盡焉，尚何過舉之有哉？抑考太甲，自厎不類，欲敗度，縱敗禮，其於所謂本然之度與夫已然之度，蓋胥失之矣。伊尹有見于此，故已投以受病之藥，而又喻以處事之要。忠愛之言，不一而足，老成之告君類如此。卒之克終允德，而配天之澤，上與湯並，謂非阿衡啓迪之力哉？

是訓是行，以近天子之光。
田滋
translation_en:
…and keep it from being swayed by external temptations. Let there be no contrived likes or dislikes, so that the highest good remains whole and complete, unburdened by human desires. Such is what is meant by reverently preserving the original condition of one's own heart.

The deeds of the former kings that can enlighten and aid later generations constitute the standards already established in practice. If one does not know how to follow them, these will ultimately fail to be put into effect [?]. One must look up to them and follow them, neither transgressing nor forgetting, adhering to the old statutes; one must be devoted to the achievements of one's predecessors, esteeming and emulating them, and invariably taking established institutions as one's guide. Regulate affairs through righteousness and regulate the heart through ritual propriety: your ancestor's house rules are all there, so do not display your cleverness and thereby disrupt them. Earnestly revere virtue and become worthy of the Lord on High: your ancestor's splendid legacy can be continued, so do not alter it on account of crooked counsel. Such is what is meant by following the precedents established by the former kings.

Ah! Reverently abiding in the good establishes the foundation; emulating one's ancestors brings it into practical use. The standards for handling affairs extend no further than these. If our king can fully accomplish both, what mistaken action could there still be?

Yet consider Tai Jia: he brought himself to an unworthy condition; his desires ruined proper standards, and his indulgence ruined ritual propriety. He had lost both what we call the original standards inherent in the heart and those already established in practice. Yi Yin perceived this. Thus, having already administered medicine for the affliction, he further explained the essentials of handling affairs. His words of loyalty and love were by no means confined to a single admonition. Such is the counsel that seasoned elders give their rulers. In the end, Tai Jia succeeded in remaining truly virtuous to the last, and his beneficence, worthy of Heaven, rose to equal that of Tang. Could one say that this was not due to the enlightening guidance of the A Heng, Yi Yin?

Follow these teachings and put them into practice, thereby drawing near to the radiance of the Son of Heaven.
Tian Zi

title: 正德八年河南鄉試錄
text:
同考試官訓導秦　批〔恭傳言是訓是行可以近天〕
〔子道德之光華此作形容親切〕
同考試官教諭桑　批〔布置齊整而不腐不渺自是作家手段〕
考試官學正王　批〔文有典則氣出渾雄科塲中佳士也〕
考試官教授陸　批〔爾雅沉着無踰此篇〕
民不違乎君之教斯不遠乎君之德蓋敷言之
教所以納民於極也民既由之而不違則於君
德其庶幾乎昔箕子衍皇極之疇以告武王至
此若謂君以建極爲教民以好德爲心是以民
===
於極之敷言以諷以誦而佩服之不違宛然耳
提面命也以歌以詠而思念之不忘恍然口傳
心授也不徒知之必躬行之而俛焉以盡其力
既允蹈之必心得之而孰焉以復其性遵義遵
道遵路會其有極者異其人而同心蕩蕩平平
正直歸其有極者殊其途而一致然民之性皆
復于善如此則可以近天子道德之光矣吾知
人慾消而天理明道德同而風俗一日月照臨
之地孰不依餘光以自新雲漢昭回之天孰不
punctuated:
同考試官訓導秦，批〔恭傳言「是訓是行，可以近天子道德之光華」，此作形容親切。〕
同考試官教諭桑，批〔布置齊整，而不腐不渺，自是作家手段。〕
考試官學正王，批〔文有典則，氣出渾雄，科塲中佳士也。〕
考試官教授陸，批〔爾雅沉着，無踰此篇。〕
民不違乎君之教，斯不遠乎君之德。蓋敷言之教，所以納民於極也。民既由之而不違，則於君德其庶幾乎！昔箕子衍皇極之疇以告武王，至此若謂：君以建極爲教，民以好德爲心。是以民於極之敷言，以諷以誦，而佩服之不違，宛然耳提面命也；以歌以詠，而思念之不忘，恍然口傳心授也。不徒知之，必躬行之，而俛焉以盡其力；既允蹈之，必心得之，而孰焉以復其性。遵義遵道遵路，會其有極者，異其人而同心；蕩蕩平平正直，歸其有極者，殊其途而一致。然民之性皆復于善如此，則可以近天子道德之光矣。吾知人慾消而天理明，道德同而風俗一。日月照臨之地，孰不依餘光以自新？雲漢昭回之天，孰不
translation_en:
Associate Examiner Qin, Assistant Instructor, comments: 〔The commentary attributed to Kong [?] says, “Follow these instructions and put them into practice, and you may approach the brilliance of the Son of Heaven’s moral virtue.” This composition conveys the meaning vividly and aptly.〕
Associate Examiner Sang, Instructor, comments: 〔The arrangement is orderly, without being stale or vague: clearly the work of an accomplished writer.〕
Examiner Wang, Instructor, comments: 〔The writing follows classical standards, and its vigor is full and majestic. Here is an outstanding scholar among the examination candidates.〕
Examiner Lu, Professor, comments: 〔For refinement and composure, nothing surpasses this essay.〕
When the people do not depart from their ruler’s teaching, they are not far from his virtue. Teaching through proclaimed words serves to bring the people to the supreme standard. Once they follow it without deviation, surely they come close to the ruler’s virtue! Long ago, Jizi expounded the section on the August Standard to King Wu. At this point, he seems to be saying: the ruler teaches by establishing the supreme standard, while the people set their hearts on loving virtue. Thus, as for the proclaimed words concerning that standard, the people recite and rehearse them, embracing them without deviation, just as though the ruler were drawing them close by the ear and instructing them face to face. They sing and chant them, holding them in their thoughts without forgetting, as though receiving oral instruction and inward understanding directly from him. They do not merely understand them: they must put them into practice themselves, diligently exerting all their strength. Having faithfully followed them in practice, they must grasp them in their hearts, becoming thoroughly versed in them so as to restore their original nature. Following righteousness, following the Way, and following the proper path, those who gather at the supreme standard are different people united in purpose. Broad and level, upright and straight, the paths by which they return to the supreme standard differ, yet lead to one end. When the people’s natures have all thus returned to goodness, they can approach the light of the Son of Heaven’s moral virtue. I know that human desires will fade and Heaven’s principle will shine forth; moral virtue will be shared, and customs will become one. Throughout the lands illuminated by the sun and moon, who would not draw upon that light to renew themselves? Beneath the heavens where the River of Stars shines and turns, who would not …

title: 正德八年河南鄉試錄
text:
覽德輝以自耀秉彛之心人所同得君有之而
民化之位雖異而性則同矣天子道德之光華
不既相近矣乎降衷之理人所均禀上行之而
下效之分雖殊而理則一矣惟皇道德之光輝
夫豈相遠矣乎吁在上者脩道以立教在下者
率性以爲道此成周之民所以爲皇極之民也
歟抑考傳曰堯舜帥天下以仁而民從之桀紂
帥天下以暴而民從之其所令反其所好而民
不從是則民之從化于其所行而不于其所言
===
也歟言之感豈特言語之所致哉蓋皇極之君
躬行心得有以爲之地耳後世詔令蓋紛紛矣
詞非不美法非不密而民終不能感化者何益
於治故爲政不在多言
詩
衆維魚矣實維豐年旐維旟矣室家溱溱
同考試官教諭黃 批
李茂元
〔宣王承懺□流離之後所願者歲熟民滋耳此篇擬爲詩人語意如身親見者然可謂善□□□矣〕
punctuated:
覽德輝以自耀？秉彛之心，人所同得；君有之而民化之，位雖異而性則同矣。天子道德之光華，不既相近矣乎？降衷之理，人所均禀；上行之而下效之，分雖殊而理則一矣。惟皇道德之光輝，夫豈相遠矣乎？吁！在上者脩道以立教，在下者率性以爲道，此成周之民所以爲皇極之民也歟！抑考傳曰：「堯舜帥天下以仁，而民從之；桀紂帥天下以暴，而民從之。其所令反其所好，而民不從。」是則民之從化，于其所行而不于其所言也歟？言之感，豈特言語之所致哉？蓋皇極之君，躬行心得，有以爲之地耳。後世詔令蓋紛紛矣，詞非不美，法非不密，而民終不能感化者，何益於治？故爲政不在多言。

詩
衆維魚矣，實維豐年；旐維旟矣，室家溱溱。
同考試官教諭黃，批。
李茂元
〔宣王承懺□流離之後，所願者歲熟民滋耳。此篇擬爲詩人語意，如身親見者然，可謂善□□□矣。〕
translation_en:
…behold the radiance of virtue and thereby shine themselves? The heart that holds fast to constant moral principles is something all people possess alike. When the ruler possesses it, the people are transformed by him: though their positions differ, their nature is the same. Have they not thus drawn close to the brilliance of the Son of Heaven’s moral virtue? The principles Heaven bestows within us are received equally by all. Those above practice them, and those below emulate them: though their stations differ, the principles are one. How, then, could the radiance of the sovereign’s moral virtue be far from them? Ah! Those above cultivate the Way to establish instruction; those below follow their nature to realize the Way. Is this not why the people of Chengzhou became the people of the August Ultimate?

Moreover, consider what the Commentary says: “Yao and Shun led the realm with benevolence, and the people followed them. Jie and Zhou led the realm with violence, and the people followed them. When their commands contradicted what they themselves delighted in, the people did not obey.” Does this not mean that the people follow and are transformed by what their rulers do, rather than by what they say? How could the moving power of words arise solely from language? It is because the ruler who embodies the August Ultimate personally practices the Way and inwardly apprehends it that his words have a foundation. In later ages, edicts and commands have indeed proliferated. Their language is certainly fine, and their regulations certainly detailed; yet if the people ultimately remain unmoved and untransformed, what benefit is there to government? Thus governing does not depend on speaking much.

The Book of Odes

“The multitudes become fish: truly, a year of abundance. The tortoise-and-serpent banners become falcon banners: households multiply in profusion.”

Comment by Associate Examiner Huang, Instructor.

Li Maoyuan

〔King Xuan succeeded after a time of [?] and displacement; all he wished for was ripening crops and a growing population. This piece adopts the poet’s voice and meaning, as though its author had witnessed these things in person. It may be called skillful in [?].〕

title: 正德八年河南鄉試錄
text:
同考試官教諭鄒　批〔周人歆吉夢于王正如此識謂　考牧之詩故爲之頌傳非也作此以祛羣疑〕
考試官學正王　批〔意思悠遠而語致從容視它作特　異〕
考試官教授陸　批〔文從理順讀之令人灑然〕
即牧人夢兆之興占國家富庶之祥蓋既富且
庶有國家者所深願也牧人夢兆有祥而所占
乃爾詩人得不備述以獻于上哉是詩言牧事
有成而牛羊衆多至此意曰國家之興必有禎
===
祥吉夢之占必有徵應蓋人惟萬物之靈魚特
鱗介之類則夫人所生固不如魚所生之多也
牧人夢人爲魚是維以少變多之象其占也不
將爲豐年之穰穰乎殆見鐵鍾之餘豐稔疊至
陰陽以和風雨以時自天降康雲漢無旱魃之
灾也五穀以熟百物以充迄用康年癸柔無捋
采之憂也然夢兆之祥不特此耳在郊野則載
旐在州里則建旟則夫旐所統固不如旟所統
之衆也牧人夢旐爲旟是又以寡得衆之象其
punctuated:
同考試官教諭鄒批〔周人歆吉夢于王，正如此。識謂考牧之詩，故爲之頌，傳非也。作此以祛羣疑。〕
考試官學正王批〔意思悠遠，而語致從容，視它作特異。〕
考試官教授陸批〔文從理順，讀之令人灑然。〕
即牧人夢兆之興，占國家富庶之祥。蓋既富且庶，有國家者所深願也。牧人夢兆有祥，而所占乃爾，詩人得不備述以獻于上哉？是詩言牧事有成，而牛羊衆多至此。意曰：國家之興，必有禎祥；吉夢之占，必有徵應。蓋人惟萬物之靈，魚特鱗介之類，則夫人所生，固不如魚所生之多也。牧人夢人爲魚，是維以少變多之象，其占也，不將爲豐年之穰穰乎？殆見鐵鍾之餘，豐稔疊至，陰陽以和，風雨以時，自天降康，《雲漢》無旱魃之灾也。五穀以熟，百物以充，迄用康年，《癸柔》無捋采之憂也。然夢兆之祥，不特此耳。在郊野則載旐，在州里則建旟，則夫旐所統，固不如旟所統之衆也。牧人夢旐爲旟，是又以寡得衆之象，其
translation_en:
Associate Examiner Zou, Instructor, comments: 〔The people of Zhou delighted in auspicious dreams for their king in precisely this way. The statement that this is a poem about inspecting the herds, and that a eulogy was therefore composed for him, is erroneous in its interpretation [?]. This essay was written to dispel the various doubts.〕
Examiner Wang, School Instructor, comments: 〔The thought is far-reaching, and the expression unhurried. Compared with other compositions, this is exceptional.〕
Examiner Lu, Professor, comments: 〔The writing flows and the reasoning is coherent; reading it leaves one refreshed.〕
From the portents appearing in the herdsmen’s dreams, one divines auspicious signs of the realm’s wealth and populousness. For wealth together with a flourishing population is what those who rule a realm profoundly desire. The herdsmen’s dreams contain auspicious portents, and their interpretation is of this kind: how could the poet fail to recount them fully and present them to his sovereign? This poem tells how livestock husbandry has succeeded, with cattle and sheep becoming so numerous. Its meaning is this: when a realm rises to prosperity, there must be auspicious signs; the interpretation of a fortunate dream must find confirmation in events.
Human beings are the most spiritually endowed of all creatures, whereas fish belong merely to the scaly and shelled kinds. Yet human offspring are certainly less numerous than those of fish. When the herdsmen dream of people becoming fish, this is an image of the few becoming many. Would its interpretation not foretell the abundance of a bountiful year? One may envision, after the ‘iron bell’ [?], abundant harvests arriving one after another. Yin and yang are harmonious; wind and rain come in their proper seasons. Well-being descends from Heaven, and there is none of the calamity wrought by the drought demon in ‘The Milky Way’ (Yun han). The five grains ripen, all produce is plentiful, and a year of plenty is finally attained: there is none of the anxiety over stripping and gathering leaves in ‘Gui rou’ [?].
But the auspicious portents of these dreams are not confined to this. In the outlying countryside the tortoise-and-serpent banner is borne; in the townships and villages the falcon banner is raised. Those mustered under the former are certainly fewer than those mustered under the latter. When the herdsmen dream of tortoise-and-serpent banners becoming falcon banners, this is another image of gaining many from few. Its…

title: 正德八年河南鄉試錄
text:
占也不將爲室家之溱溱乎殆見流離之後生
聚日繁往者還之擾者定之究安宅而閭閻相
望鴻鴈無中澤之勞也危者安之散者復之達
四境而雞犬相聞黃鳥無此邦之嘆也是知年
豐則國用以足民衆則國本以固宣王牧事有
成而獻吉夢者如是中興氣象亦可以想見也
夫抑考厲王之時百姓背叛四夷交侵宗周之
業已板蕩矣宣王即位遇災而懼撥亂反正內
脩外攘天下喜於王化復行而頌禱之詩洋洋
===
盈耳矣何末年失政債千畝之師料太原之民
拒樊穆仲之諫而令終不保此牂羊之歌作而
無羊之迹熄矣可不畏哉
休矣皇考以保明其身
杜桐
同考試官教諭費　批〔成王始即政深懲管蔡之事恒以不能保明其身是惧故惓惓以是延訪羣臣學詩者多不能體認率〕
同考試官教諭鄒　批〔詩人思慕懇氣發渾觀切庶以浮詞長語敷衍其義殊較可厭及得是卷爲之喜見顏色〕
punctuated:
占也，不將爲室家之溱溱乎？殆見流離之後，生聚日繁，往者還之，擾者定之，究安宅而閭閻相望，鴻鴈無中澤之勞也；危者安之，散者復之，達四境而雞犬相聞，黃鳥無此邦之嘆也。是知年豐則國用以足，民衆則國本以固。宣王牧事有成，而獻吉夢者如是，中興氣象亦可以想見也夫！抑考厲王之時，百姓背叛，四夷交侵，宗周之業已板蕩矣。宣王即位，遇災而懼，撥亂反正，內脩外攘，天下喜於王化復行，而頌禱之詩洋洋盈耳矣。何末年失政，債千畝之師，料太原之民，拒樊穆仲之諫，而令終不保？此牂羊之歌作，而無羊之迹熄矣。可不畏哉！
休矣皇考，以保明其身。
杜桐
同考試官教諭費　批〔成王始即政，深懲管蔡之事，恒以不能保明其身是惧，故惓惓以是延訪羣臣。學詩者多不能體認，率〕
同考試官教諭鄒　批〔詩人思慕懇氣發渾觀切庶，以浮詞長語敷衍其義，殊較可厭。及得是卷，爲之喜見顏色〕
translation_en:
…Would its divination not portend households in abundance? Surely, after displacement and dispersal, the population would multiply daily. Those who had departed would be brought back, and those in turmoil settled. Everywhere people would dwell securely, with village homes within sight of one another; the wild geese would no longer toil in the marshes. Those in danger would be made safe, and those scattered would return. Throughout the realm, chickens and dogs would be heard from one settlement to the next; the yellow birds would no longer lament their sojourn in this land. Thus we know that abundant harvests provide sufficient resources for the state, while a numerous population secures its foundations. King Xuan achieved success in livestock husbandry, and such were the auspicious dreams presented to him. From these one can imagine the flourishing circumstances of his restoration!
Yet consider the time of King Li: the common people rebelled, peoples beyond the borders invaded from every direction, and the royal enterprise of Zhou had already fallen into disorder. When King Xuan ascended the throne, he met calamities with apprehension, quelled disorder and restored proper rule, cultivated government within, and repelled enemies without. All under Heaven rejoiced that the king’s transforming influence prevailed once more, and poems of praise and prayer filled the ears. Why, then, did he misgovern in his final years, suffer the defeat of his army at Qianmu [?], count the population of Taiyuan, reject Fan Muzhong’s remonstrance, and fail to preserve a good end to his reign? Thus the song of the ewe arose, and the achievements celebrated in “No Sheep” disappeared. Is this not cause for fear?
“Glorious was my august father; thereby may I preserve and illuminate my own person.”
Du Tong
Associate Examiner Fei, Instructor, comments: 〔When King Cheng first assumed government, he took the affair of Guan and Cai deeply to heart as a warning. Constantly fearing that he could not preserve and illuminate his own person, he earnestly consulted his assembled ministers on this matter. Most students of the Book of Odes fail to grasp this fully and generally…〕
Associate Examiner Zou, Instructor, comments: 〔The poet’s yearning and earnest feeling [the following wording is garbled: ?]; they elaborate its meaning with empty phrases and lengthy verbiage, which is particularly tiresome [?]. When I obtained this essay, however, delight showed on my face…〕

title: 正德八年河南鄉試錄
text:
〔幾可與説詩者〕
考試官學正王　批〔用本色語組織成章舉子中之親於〕
〔經學者〕
考試官教授陸　批〔寫出訪落之意〕
嗣王之延訪羣臣惟欲賴先王之休以自善而
已夫保明其身則嗣王之所以爲善者有其道
矣然非仰賴先王之遺休抑亦何由而致此乎
昔成王既朝武王之廟因作詩以道延訪羣臣
之意至此意謂我昭考武王之道仰之而不可
===
及就之而未能合然豈無以恤我乎哉蓋上下
於庭乃昭考燕翼之迹于此而思所以紹之庶
幾賴其休於上下之時臨之如在前也質之如
在旁也陟降於家乃昭考貽謀之地于此而思
所以嗣之庶幾藉其休於陟降之餘坐則見於
墻也食則見於羹也夫浅以家之多難國方罹
危殆之憂質之不聰又未免昏塞之患幸而昭
考遺休足爲顧藉是引是翼有以保吾身於不
危患生而能備害至而能防九重之尊即吾優
punctuated:
〔幾可與説詩者。〕
考試官學正王　批〔用本色語組織成章，舉子中之親於〕〔經學者。〕
考試官教授陸　批〔寫出訪落之意。〕

嗣王之延訪羣臣，惟欲賴先王之休以自善而已。夫保明其身，則嗣王之所以爲善者有其道矣。然非仰賴先王之遺休，抑亦何由而致此乎？昔成王既朝武王之廟，因作詩以道延訪羣臣之意。至此，意謂：「我昭考武王之道，仰之而不可及，就之而未能合，然豈無以恤我乎哉？蓋上下於庭，乃昭考燕翼之迹；于此而思所以紹之，庶幾賴其休於上下之時，臨之如在前也，質之如在旁也。陟降於家，乃昭考貽謀之地；于此而思所以嗣之，庶幾藉其休於陟降之餘，坐則見於墻也，食則見於羹也。夫浅以家之多難，國方罹危殆之憂；質之不聰，又未免昏塞之患。幸而昭考遺休足爲顧藉，是引是翼，有以保吾身於不危，患生而能備，害至而能防，九重之尊即吾優
translation_en:
〔…one with whom one might almost discuss the Odes.〕
Examiner Wang, Instructor, comments: 〔He composes his essay in natural, unaffected language: among examination candidates, he is one closely acquainted with〕〔classical learning.〕
Examiner Lu, Professor, comments: 〔He brings out the meaning of “Seeking Counsel” (Fang luo).〕

In seeking counsel from his assembled ministers, the succeeding king wished only to rely upon the blessings of the former king to perfect himself. Preserving and enlightening his own person, then, was the way by which the succeeding king could achieve goodness. Yet without relying upon the blessings bequeathed by the former king, how could he accomplish this?

After King Cheng had paid his respects at King Wu’s ancestral temple, he composed an ode to express his intention in seeking counsel from his assembled ministers. At this point, his meaning was: “The Way of my illustrious deceased father, King Wu—I look up to it but cannot reach it; I approach it but cannot yet conform to it. Yet could he have left nothing by which to care for me? As I move up and down in the court, here are the traces of my illustrious father’s provision for the security of his descendants. Here I ponder how to carry on his work, hoping to draw upon his blessings as I move about: I stand before him as though he were in front of me, and submit my conduct to his judgment as though he were beside me. As I ascend and descend within the house, here is the place where my illustrious father left plans for his descendants. Here I ponder how to succeed him, hoping to draw upon his blessings in the course of my movements: when seated, I see him upon the wall; when eating, I see him in my soup.

“Because of the many troubles of the royal house [?], the state now faces the fear of peril; and because my natural endowment lacks discernment, I am still subject to the affliction of benightedness. Fortunately, the blessings left by my illustrious father suffice to sustain me. They guide and assist me, enabling me to preserve my person from danger: when trouble arises, I can prepare for it; when harm approaches, I can guard against it. The exalted position within the ninefold palace gates is thus my place of ease…

title: 正德八年河南鄉試錄
text:
游之境矣莽蜂辛螫寧復自求矣乎是啓是迪
有以明吾身於不昧物來而先知事至而先覺
萬幾之務在吾洞察之中矣桃虫拚飛寧不自
戢矣乎噫先王之道遠矣即其事而求之則道
之在先王者在吾身也爾羣臣尚堪爲我一盼
焉大抵成王以幼冲踐祚乃能延訪羣臣如此
此其所以緝熈宥密而能安靖天下他日訓迪
百官既曰制治未亂保邦未危又曰亂爾有政
以佑乃辟亦知慎終如始而永保大命也已持
===
盈守成者當以成王爲法
春秋
諸侯遂救許〔僖公六年〕諸侯遂圍許〔僖公〕
二十有八年
張景
考試官學正王　批〔聖筆襃貶於一字之間此作闡揚微意既明且盡而下筆不苟不迫整於文體甚高非重是可以式矣〕
考試官教授陸　批〔春秋經世大旨重在夷夏君臣之間此題文救許圍許之事所以可善是篇筆力簡健而經旨甚明必探有得於孫徒者〕
punctuated:
游之境矣，莽蜂辛螫，寧復自求矣乎？是啓是迪，有以明吾身於不昧。物來而先知，事至而先覺，萬幾之務在吾洞察之中矣。桃虫拚飛，寧不自戢矣乎？噫！先王之道遠矣，即其事而求之，則道之在先王者在吾身也。爾羣臣尚堪爲我一盼焉。大抵成王以幼冲踐祚，乃能延訪羣臣如此，此其所以緝熈宥密而能安靖天下。他日訓迪百官，既曰「制治未亂，保邦未危」，又曰「亂爾有政，以佑乃辟」，亦知慎終如始而永保大命也已。持盈守成者，當以成王爲法。

春秋

諸侯遂救許〔僖公六年〕。諸侯遂圍許〔僖公〕二十有八年。

張景

考試官學正王　批〔聖筆襃貶於一字之間，此作闡揚微意，既明且盡，而下筆不苟不迫，整於文體甚高，非重是可以式矣。〕

考試官教授陸　批〔春秋經世大旨，重在夷夏君臣之間。此題文救許圍許之事，所以可善。是篇筆力簡健，而經旨甚明，必探有得於孫徒者。〕
translation_en:
…a realm in which I may move at ease. Would I again bring upon myself the painful sting of the great bee [?]? Such guidance and instruction can keep me enlightened and free from obscurity. Before things come, I shall know them; before affairs arise, I shall perceive them. The myriad affairs of government will lie within my clear understanding. Seeing the little bird take flight, would I not restrain myself? Ah! The Way of the former kings is distant indeed. Yet if I seek it through their deeds, the Way that resided in the former kings will reside in me. You, my assembled ministers, may yet cast a watchful eye on my behalf [?].

In general, King Cheng ascended the throne while still a child, yet was able to summon and consult his ministers in this manner. This was how he continued in luminous virtue, profound and tranquil, and brought peace to the world. Later, in instructing the various officials, he said both, “Establish order before disorder arises; safeguard the state before danger appears,” and, “Put your governmental duties in order, thereby assisting your sovereign.” He thus understood that, by being as cautious at the end as at the beginning, he could preserve the great Mandate forever. Those who maintain prosperity and preserve an inherited achievement should take King Cheng as their model.

Spring and Autumn Annals

“The feudal lords thereupon came to the rescue of Xu.” 〔Sixth year of Duke Xi〕 “The feudal lords thereupon besieged Xu.” 〔Duke Xi〕 Twenty-eighth year.

Zhang Jing

Comment by Examiner Wang, School Instructor: 〔The sage’s brush conveys praise and blame through a single character. This composition elucidates those subtle meanings both clearly and fully. Its writing is neither careless nor hurried; its literary form is orderly and of a very high standard. The final phrase is doubtful, but appears to commend it as a model [?].〕

Comment by Examiner Lu, Prefectural School Instructor: 〔The overarching purpose of the Spring and Autumn Annals in ordering the world places particular weight on the distinctions between the Yi peoples and the Xia, and between ruler and minister. This topic concerns the rescue and siege of Xu and the grounds on which these actions deserve approval [?]. This essay’s writing is concise and vigorous, and it makes the meaning of the Classic very clear. The author must have gained something through studying the followers of Sun [?].〕

title: 正德八年河南鄉試錄
text:
霸主急於恤患春秋深善之霸主明於討罪春
秋亦善之此齊桓之遂救許晉文之遂圍許皆
有得於大義之所當爲者何莫而非春秋之所
善也哉且伐鄭新城之役非許所專楚人欲救
而圍乃及許固將以撓我師也然當是時鄭尚
未服雖幾恤之也何嫌桓以爲救分之禮在所
當急爰得猾夏伊誰之咎況致圍者以吾收貳
之故乎吾寧舍鄭不可以負吾許于是遂解新
城之圍往爲許人之救水火之害惟恐其拯之
===
不早簡書之畏惟恐其爲之不力雖墮楚之詭
計不恤也是非勇於義者其能急人之急如此
桓之此舉安攘之功於是爲大春秋書曰遂救
許救固爲善其曰遂救者善之尤者也非深善
之而何若踐土河陽之地於許爲近天子再至
而朝獨無許固可謂慢其職也然當是時蹕巳
反旋雖姑置之也何傷文則以征討之法在所
當明臣敢慢君人得而討況出覲者又吾舉廢
之志乎吾欲尊周不可以追此許于是遂率于
punctuated:
霸主急於恤患，《春秋》深善之；霸主明於討罪，《春秋》亦善之。此齊桓之遂救許、晉文之遂圍許，皆有得於大義之所當爲者，何莫而非《春秋》之所善也哉？且伐鄭新城之役，非許所專；楚人欲救，而圍乃及許，固將以撓我師也。然當是時，鄭尚未服，雖幾恤之也，何嫌？桓以爲：「救分之禮，在所當急。爰得猾夏，伊誰之咎？況致圍者，以吾收貳之故乎？吾寧舍鄭，不可以負吾許。」于是遂解新城之圍，往爲許人之救。水火之害，惟恐其拯之不早；簡書之畏，惟恐其爲之不力。雖墮楚之詭計，不恤也。是非勇於義者，其能急人之急如此？桓之此舉，安攘之功于是爲大。《春秋》書曰：「遂救許。」救固爲善，其曰「遂救」者，善之尤者也。非深善之而何？

若踐土、河陽之地，於許爲近，天子再至，而朝獨無許，固可謂慢其職也。然當是時，蹕巳反旋，雖姑置之也，何傷？文則以：「征討之法，在所當明。臣敢慢君，人得而討。況出覲者，又吾舉廢之志乎？吾欲尊周，不可以追此許。」于是遂率于
translation_en:
When a hegemon hastens to relieve distress, the Spring and Autumn Annals deeply approves; when a hegemon clearly upholds the punishment of wrongdoing, the Annals likewise approves. Thus Duke Huan of Qi’s proceeding to rescue Xu and Duke Wen of Jin’s proceeding to besiege Xu both accorded with what the greater demands of righteousness required. How could either fail to win the approval of the Annals?

Now, the campaign against Zheng at Xincheng was not an undertaking for which Xu alone was responsible. The men of Chu wished to rescue Zheng, but their siege fell instead upon Xu: their intention was certainly to disrupt our army. At that time, however, Zheng had not yet submitted. What objection could there have been to giving some consideration to this [?]? Duke Huan reasoned: “The ritual obligation to give aid [?] demands urgent attention. How could they be allowed to wreak havoc upon the Xia states, and whose fault would that be [?]? Moreover, was it not because I sought to bring a wavering state to obedience that Xu came under siege? I would rather abandon Zheng than fail our ally Xu.” Thereupon he lifted the siege of Xincheng and went to rescue the people of Xu. Faced with suffering like that of fire and flood, he feared only that relief would come too late; mindful of the obligations conveyed in the written summons, he feared only that his efforts would be insufficient. Even if he fell into Chu’s cunning trap, he did not care. Could anyone who lacked courage in righteousness have responded to another’s emergency with such urgency? Through this action, Duke Huan’s achievement in securing the Chinese states and repelling outsiders became great. The Annals records: “They thereupon rescued Xu.” A rescue was certainly commendable; by saying “thereupon rescued,” it expressed particular approval. What could this be but deep approval?

As for Jiantu and Heyang, these places were close to Xu. The Son of Heaven came twice, yet Xu alone was absent from the court audience. This could certainly be called neglect of its duties. At that time, however, the imperial carriage had already returned. What harm would there have been in letting the matter rest for the moment? Duke Wen, however, reasoned: “The rules governing punitive expeditions must be clearly upheld. If a subject dares to slight his ruler, others are entitled to punish him. Moreover, the ruler’s coming forth to receive homage accords with my purpose of restoring neglected observances. I wish to honor Zhou; I cannot let this Xu pass [?].” Thereupon he led the forces at …

title: 正德八年河南鄉試錄
text:
溫之衆往爲許入之圍數其一不朝也而不臣
之罪以聲數其再不朝也而無君之惡以懲雖
非周之發禁不討也是非明於義者其能不後
其君如此文之此舉尊奬之名於是爲正春秋
書曰遂圍許圍不爲甚其曰遂者繼事之詞也
又非善之而何是則許之遂救也而夷夏之大
防以立其遂圍也而君臣之大分以明桓文之
霸此其所以爲可稱與雖然救許善矣臧黃敗
徐之坐視何不克終圍許可矣翟泉子虎之上
===
盟何不自考要之均未聞王者之道而不免假
之者也君子於二公取人之恕衛道之嚴又可
兩偏也哉
齊侯使國佐如師　及國佐盟于袁婁　成
公二年
鄭重
考試官學正王　批〔是作依經據傳筆下操縱老健說出晉人服敵待敵之失詳盡無遺非得春秋心法者不能篤之必有用之學〕
punctuated:
溫之衆，往爲許入之圍，數其一不朝也，而不臣之罪以聲；數其再不朝也，而無君之惡以懲。雖非周之發禁，不討也，是非明於義者，其能不後其君如此？文之此舉，尊奬之名於是爲正。《春秋》書曰：「遂圍許。」圍不爲甚，其曰「遂」者，繼事之詞也，又非善之而何？是則許之遂救也，而夷夏之大防以立；其遂圍也，而君臣之大分以明。桓文之霸，此其所以爲可稱與！雖然，救許善矣，臧黃敗徐之坐視，何不克終？圍許可矣，翟泉子虎之上盟，何不自考？要之，均未聞王者之道，而不免假之者也。君子於二公，取人之恕、衛道之嚴，又可兩偏也哉？
齊侯使國佐如師，及國佐盟于袁婁。成公二年。
鄭重
考試官學正王，批〔是作依經據傳，筆下操縱老健，說出晉人服敵待敵之失，詳盡無遺。非得春秋心法者不能篤之，必有用之學。〕
translation_en:
…the forces at Wen, and went to lay siege to Xu [?]. He enumerated its ruler’s first failure to attend court, proclaiming his crime of failing in a subject’s duty; he enumerated his second failure to attend court, punishing his wicked disregard for his sovereign. Although Zhou had issued no prohibition, he would not leave the offense unpunished. Could anyone without a clear understanding of righteousness have refused so firmly to put his sovereign second? Through this action, Duke Wen rightly earned a reputation for honoring and supporting the royal house. The Spring and Autumn Annals records: “He thereupon besieged Xu.” The siege was not excessive; “thereupon” is a word linking successive events. How could this, too, be anything but approval? Thus, by proceeding to rescue Xu, the great boundary between the Yi and the Xia was established; by proceeding to besiege Xu, the great distinction between ruler and subject was clarified. Was this not what made the hegemony of Dukes Huan and Wen worthy of praise?
Nevertheless, rescuing Xu was good, but why did Duke Huan fail to sustain his conduct to the end, standing idly by at the destruction of Huang [?] and the defeat of Xu? Besieging Xu was acceptable, but why did Duke Wen fail to examine himself when entering the covenant at Diquan above Zihu [?]? In essence, neither had learned the Way of the true king, and neither escaped merely borrowing its forms. In judging these two dukes, could the gentleman favor either generous recognition of others’ merits or strict defense of the Way to the exclusion of the other?
“The Marquis of Qi sent Guo Zuo to the army.” “A covenant was made with Guo Zuo at Yuanlou.” Second year of Duke Cheng.
Zheng Zhong
Comment by Examiner Wang, Instructor: 〔This composition rests on the Classic and draws its evidence from the commentaries. Its handling of the written argument is seasoned and vigorous. It explains the failings of the men of Jin in subduing and treating their enemy exhaustively, leaving nothing out. Only someone who has grasped the essential principles of the Spring and Autumn Annals could affirm these judgments with such conviction. This is surely learning that will prove useful.〕

title: 正德八年河南鄉試錄
text:
考試官教授陸　批〔不熟讀三傳恐不能作此〕
春秋紀霸臣於敵至而要信也原其無服人之
義責其無待人之禮此國佐之如師晉但能使
之求免而袁婁之及盟晉不能制之甘心也春
秋致意於是良有以哉嘅昔于鞌有戰齊師告
北侵車東巡晉忿未息於是齊有國佐之遣而
晉因爲袁婁之盟焉夫以齊之強而晉能致之
人固謂其與齊桓之致屈完者等爾不知服人
有義以力屈者非所謂服也齊之暴不如楚而
===
憒不可逞晉苟負擊強扶弱之心數其罪而不
加兵馬則所仗者正而齊固自服矣今者得國
佐之如師是果義以服人乎雪一笑之恥至於
殘民毒衆之慘不道之加爲暴已甚亦何以厭
其心哉但見賂持甗磬惟知求免雖曰如我師
也彼特懼吾之迫而勉強於一時焉耳在晉也
者豈知所以服齊若屈完之欵者哉夫國佐既
返而晉乃盟之人亦謂其與齊桓之盟召陵者
等爾不知待人有禮以盟要者非所謂待也國
punctuated:
考試官教授陸，批〔不熟讀三傳，恐不能作此。〕

春秋紀霸臣於敵至而要信也，原其無服人之義，責其無待人之禮。此國佐之如師，晉但能使之求免；而袁婁之及盟，晉不能制之甘心也。春秋致意於是，良有以哉！嘅昔于鞌有戰，齊師告北，侵車東巡，晉忿未息。於是齊有國佐之遣，而晉因爲袁婁之盟焉。夫以齊之強，而晉能致之，人固謂其與齊桓之致屈完者等爾。不知服人有義，以力屈者非所謂服也。齊之暴不如楚，而憒不可逞。晉苟負擊強扶弱之心，數其罪而不加兵馬，則所仗者正，而齊固自服矣。今者得國佐之如師，是果義以服人乎？雪一笑之恥，至於殘民毒衆之慘，不道之加，爲暴已甚，亦何以厭其心哉？但見賂持甗磬，惟知求免。雖曰如我師也，彼特懼吾之迫，而勉強於一時焉耳。在晉也者，豈知所以服齊若屈完之欵者哉？夫國佐既返，而晉乃盟之，人亦謂其與齊桓之盟召陵者等爾。不知待人有禮，以盟要者非所謂待也。國
translation_en:
Examiner Lu, Professor, comments: 〔Without a thorough reading of the Three Commentaries, one could hardly compose this.〕

In recording how a minister serving a hegemon exacted a pledge when the adversary arrived, the Spring and Autumn Annals probes his failure to bring others into submission through righteousness and censures his failure to treat others with ritual propriety. When Guo Zuo went to the army, Jin could only make him seek deliverance; when they covenanted at Yuanlou, Jin could not compel his willing assent. The Annals had good reason to draw attention to this!

Alas, in the former battle at An, Qi’s army suffered defeat. The invading chariots ranged eastward, yet Jin’s anger remained unappeased. Qi therefore dispatched Guo Zuo, and Jin thereupon concluded the covenant at Yuanlou. Since Jin could induce so powerful a state as Qi to send an envoy, people naturally considered this equal to Duke Huan of Qi’s bringing Qu Wan to him. They did not understand that bringing others into submission requires righteousness: bending them by force is not true submission. Qi’s violence did not equal Chu’s, yet its reckless folly could not be allowed free rein [?]. Had Jin harbored the intention of striking the strong and supporting the weak, enumerating Qi’s offenses without bringing troops and horses against it, its cause would have been upright, and Qi would naturally have submitted. Now that Jin had secured Guo Zuo’s coming to its army, had it truly brought another into submission through righteousness? To efface the humiliation of a single laugh, it went so far as cruelly to injure the people and afflict the multitude. Such an unrighteous assault was violence carried to excess: how could it win their heartfelt acceptance? We see only gifts brought—a yan cooking vessel and a chime stone—and a single-minded pursuit of deliverance. Although it was said that he “went to our army,” he merely feared our pressure and reluctantly yielded for the moment. How could those in Jin understand how to secure Qi’s submission with sincerity like Qu Wan’s?

After Guo Zuo had returned, Jin then made a covenant with him. People likewise considered this equal to Duke Huan of Qi’s covenant at Shaoling. They did not understand that treating others requires ritual propriety: coercing them through a covenant is not proper treatment. Guo…

title: 正德八年河南鄉試錄
text:
佐之服不如完而勢不可挾晉苟知招携懷貳
之德綏以誠而不敢遂焉則所示者大而齊固
自幸矣今者逮衷婁以與盟是果禮以下敵乎
恃一戰之捷至有質母東畝之命不衷之發爲
悖已甚亦何以免其倨哉卒之假使魯衛去而
復要雖曰聽于盟也彼蓋陋吾之識而勉強於
一與焉爾在晉也者豈知所以待齊若召陵之
盟者哉聖人以爲制敵莫如仗義天下莫大於
理而強有力不與焉故於國佐如師之下而反
===
以及盟在晉若曰晉之不義不能致其服而其
悖理徒以強其盟也一變文間而晉之曲於此
焉見春秋曲直之繩墨有如是夫雖然齊果無
罪乎房帷不謹而至於喪師失地幾見執獲固
先有以自取矣特郤克挾主盟之勢行其私憤
是以反爲國佐所折非齊之本直也噫晉有郤
克雖嘗敗齊也而已大至於損威齊有國佐雖
嘗見敗也而亦差能以伸氣此于蒲之盟晉不
免於收拾而雞澤以後齊率至於抗衡矣國
punctuated: 佐之服不如完，而勢不可挾。晉苟知招携懷貳之德，綏以誠而不敢遂焉，則所示者大，而齊固自幸矣。今者逮衷婁以與盟，是果禮以下敵乎？恃一戰之捷，至有質母東畝之命，不衷之發，爲悖已甚，亦何以免其倨哉？卒之假使魯衛，去而復要，雖曰聽于盟也，彼蓋陋吾之識，而勉強於一與焉爾。在晉也者，豈知所以待齊若召陵之盟者哉？聖人以爲制敵莫如仗義，天下莫大於理，而強有力不與焉。故於國佐如師之下，而反以及盟在晉，若曰晉之不義，不能致其服，而其悖理，徒以強其盟也。一變文間，而晉之曲於此焉見。《春秋》曲直之繩墨有如是夫！雖然，齊果無罪乎？房帷不謹，而至於喪師失地，幾見執獲，固先有以自取矣。特郤克挾主盟之勢，行其私憤，是以反爲國佐所折，非齊之本直也。噫！晉有郤克，雖嘗敗齊也，而已大至於損威；齊有國佐，雖嘗見敗也，而亦差能以伸氣。此于蒲之盟，晉不免於收拾，而雞澤以後，齊率至於抗衡矣。國
translation_en:
…Zuo's submission was unlike Qu Wan's, and superior force could not be used to coerce him. Had Jin understood the virtue of drawing back those who had become estranged and winning over those whose allegiance wavered, reassuring them with sincerity and not daring to pursue its demands to the utmost, it would have shown magnanimity, and Qi would certainly have considered itself fortunate. Yet now it went to Zhonglou [?] to enter into a covenant: was this truly treating an adversary with ritual courtesy and humility? Relying on victory in a single battle, it went so far as to demand that a mother be given as a hostage and that the field furrows run eastward. Such immoderate demands were utterly perverse. How could Jin escape the charge of arrogance? In the end, it employed envoys from Lu and Wei [?], who departed and then renewed the request. Although Qi was said to have consented to the covenant, it actually despised Jin's judgment and reluctantly agreed to participate on this one occasion. How could those in Jin have understood how to treat Qi as it had been treated at the covenant of Shaoling?

The Sage held that nothing surpasses righteousness in bringing an adversary under control, and that nothing under Heaven is greater than moral principle; sheer strength has no place in this. Thus, after recording that Guo Zuo went to the army, he instead made Jin the party responsible for entering into the covenant. It is as though he were saying that Jin's unrighteousness could not secure Qi's submission, and that its violation of principle merely forced Qi into a covenant. Through a single change in wording, Jin's being in the wrong becomes apparent. Such is the Spring and Autumn Annals' standard for judging right and wrong!

Nevertheless, was Qi truly without fault? Its lack of circumspection within the women's quarters led to the loss of its army and territory, and its ruler nearly being captured. It had certainly brought this upon itself in the first place. It was only because Xi Ke exploited his position as leader of the covenant to vent his personal resentment that he was, in turn, rebuffed by Guo Zuo. It was not that Qi had been in the right from the outset. Alas! With Xi Ke serving Jin, although Jin defeated Qi, it nevertheless suffered a serious loss of prestige. With Guo Zuo serving Qi, although Qi suffered defeat, it was still able to recover some of its spirit. Thus, at the covenant of Pu, Jin had to repair the situation, while after Jize, Qi generally came to stand against it as an equal. A state's…

記者引言人道莫大於樂以其為化民之本也

Comment by Associate Examiner Lin, Instructor: 〔The Record of Music frequently discusses how the Way of music transforms people. Yet no passage matches this one in directly revealing the wondrous process by which gentlemen and common people alike come under the transforming influence of the Way. This essay fully reveals how the transformative power of the sages' music resides in〕〔its sounds and movements, making this meaning vividly apparent. The compiler quotes a saying that, among the ways of guiding human beings, nothing surpasses music, because it is the foundation for transforming the people. Music's power to move and transform human beings is indeed profound. Could anyone claim that, among the ways of guiding the people, it should not be deemed paramount? Having discussed how music and dance embody the principles by which the people are transformed, the gentleman who composed the Record of Music quotes an ancient saying to conclude his discussion. His meaning is that the Way of music issues from the sages and moves all under Heaven: it is supremely great, and nothing surpasses it. How can this be seen? The people, in their lives, are not necessarily all of one mind. Unless there is something to unite their minds, their prevailing ways cannot be changed. Their feelings are not necessarily all alike. Unless there is something to bring their feelings into accord, their customs cannot be altered. title: 正德八年河南鄉試錄
text:
也者本諸復情和志之功而有窮本知變之妙
其作也極聲音之和而鐘皷管磬之相宜凡心
之所動莫不形見而無遺所謂天地之命者在
是極動靜之變而羽籥干戚之迭舞凡情之所
蘊莫不表暴而無餘所謂中和之紀者在是人
惟無聞於樂也一有聞焉則慾心自釋躁心自
平君子以之而好善非特使學之者不厭其道
而已矣人惟無聽於樂也一有聽焉則佚能思
初安能惟始小人以之而知過非特使教之者
===
不私其欲而已矣夫化於此或遺於彼非大也
君子化之而小人亦化之則心一情同有舉世
甄陶之氣象小補不足以並稱也感於彼或遺
於此非大也小人感之而君子亦感之則風移
俗易有同歸道化之規模小康不足以儷美也
謂之曰樂爲大焉不亦信哉抑又論之人道以
樂爲大固也然自節事天地之神辨君臣上下
長幼之位別男女父子兄弟之親昏姻䟽數之
交而言則有禮以爲大自夫婦別父子親君臣
punctuated:
也者，本諸復情和志之功，而有窮本知變之妙。其作也，極聲音之和，而鐘皷管磬之相宜，凡心之所動，莫不形見而無遺，所謂天地之命者在是；極動靜之變，而羽籥干戚之迭舞，凡情之所蘊，莫不表暴而無餘，所謂中和之紀者在是。人惟無聞於樂也，一有聞焉，則慾心自釋，躁心自平。君子以之而好善，非特使學之者不厭其道而已矣。人惟無聽於樂也，一有聽焉，則佚能思初，安能惟始。小人以之而知過，非特使教之者不私其欲而已矣。夫化於此，或遺於彼，非大也；君子化之，而小人亦化之，則心一情同，有舉世甄陶之氣象，小補不足以並稱也。感於彼，或遺於此，非大也；小人感之，而君子亦感之，則風移俗易，有同歸道化之規模，小康不足以儷美也。謂之曰樂爲大焉，不亦信哉？

抑又論之，人道以樂爲大，固也。然自節事天地之神，辨君臣上下長幼之位，別男女父子兄弟之親、昏姻䟽數之交而言，則有禮以爲大；自夫婦別、父子親、君臣
translation_en:
…is rooted in the work of restoring the feelings and harmonizing the will, and possesses the subtle power to fathom origins and comprehend change. When music is performed, it brings the harmony of sounds to its utmost, with bells, drums, pipes, and chime stones fitting together. Whatever stirs in the heart finds expression, with nothing left out: herein lies what is called the mandate of Heaven and Earth. It brings the variations of movement and stillness to their utmost, with alternating dances using feathers and flutes, shields and axes. Whatever the feelings hold within is fully displayed, with nothing remaining concealed: herein lies what is called the ordering principle of centrality and harmony. People need only hear music: once they hear it, their desires naturally dissolve and their agitation naturally subsides. Through it, the gentleman comes to love goodness; its effect is not merely to keep those who study it from tiring of its way. People need only listen to music: once they listen, even in ease they can reflect upon their beginnings, and even in security they can recall how things started. Through it, the common person comes to recognize his faults; its effect is not merely to keep those who teach it from indulging their private desires.

To transform those here while perhaps leaving out those there is not greatness. When gentlemen are transformed and common people are transformed as well, their hearts become united and their feelings accord. There is the prospect of molding the entire world: minor benefits cannot be mentioned in the same breath. To move those there while perhaps leaving out those here is not greatness. When common people are moved and gentlemen are moved as well, prevailing ways change and customs are renewed. There is a comprehensive order in which all alike come under the transforming influence of the Way: a state of modest peace cannot rival its excellence. Is it not indeed true, then, to say that music is great?

Let us consider this further. It is certainly true that music is of the greatest importance in the human way. Yet, viewed in terms of regulating service to the spirits of Heaven and Earth, distinguishing the stations of ruler and minister, superior and inferior, elder and younger, and differentiating the relationships between men and women, fathers and sons, and elder and younger brothers, as well as marriage ties and the infrequency or frequency of social intercourse, ritual is of the greatest importance. Viewed in terms of distinction between husband and wife, affection between father and son, and ruler and minister…

title: 正德八年河南鄉試錄
text:
者矣彼人於日用常行之間莫不有言焉言也
者物感於外情動於中本之氣以宣其藴者也
使言藏於心則無迹之可求固有傾耳而聽之
不可得而聞者矣惟宣之言也則因文以達其
志而清濁高下之有倫由辭以發其情而喜怒
哀樂之殊應故善言出則仁義之聲入於人不
善之言出則非僻之聲入於人未有有言而無
聲有聲而無聞者也言之有徵也蓋如此人於
應事接物之際亦莫不有行焉行也者有踐履
===
之方施爲之序本諸身以體夫事者也使言而
不行則無形之可驗固有正明目而視之不可
得而見者矣惟涉於行也則發乎邇而見乎遠
有卓然不易之規加於身而措於前有巍然不
動之象故行之而善則人莫不見其德之成行
之而弗善則人莫不見其過之成未有有行而
無成有成而無見者也行之有徵也又如此吁
言必有聲行必有成然則君子於言行可不謹
哉抑考此章上文有曰苟有車必見其軾苟有
punctuated: 者矣。彼人於日用常行之間，莫不有言焉。言也者，物感於外，情動於中，本之氣以宣其藴者也。使言藏於心，則無迹之可求，固有傾耳而聽之，不可得而聞者矣。惟宣之言也，則因文以達其志，而清濁高下之有倫；由辭以發其情，而喜怒哀樂之殊應。故善言出，則仁義之聲入於人；不善之言出，則非僻之聲入於人。未有有言而無聲，有聲而無聞者也。言之有徵也，蓋如此。人於應事接物之際，亦莫不有行焉。行也者，有踐履之方、施爲之序，本諸身以體夫事者也。使言而不行，則無形之可驗，固有正明目而視之，不可得而見者矣。惟涉於行也，則發乎邇而見乎遠，有卓然不易之規；加於身而措於前，有巍然不動之象。故行之而善，則人莫不見其德之成；行之而弗善，則人莫不見其過之成。未有有行而無成，有成而無見者也。行之有徵也，又如此。吁！言必有聲，行必有成，然則君子於言行可不謹哉？抑考此章上文有曰：「苟有車，必見其軾；苟有
translation_en:
…that cannot be prevented. In the course of everyday life and ordinary conduct, everyone speaks. Speech arises when things stir us from without and feelings move within; it draws upon vital energy to express what is held inside. If words remain hidden in the heart, there is no trace to seek: even if one inclines an ear to listen, nothing can be heard. Only when they are expressed in speech does one convey one’s intentions through patterned utterance, with an ordered arrangement of clear and thick, high and low tones, and express one’s feelings through words, with distinct responses of joy, anger, sorrow, and delight. Thus, when good words issue forth, the sound of benevolence and righteousness enters others’ ears; when bad words issue forth, the sound of wrongdoing and perversity enters their ears. There has never been speech without sound, or sound without its being heard. Such is the evidence that speech leaves.

Likewise, in responding to affairs and engaging with things, everyone acts. Action has its methods of practice and its sequence of execution; it is grounded in one’s own person and gives concrete embodiment to affairs. If one speaks but does not act, there is no visible form to examine: even if one directs one’s clear gaze toward it [?], nothing can be seen. Only when one proceeds to action does what begins nearby become manifest afar, presenting a distinctly established and unchanging standard; what one undertakes in person and sets forth before others presents a lofty and unwavering form. Thus, if one’s actions are good, everyone sees the resulting achievement of one’s virtue; if one’s actions are not good, everyone sees the resulting manifestation of one’s faults. There has never been action without a result, or a result without its being seen. Such, too, is the evidence that action leaves.
