聖人能使天下順治
李濂
同考試官訓導秦批〔論場正要於議論中看人〕見識。論理要得理趣，論事要得事情，反覆委曲，含蓄痛快，乃見胸次，乃見筆力。而近時士子科舉之作，承習學究一種活套文字，遇題不問出處，但字面有近似者，輒移其意以入其說，陳俗腐爛有所不計。主司以其說偶合而備選者多矣。古人以言觀人之法，將何所施？此弊何時而改邪？檢閱數日，食次忽得此論，為之三歎。其人胸次、筆力俱不凡，必是學有根據，且能為古文者。錄之，可以祛場中
translation_en:
…clothing, its wear must be visible.” These statements all mean that where a thing exists, its corresponding manifestations must exist. Once a carriage is actually set out, one cannot deceive others by claiming it has no crossbar; once clothing is actually worn, one cannot deceive others by claiming it shows no wear. How much more is this true of words and conduct! The gentleman knows that these cannot be concealed through deception. Thus, in speaking he chooses what is appropriate and says nothing that does not conform to proper standards; in acting he chooses what is appropriate and does nothing that does not accord with the Way. Here the Master introduces the point without fully developing his explanation, surely wishing learners to apprehend it in their hearts and grasp it for themselves. Otherwise, if their words fail to conform to proper standards and their conduct fails to accord with the Way, could they reflect at daybreak without feeling shame in their hearts?
Second Session
Discourse
“The Sage Can Bring All under Heaven into Obedience and Good Order”
Li Lian
Comment by Associate Examiner Qin, Assistant Instructor: 〔In the discourse session, the essential thing is to discern a candidate’s〕 understanding through his argument. In discussing principles, one must grasp their significance; in discussing affairs, one must grasp their actual circumstances. Only through exploring a subject repeatedly and in all its intricacies, with both reserve and forceful clarity, can one reveal the scope of one’s mind and the power of one’s writing. Yet candidates’ examination compositions nowadays perpetuate a kind of stock, adaptable wording used by pedantic scholars. On encountering a topic, they do not inquire into its source: whenever they find some superficial resemblance in the wording, they simply transfer the meaning of another passage into their argument, disregarding its staleness, vulgarity, and decay. There have been many whom the examiners included among their selections merely because their arguments happened to accord with their own. Where, then, can the ancient method of judging people through their words be applied? When will this abuse be corrected? After reviewing papers for several days, I unexpectedly came upon this discourse at mealtime and sighed three times in admiration. Both this man’s breadth of mind and his literary power are extraordinary. He must be someone whose learning has a firm foundation and who can also write ancient-style prose. Selecting it for inclusion can dispel from the examination hall…

title: 正德八年河南鄉試錄
text:
之隨習矣
同考試官教諭桑　批　〔因程子之言而發明周易艮止之義得其旨矣且立意高遠措詞老成而開闔起伏自有法度可取可嘉〕
考試官學正王　批　〔不古不今長江大河說去而意態層出無一字着人俗格允宜錄出〕
考試官教授陸　批　〔觀其論和其人使厥秉公司文柄亦當讓子出一頭地也〕
天下安聖人之所止者有理爲之據耳天
===
下無理外之物無事外之理萬物庶事必
有所止無所止則不得其所歸止必有所
據無所據則不得其所止聖人天下之所
歸也聖人之止將以歸天下者也天下於
我乎歸而不爲之所其止矣爲之
所矣爲我止矣而不爲之據其能爲我安
乎我之止有未得其所我之止之所有未
得所據欲止而安一身有未易者况天下
乎是有理焉理聖人之止之所也聖人之
punctuated:
之隨習矣。

同考試官教諭桑，批：〔因程子之言而發明周易艮止之義，得其旨矣。且立意高遠，措詞老成，而開闔起伏自有法度，可取可嘉。〕

考試官學正王，批：〔不古不今，長江大河說去，而意態層出，無一字着人俗格，允宜錄出。〕

考試官教授陸，批：〔觀其論，和其人，使厥秉公司文柄，亦當讓子出一頭地也。〕

天下安聖人之所止者，有理爲之據耳。天下無理外之物，無事外之理。萬物庶事必有所止，無所止則不得其所歸；止必有所據，無所據則不得其所止。聖人，天下之所歸也；聖人之止，將以歸天下者也。天下於我乎歸，而不爲之所，其止矣？爲之所矣，爲我止矣，而不爲之據，其能爲我安乎？我之止有未得其所，我之止之所有未得所據，欲止而安一身，有未易者，况天下乎？是有理焉。理，聖人之止之所也。聖人之
translation_en:
…the habit of following convention.

Associate Examiner Sang, Instructor, comments: 〔By drawing upon Master Cheng’s words to elucidate the meaning of stopping in the Gen hexagram of the Changes of Zhou, the author has grasped its essential purport. Moreover, his conception is lofty and far-reaching, his diction mature, and the opening and closing, rising and falling of his argument follow their own orderly method. It deserves selection and praise.〕

Examiner Wang, School Director, comments: 〔Neither ancient nor modern in manner, his exposition flows like the Yangzi or the Yellow River, with ideas and expressive turns emerging in succession. Not a single word falls into others’ commonplace patterns. It certainly deserves inclusion.〕

Examiner Lu, Professor, comments: 〔Reading his discourse, [one …] the man [?]. Whoever impartially wields the authority to judge literary compositions would likewise have to let this gentleman stand a head above the rest.〕

That all under Heaven find peace in the point at which the sage rests is simply because principle provides its foundation. Under Heaven there are no things outside principle, and no principle outside affairs. The myriad things and manifold affairs must each have a point at which to rest. Without such a point, they cannot find where they belong. Resting must have a foundation; without a foundation, one cannot attain the proper point of rest. The sage is the one to whom all under Heaven turn; the sage’s resting is intended to give all under Heaven somewhere to turn. If all under Heaven turn to me, yet I do not provide them a place, can they rest [?]? Even if I provide them a place and they rest with me [?], unless I establish a foundation for them, can they find peace with me? If my resting has not found its proper place, or if the place where I rest has not found its foundation, even wishing to rest and bring peace to my own person is no easy matter—how much more so for all under Heaven! Here there is principle. Principle is the place where the sage rests. The sage’s …

title: 正德八年河南鄉試錄
text:
止之所聖人之所據而與天下共之者也
天下事物莫不有理莫不各有其所理之
所在事物所當止之所也聖人於此以為
天下所與共之者也是故其所止也不敢
以私于其身而止之也亦非有强於人是
故聖人之止天下歸之而聖人止之天下
無不安之程子曰聖人能使天下順治其
理如此甚矣天下之生也物有萬焉事有
萬焉有萬其情喜怒哀樂發焉有萬其變
===
吉凶悔吝出焉尊卑異賾大小異行親疏
異分内外異制遠近異視衆獨異處重輕
異置今故異襲久暫異習同異異識孰者
為得孰者為失孰者為過孰為不及孰是
孰非孰美孰惡孰公孰私孰順孰逆紛紜
膠轕將迎滿目舉天下何等非物物接乎
我何等非事擾擾貿貿於何所歸聖人者
出治之何而歸之歸之未易若之何而止
之止之未易又若之何安之噫是亦有理
punctuated: 止之所，聖人之所據而與天下共之者也。天下事物莫不有理，莫不各有其所。理之所在，事物所當止之所也。聖人於此，以為天下所與共之者也。是故其所止也，不敢以私于其身，而止之也，亦非有强於人。是故聖人之止，天下歸之；而聖人止之，天下無不安之。程子曰：「聖人能使天下順治，其理如此。」甚矣，天下之生也！物有萬焉，事有萬焉，有萬其情，喜怒哀樂發焉；有萬其變，吉凶悔吝出焉。尊卑異賾，大小異行，親疏異分，内外異制，遠近異視，衆獨異處，重輕異置，今故異襲，久暫異習，同異異識。孰者為得？孰者為失？孰者為過？孰為不及？孰是孰非？孰美孰惡？孰公孰私？孰順孰逆？紛紜膠轕，將迎滿目。舉天下何等非物？物接乎我，何等非事？擾擾貿貿，於何所歸？聖人者出，治之，何而歸之？歸之未易，若之何而止之？止之未易，又若之何安之？噫！是亦有理
translation_en: …the place where he rests is what the sage relies upon and shares with all under Heaven. All affairs and things under Heaven possess principle, and each has its proper place. Where principle resides is the place where affairs and things ought to rest. The sage regards this as something to share with all under Heaven. Thus, in choosing where to rest, he dares not reserve it for his own private benefit; and in bringing others to rest there, he does not impose anything upon them. Hence, where the sage rests, all under Heaven turn to him; and when the sage brings them to rest, none under Heaven fails to find peace there. Master Cheng said: “The sage can bring all under Heaven into harmonious order; the principle is thus.” How vast is the unfolding of life under Heaven! Things are myriad, and affairs are myriad. Their feelings are myriad, giving rise to joy, anger, sorrow, and delight; their changes are myriad, giving rise to good fortune, misfortune, regret, and humiliation. The honored and the lowly differ in their complexities [?]; the great and the small differ in their conduct; the close and the distant differ in their allotted relationships; those within and without differ in their regulations; the far and the near are viewed differently; the multitude and the solitary are situated differently; the weighty and the slight are placed differently; the present and the past differ in what they inherit; the enduring and the temporary differ in their habitual practices; sameness and difference are discerned differently. Which counts as attaining what is proper? Which as losing it? Which as excess? Which as falling short? Which is right, and which wrong? Which is good, and which bad? Which is public-minded, and which selfish? Which accords, and which runs counter? Confused and entangled, things departing and arriving fill the eyes. Throughout all under Heaven, what is not a thing? When things come into contact with me, what is not an affair? Amid this restless bustle and bewilderment, where can one turn? The sage comes forth to govern them: how can he bring them to their proper destination? Bringing them there is not easy; how, then, can he bring them to rest? Bringing them to rest is not easy; how, then, can he bring them peace? Ah! Here too there is principle…

title: 正德八年河南鄉試錄
text:
馬爾矣理在天下在萬物在萬事理在聖
人在其身心天下事物有一物即有一物
理有一理即有一理事事物有萬理亦有
萬萬物備於聖人而聖人之心具乎萬理
聖人所治舉天下萬物庶事又何等而非
理之所在邪嗚呼此聖人所以為天下歸
聖人之止之所之所據所以共乎天下天
下事物所以各有當止之所而聖人止之
所以安其所而止也無尊卑無大小無親
===
踈無內外無遠近無衆獨無重輕無今故
無久暫無同異而能得之是審失之是察
謹抑其過勉其不及去非即是棄惡成美
革私從公遠逆依順隨所居之位而不違
乎當然之則嗚呼此固聖人所以公天下
之人而為止之之理也止之止止之得
其所也止得其所得其理也其理則其所
據之具也物得當然之則以為之據金之
於範泥之於鈞奔者之於衹休者之於喬
punctuated: 馬爾矣。理在天下，在萬物，在萬事；理在聖人，在其身心。天下事物，有一物即有一物理，有一理即有一理事。事物有萬，理亦有萬。萬物備於聖人，而聖人之心具乎萬理。聖人所治，舉天下萬物庶事，又何等而非理之所在邪？嗚呼！此聖人所以為天下歸。聖人之止之所之所據，所以共乎天下；天下事物所以各有當止之所，而聖人止之，所以安其所而止也。無尊卑，無大小，無親踈，無內外，無遠近，無衆獨，無重輕，無今故，無久暫，無同異，而能得之是審，失之是察，謹抑其過，勉其不及，去非即是，棄惡成美，革私從公，遠逆依順，隨所居之位而不違乎當然之則。嗚呼！此固聖人所以公天下之人而為止之之理也。止之止，止之得其所也。止得其所，得其理也。其理則其所據之具也。物得當然之則以為之據，金之於範，泥之於鈞，奔者之於衹，休者之於喬
translation_en: …that is all [?]. Principle resides in all under Heaven, in the myriad things, and in every affair; principle resides in the sage, in his person and mind. Among the things and affairs of the world, wherever there is a thing, there is that thing’s principle; wherever there is a principle, there is an affair corresponding to that principle. Things and affairs number in the myriad, and so do principles. The myriad things are complete within the sage, and the sage’s mind contains their myriad principles. Of all the myriad things and numerous affairs under Heaven that the sage governs, which is not a place where principle resides? Ah! This is why all under Heaven turn to the sage. The foundation of the place where the sage brings things to rest [?] is shared throughout the world. Thus each thing and affair under Heaven has its proper resting place, and the sage brings it to rest so that it settles securely in that place. Without distinction between honored and lowly, great and small, close and distant kin, inner and outer, near and far, the many and the solitary, weighty and slight, present and past, enduring and temporary, or same and different, he can scrutinize what is right and examine what is wrong, carefully restrain excess and encourage what falls short, remove error and embrace what is right, discard evil and bring goodness to fruition, reform selfishness and follow impartiality, distance himself from defiance and adhere to compliance. Whatever position he occupies, he does not depart from the standard of what ought to be. Ah! This indeed is how the sage treats the people of the world impartially, and it is the principle by which he brings them to rest. Bringing to rest means bringing to rest in the proper place [?]. To rest in the proper place is to attain its principle. That principle supplies the basis on which it rests. Things obtain the standard of what ought to be and take it as their foundation: metal in relation to a mold, clay in relation to a potter’s wheel, those running in relation to zhi [?], and those resting in relation to tall …

title: 正德八年河南鄉試錄
text:
木而有不止不安者乎是理也在書曰皇
極在詩曰物則在周易之艮則所謂背而
孔氏於大學直指爲至善者也昔者聖人
作易次艮於震而吾夫子傳之於止之而
止之理言之悉矣猶懼學者或有所未達
也於是授門人以大學之道其綱領三其
條目八二百五字之間泄露無餘其示虞
人之的而授匠氏之規矩乎聖人至善之
止不獨止乎其德之明將民之新也物格
===
知至意誠心正而身之脩固將家之齊國
之治而天下之平也易有之曰艮其背矣
曰艮其身矣艮其背其止以天下天下之
止聖人之止也艮其身其止一身而已聖
人弗取也聖人之止公乎天下如是是理
固聖人所與天下共之非可得私而所謂
明德者聖人與人同得於天不此有彼無
不彼豐此嗇者也特人不能無氣質物欲
之累而無以充其全體故天下之明德不
punctuated: 木，而有不止不安者乎？是理也，在《書》曰皇極，在《詩》曰物則，在《周易》之《艮》則所謂背，而孔氏於《大學》直指爲至善者也。昔者聖人作《易》，次《艮》於《震》，而吾夫子傳之，於止之而止之理言之悉矣。猶懼學者或有所未達也，於是授門人以《大學》之道。其綱領三，其條目八，二百五字之間，泄露無餘。其示虞人之的而授匠氏之規矩乎？聖人至善之止，不獨止乎其德之明，將民之新也。物格知至，意誠心正，而身之脩，固將家之齊、國之治而天下之平也。《易》有之，曰「艮其背」矣，曰「艮其身」矣。艮其背，其止以天下，天下之止，聖人之止也；艮其身，其止一身而已，聖人弗取也。聖人之止公乎天下如是。是理固聖人所與天下共之，非可得私。而所謂明德者，聖人與人同得於天，不此有彼無，不彼豐此嗇者也。特人不能無氣質物欲之累，而無以充其全體，故天下之明德不
translation_en:
…trees: could any fail to come to rest and find repose? This principle is called the August Ultimate in the Book of Documents and the norm of things in the Book of Odes. In Gen (Keeping Still) in the Changes of Zhou, it is what is meant by the “back”; in the Great Learning, Confucius directly identifies it as the highest good.

In ancient times, when the sage composed the Changes, he placed Gen after Zhen (Arousing). Our Master supplied its commentary, explaining exhaustively the principle of bringing things to rest and resting therein [?]. Still fearing that learners might not fully understand, he taught his disciples the Way of the Great Learning. Its guiding principles number three and its constituent steps eight. Within its 205 characters, everything is disclosed, with nothing left concealed. Is this not like showing a gamekeeper his target and giving a craftsman his compass and square?

The sage’s resting in the highest good does not end with making his own virtue luminous: he also intends to renew the people. When things have been investigated, knowledge fully attained, intentions made sincere, and the mind rectified, the cultivation of his person is assuredly directed toward ordering the family, governing the state, and bringing peace to all under Heaven. The Changes says, “Keeping his back still,” and also, “Keeping his body still.” In keeping his back still, he takes all under Heaven as the scope of his stillness: the resting of all under Heaven is the sage’s resting. In keeping his body still, his resting extends only to his own person; the sage does not choose this. Such is the way the sage’s resting encompasses all under Heaven impartially.

This principle is inherently something the sage shares with all under Heaven; it cannot be privately possessed. As for what is called luminous virtue, sages and other people alike receive it from Heaven. It is not present in one and absent in another, nor abundant in one and scant in another. Yet people cannot avoid the encumbrances of their material endowment and desires for things, and so cannot fully realize its entire substance. Thus the luminous virtue of all under Heaven cannot…

title: 正德八年河南鄉試錄
text:
能不賴于聖人以明而新民之責聖人不
得不以之自任雖然非人力私意有所付
畀增益之也人有之不及知知之不及行
而行之者不及至也聖人於是歸之于當
止之所而止之以當然之則立必俱立成
不獨成亦何事於強哉至善之止聖人無
分已所有於人之惠而人亦無受其所有
於聖人之謝止之各於其所而已矣止之
不於其所則無可止之理天下事物得其
===
所則安失其所則悖其安其悖一視乎理
而已矣愚故曰天下安聖人之所止者有
理爲之據耳止則治安則順矣此程子順
治之說所以爲易良止而發而有及乎孔
氏門人傳釋大學所引之言朱子深有契
焉二書之註交明互舉曲暢旁通伊川示
我無欲無思之境紫陽勉我必至不遷之
地當止之所於是爲極學者於是地而求
之可以立仁宅可以闢義路可以設禮門
punctuated: 能不賴于聖人以明，而新民之責，聖人不得不以之自任。雖然，非人力私意有所付畀增益之也。人有之不及知，知之不及行，而行之者不及至也。聖人於是歸之于當止之所，而止之以當然之則。立必俱立，成不獨成，亦何事於強哉？至善之止，聖人無分已所有於人之惠，而人亦無受其所有於聖人之謝，止之各於其所而已矣。止之不於其所，則無可止之理。天下事物得其所則安，失其所則悖。其安其悖，一視乎理而已矣。愚故曰：天下安聖人之所止者，有理爲之據耳。止則治，安則順矣。此程子順治之說所以爲《易》良止而發，而有及乎孔氏門人傳釋《大學》所引之言，朱子深有契焉。二書之註，交明互舉，曲暢旁通。伊川示我無欲無思之境，紫陽勉我必至不遷之地。當止之所，於是爲極。學者於是地而求之，可以立仁宅，可以闢義路，可以設禮門。
translation_en:
…cannot but depend on the sage to make it bright; and the sage cannot but take upon himself the responsibility of renewing the people. Nevertheless, this does not mean that human effort or private intention bestows anything upon them or adds to what they possess. People possess it but fail to know it; they know it but fail to put it into practice; and those who practise it fail to reach its fullest extent. The sage therefore brings them back to the place where they ought to rest and settles them there according to the norms of what is right. In establishing himself, he must establish others alongside him; in attaining fulfilment, he does not attain it alone. What need, then, is there for coercion? In resting in the highest good, the sage confers no favour by sharing with others something that belongs to himself, nor do people owe the sage thanks for receiving from him what they themselves already possess. It is simply a matter of each resting in the proper place. If one rests somewhere other than the proper place, there is no principle that warrants resting there. When the affairs and things of the world find their proper places, they are at ease; when they lose their proper places, they fall into disorder. Whether they are at ease or in disorder depends entirely upon principle.
Thus I humbly say: the reason the world finds repose where the sage rests is simply that principle provides the foundation. Resting there brings order; being at ease brings accord. This is why Master Cheng’s explanation of accord and order arose in connection with “good stopping” [?; apparently referring to the Gen hexagram’s teaching on resting] in the Book of Changes, and extended to the words quoted by Confucius’s disciples in their commentary explaining the Great Learning. Master Zhu understood this profoundly. His annotations to the two books illuminate one another and refer to each other, fully unfolding the subtleties and drawing out their wider connections. Yichuan [Cheng Yi] shows us the realm free of desire and deliberation; Ziyang [Zhu Xi] urges us toward the place we must reach and from which we must never depart. The place where one ought to rest thus becomes the ultimate standard. If students pursue it in this realm, they can establish the dwelling of benevolence, open the road of righteousness, and set up the gate of ritual propriety…

title: 正德八年河南鄉試錄
text:
可以開智牖可以升孔子之堂而入其室
矣謹論
表
擬宋司馬光進稽古錄表〔元祐元年〕
車富
同考試官教諭楊　批〔司馬公進稽古錄表自有手筆〕
此篇擬之頗相類
同考試官學正鄧　批〔駢儷有則亦非不能為四六者〕

頗悉君父之志
